title: 4  Exercises: Hypothesis testing
text:
4.9 Certifying a low rate

Exercise 9. How many negatives with zero false positives do you need to claim FPR \(< 10^{-3}\) at 95% confidence? Check: 2,995. (Clopper–Pearson, rule of three)







TipSolution






The one-sided bound. “FPR below \(u\) at 95% confidence” is a one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound. Rerun the upper-end derivation of Section 4.11 with \(a/2\) replaced by \(0.05\): if \(u\) solves \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le k] = 0.05\), then \(\Pr[p \ge u(K)] \le 0.05\).
Zero counts. At \(k = 0\), \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le 0] = (1 - u)^n\), so \(u\) solves \((1 - u)^n = 0.05\).
The requirement. You need \(u \le 10^{-3}\). \((1 - u)^n\) is decreasing in \(u\), so this holds exactly when \((1 - 10^{-3})^n \le 0.05\).
Solve for \(n\). Take logs and divide by \(\ln(1 - 10^{-3}) < 0\), which flips the inequality: \[n \ge \frac{\ln 20}{-\ln(1 - 10^{-3})} = 2{,}994.2, \tag{4.9}\] so \(n = 2{,}995\).
Check both sides. \(0.999^{2994} = 0.05001 > 0.05\) but \(0.999^{2995} = 0.04996 \le 0.05\). The chapter’s two-sided Clopper–Pearson routine at 90% has the same upper end as the one-sided 95% bound. At \(k = 0\) it gives \(1.0001\times10^{-3}\) for \(n = 2{,}994\) and \(9.9974\times10^{-4}\) for \(n = 2{,}995\).

As a hypothesis test. Step 3 is a test of “FPR \(\ge 10^{-3}\)” against “FPR \(< 10^{-3}\)” that rejects the first when it sees no false positive. If the true FPR is at least \(10^{-3}\), it sees none with probability at most \(0.999^n\), its type I error. That is at most 0.05 from \(n = 2{,}995\) on. The rule of three, \(3/10^{-3} = 3{,}000\), is within five of it. If you report the two-sided 95% interval instead, its upper end uses \(0.025\), and you need \(\ln 40/(-\ln 0.999) = 3{,}687.0\), so 3,688 negatives.
Certifying a rate of \(10^{-3}\) needs about \(3/10^{-3}\) clean trials, and that only bounds the rate. Measuring it to within about 20% needs on the order of \(100/10^{-3} = 10^5\), over thirty times more.

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
text:
5.1 Entropy of a geometric variable
Exercises for Information theory, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_information_theory.py computes every number quoted here; run it from the repository root with uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_information_theory.py.

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
text:
Exercise 1. Entropy of a geometric variable. \(X\) takes value \(k \ge 1\) with probability \(2^{-k}\). Show that \(H(X) = 2\) bits, while \(H_\infty(X) = 1\). Hint: \(\sum_k k2^{-k} = 2\). (Entropy definition)







TipSolution






Surprisal of each outcome. \(p(k) = 2^{-k}\), so \(\log\frac{1}{p(k)} = k\) bits. The outcome \(k\) costs exactly \(k\) bits, as in the code \(1, 01, 001, \dots\)
Average it (definition of entropy): \[H(X) = \sum_{k \ge 1} p(k)\log\frac{1}{p(k)} = \sum_{k \ge 1} k\,2^{-k}. \tag{5.1}\]
Sum the series (the hint). Let \(S = \sum_{k \ge 1} k\,2^{-k}\). Then \(S/2 = \sum_{k \ge 1} k\,2^{-(k+1)} = \sum_{k \ge 2}(k - 1)2^{-k}\). Subtract term by term: \(S - S/2 = \sum_{k \ge 1} 2^{-k} = 1\), so \(S = 2\) and \(H(X) = 2\) bits.
Min-entropy. The most likely value is \(k = 1\), so \(V(X) = \max_k 2^{-k} = \frac12\) and \(H_\infty(X) = -\log\frac12 = 1\) bit.

The series converges fast. The partial sums up to \(k = 5\), \(10\) and \(20\) are 1.7812, 1.9883 and 2.0000. As predicted by \(H_\infty \le H\), the min-entropy is below the entropy. The bound \(H \le \log\lvert\mathcal X\rvert\) says nothing here, because \(X\) has infinitely many values.
A variable with infinitely many values can still have a small finite entropy, and its best single guess (here \(X = 1\)) succeeds half the time.

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
text:
5.2 Information from independent observations

Exercise 2. Information from independent observations. If \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are independent given \(X\), show that \(I(X; Y_1, Y_2) \le I(X; Y_1) + I(X; Y_2)\). Find an example where \(Y_1, Y_2\) are not conditionally independent and the inequality fails. Hint for the counterexample: \(X = Y_1 \oplus Y_2\) for independent fair bits. (Chain rule)







TipSolution





The inequality. Use the symmetric form \(I(X; Y_1, Y_2) = H(Y_1, Y_2) - H(Y_1, Y_2 \mid X)\).

The noise part splits. Apply Equation 5.9 conditioned on \(X\) throughout, as in the Fano derivation: \(H(Y_1, Y_2 \mid X) = H(Y_1 \mid X) + H(Y_2 \mid Y_1, X)\). Given \(X\), \(Y_2\) is independent of \(Y_1\), so the posterior of \(Y_2\) given \((Y_1, X)\) is its posterior given \(X\), and \(H(Y_2 \mid Y_1, X) = H(Y_2 \mid X)\). So \(H(Y_1, Y_2 \mid X) = H(Y_1 \mid X) + H(Y_2 \mid X)\).
The total part is subadditive. By the chain rule and “conditioning reduces entropy”, \(H(Y_1, Y_2) = H(Y_1) + H(Y_2 \mid Y_1) \le H(Y_1) + H(Y_2)\) (the second Check yourself question under Shannon entropy).
Subtract. Combining steps 1 and 2: \[I(X; Y_1, Y_2) \le \big[H(Y_1) - H(Y_1 \mid X)\big] + \big[H(Y_2) - H(Y_2 \mid X)\big] = I(X; Y_1) + I(X; Y_2). \tag{5.2}\]

Two observations that are independent given \(X\) can repeat each other’s information, but they cannot create information together that neither has alone. Take for example a fair bit \(X\) sent twice through a binary symmetric channel (BSC) with flip probability 0.1, with independent noise each time. Each copy carries \(I(X; Y_i) = 0.5310\) bits, and the pair carries \(I(X; Y_1, Y_2) = 0.7421 \le 1.0620\) bits.
The counterexample. Let \(Y_1, Y_2\) be independent fair bits and \(X = Y_1 \oplus Y_2\). All four pairs are equally likely:



Table 5.1: The exclusive-or counterexample: every row has probability 1/4.

One observation tells nothing. In Table 5.1, fix \(Y_1 = 0\). The two remaining rows have \(X = 0\) and \(X = 1\), equally likely. The same happens for \(Y_1 = 1\). So \(X\) is a fair bit whatever \(Y_1\) is, \(X\) and \(Y_1\) are independent, and \(I(X; Y_1) = 0\). By symmetry, \(I(X; Y_2) = 0\).
Both observations tell everything. Given \((Y_1, Y_2)\), \(X\) is determined, so \(H(X \mid Y_1, Y_2) = 0\) and \(I(X; Y_1, Y_2) = H(X) - 0 = 1\) bit.
The inequality fails: \(1 > 0 + 0\). The script confirms \(I(X; Y_1) = I(X; Y_2) = 0.0000\) and \(I(X; Y_1, Y_2) = 1.0000\).
Why the proof breaks. Given \(X = 0\), the pair is \((0, 0)\) or \((1, 1)\): \(Y_2 = Y_1\). So \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are fully dependent given \(X\), \(H(Y_1, Y_2 \mid X) = 1\), while \(H(Y_1 \mid X) + H(Y_2 \mid X) = 2\). Step 1 above fails.

Information about \(X\) can sit in the combination of features and in neither feature alone. This is why ranking features one at a time by information gain can miss useful pairs.

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
section: 5.3 Min-capacity bounds capacity for the binary symmetric channel
text:
5.3 Min-capacity bounds capacity for the binary symmetric channel

Exercise 3. Min-capacity bounds capacity for the binary symmetric channel. Show that \(1 - h(p) \le \log_2\big(2\max(p, 1 - p)\big)\) for every \(p\). Hint: \(H_\infty \le H\) applied to a \(\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\) variable. Check: at \(p = 0.25\), \(0.1887 \le 0.5850\). (Min-entropy vs Shannon)







TipSolution






Min-entropy of a coin. For \(B \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\), \(V(B) = \max(p, 1 - p)\), so \(H_\infty(B) = -\log\max(p, 1 - p)\).
Apply \(H_\infty \le H\) (Min-entropy and guessing): \(-\log\max(p, 1 - p) \le h(p)\).
Rearrange. Subtract both sides from 1: \(1 - h(p) \le 1 + \log\max(p, 1 - p) = \log_2 2 + \log_2\max(p, 1 - p) = \log_2\big(2\max(p, 1 - p)\big)\).
Read the two sides. The left side is the capacity Equation 5.17. The right side is Equation 5.22 for \(\mathrm{BSC}(p)\), whose two column maxima are both \(\max(p, 1 - p)\).
Check. At \(p = 0.25\): \(1 - h(0.25) = 0.1887\) and \(\log_2(2 \cdot 0.75) = \log_2 1.5 = 0.5850\). At \(p = 0.11\) the two are 0.5001 and 0.8319. On a grid of 1,001 values of \(p\), the smallest gap between the two sides is 0.0000.

Equality holds exactly when \(H_\infty(B) = H(B)\), that is when \(B\) is uniform on its support: \(p \in \{0, \frac12, 1\}\). That is where the grid finds the zero gap.
For this channel the min-capacity is always at least the Shannon capacity. The two measures disagree, and the one-guess measure is the larger.

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
text:
5.4 The Z-channel

Exercise 4. The Z-channel. Input 0 always arrives as 0; input 1 arrives as 0 with probability \(\frac12\). Show that \(I(X; Y) = h(q/2) - q\) for \(q = \Pr[X = 1]\), maximize over \(q\), and confirm that the uniform input is not optimal. Check: the optimum is \(q = 0.4\) and the capacity is \(\log_2(5/4) = 0.3219\) bits; the script confirms both with Blahut–Arimoto. (Capacity)







TipSolution





The formula. Use \(I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\), as for the binary symmetric channel.

Output distribution. \(Y = 1\) only if \(X = 1\) and the bit survives: \(\Pr[Y = 1] = q \cdot \frac12 = q/2\). So \(H(Y) = h(q/2)\).
Noise entropy. Given \(X = 0\), \(Y = 0\) for certain: \(H(Y \mid X = 0) = 0\). Given \(X = 1\), \(Y\) is a fair bit: \(H(Y \mid X = 1) = h(\frac12) = 1\). Averaging over \(X\): \(H(Y \mid X) = (1 - q)\cdot0 + q\cdot1 = q\).
Subtract: \(I(X; Y) = h(q/2) - q\). The script compares this with the general joint-table formula on a grid of 1,001 values of \(q\); they agree to \(3.1\times10^{-16}\).

The maximum.

Derivative of \(h\). Differentiating \(h(t) = -t\log t - (1 - t)\log(1 - t)\) gives \(h'(t) = \log\frac{1 - t}{t}\) (the \(\pm 1/\ln 2\) terms cancel).
Derivative of \(I\). By the chain rule of calculus, \(\frac{d}{dq}h(q/2) = \frac12\log\frac{1 - q/2}{q/2} = \frac12\log\frac{2 - q}{q}\). So \[\frac{dI}{dq} = \frac12\log_2\frac{2 - q}{q} - 1. \tag{5.3}\]
Set it to zero. \(\log_2\frac{2 - q}{q} = 2\), so \(\frac{2 - q}{q} = 4\) and \(q = \frac25 = 0.4\).
It is a maximum. \(h\) is concave and \(q \mapsto q/2\) is linear, so \(h(q/2)\) is concave, and subtracting the linear \(q\) keeps it concave. A stationary point of a concave function is its maximum.
The capacity. \(h(0.2) = 0.2\log_2 5 + 0.8\log_2\frac54 = \log_2 5 - 0.8\cdot 2 = \log_2 5 - 1.6\). So \(I = \log_2 5 - 1.6 - 0.4 = \log_2 5 - 2 = \log_2\frac54 = 0.3219\) bits.
Uniform input. At \(q = \frac12\), \(I = h(\frac14) - \frac12 = 0.8113 - 0.5 = 0.3113\) bits, less than 0.3219. So the uniform input is not optimal.
Numerical check. A grid search over \(q\) in steps of 0.001 peaks at \(q = 0.4000\). Blahut–Arimoto gives capacity 0.3219 at \(\Pr[X = 1] = 0.4000\).

The optimum puts less weight on input 1 because sending a 1 is expensive: half of the time it is lost, and that loss costs a full bit of noise entropy \(H(Y \mid X = 1) = 1\).
When a channel is not symmetric, the capacity-achieving input is not uniform.

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
section: 5.5 Capacities of the M-ary symmetric channel
text:
5.5 Capacities of the M-ary symmetric channel

Exercise 5. Capacities of the \(M\)-ary symmetric channel. Show that its Shannon capacity is \(\log M - h(\varepsilon) - \varepsilon\log(M - 1)\) and its min-capacity is \(\log\big(M(1 - \varepsilon)\big)\) when \(1 - \varepsilon \ge \varepsilon/(M - 1)\). Check: at \(M = 8\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.3\), 1.2765 and 2.4854 bits. (Capacity, min-capacity)







TipSolution





The channel keeps the input with probability \(1 - \varepsilon\) and otherwise sends one of the other \(M - 1\) symbols, each with probability \(\varepsilon/(M - 1)\). Every row of \(C\) holds one entry \(1 - \varepsilon\) and \(M - 1\) entries \(\varepsilon/(M - 1)\), and so does every column.
Shannon capacity. Follow the binary symmetric channel derivation.

Noise entropy does not depend on the input. Row \(x\) has entropy \[H(Y \mid X = x) = -(1 - \varepsilon)\log(1 - \varepsilon) - (M - 1)\frac{\varepsilon}{M - 1}\log\frac{\varepsilon}{M - 1} = h(\varepsilon) + \varepsilon\log(M - 1), \tag{5.4}\] using \(-\varepsilon\log\frac{\varepsilon}{M - 1} = -\varepsilon\log\varepsilon + \varepsilon\log(M - 1)\). The rows are permutations of each other, so this holds for every \(x\), and \(H(Y \mid X) = h(\varepsilon) + \varepsilon\log(M - 1)\) for every prior.
Maximize \(H(Y)\). \(Y\) takes \(M\) values, so \(H(Y) \le \log M\), with equality iff \(Y\) is uniform (the entropy upper bound).
The uniform input attains it. With \(\pi(x) = 1/M\), \(\Pr[Y = y] = \frac1M\sum_x C[x, y] = \frac1M\big[(1 - \varepsilon) + (M - 1)\frac{\varepsilon}{M - 1}\big] = \frac1M\).
So \(\mathcal C = \log M - h(\varepsilon) - \varepsilon\log(M - 1)\).

At \(M = 8\), \(\varepsilon = 0.3\): \(h(0.3) = 0.8813\) and \(0.3\log_2 7 = 0.8422\), so \(\mathcal C = 3 - 0.8813 - 0.8422 = 1.2765\) bits. Blahut–Arimoto gives 1.2765, and the input distribution it finds is exactly uniform.
Min-capacity.

Column maxima. Each column holds one entry \(1 - \varepsilon\) and \(M - 1\) entries \(\varepsilon/(M - 1)\). Under the condition \(1 - \varepsilon \ge \varepsilon/(M - 1)\), its maximum is \(1 - \varepsilon\).
Apply Equation 5.22: \(\mathcal{ML}(C) = \log\sum_{y=1}^{M}(1 - \varepsilon) = \log\big(M(1 - \varepsilon)\big)\).

At \(M = 8\), \(\varepsilon = 0.3\): \(\varepsilon/(M - 1) = 0.0429 \le 0.7\), so the condition holds, and \(\mathcal{ML} = \log_2 5.6 = 2.4854\) bits. The general column-maxima formula gives the same. If the condition fails, the column maximum is \(\varepsilon/(M - 1)\) and \(\mathcal{ML} = \log\frac{M\varepsilon}{M - 1}\).
Under the same channel, a one-try guesser gains almost twice as many bits (2.4854) as the Shannon capacity (1.2765) suggests.

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
section: 5.6 Smith versus the average of logs
text:
5.6 Smith versus the average of logs

Exercise 6. Smith versus the average of logs. Prove that \(H_\infty(X \mid Y) \le \sum_y p(y)H_\infty(X \mid Y = y)\), and find a joint table where the gap is large. Check: the walk-through gives 0.5995 vs 0.6548. (Jensen)







TipSolution





The inequality.

Write Smith’s value as a log of an average. By the derivation of Equation 5.20, \(V(X \mid Y) = \sum_y p(y)\,V(X \mid Y = y)\), where \(V(X \mid Y = y) = \max_x p(x \mid y)\). Let \(g(y) = V(X \mid Y = y)\) and \(Z = g(Y)\), a positive random variable. Then \(H_\infty(X \mid Y) = -\log\mathbb E[Z]\).
Write the other side as an average of logs. \(\sum_y p(y)H_\infty(X \mid Y = y) = \sum_y p(y)\big(-\log V(X \mid Y = y)\big) = \mathbb E[-\log Z]\).
Apply Fact 1 in its mirror form for the convex \(-\log\): \(-\log\mathbb E[Z] \le \mathbb E[-\log Z]\). That is the claim. Equality holds iff \(Z\) is constant, that is, when the best guess is equally likely to be right after every observation.

In the walk-through, Smith’s value is 0.5995 bits and the average of logs is 0.6548, as the check says.
A large gap. Reuse reveal-if-zero(1) from Section 5.8: \(X\) is uniform on \(n\)-bit strings, and \(Y\) is \(X\) itself if its lowest bit is 0 (probability \(\frac12\)), and \(\perp\) otherwise.

If \(Y\) is a string, the posterior is a point mass: \(V(X \mid Y = y) = 1\) and \(H_\infty(X \mid Y = y) = 0\).
If \(Y = \perp\), the posterior is uniform on the \(2^{n-1}\) odd strings: \(V(X \mid Y = \perp) = 2^{-(n-1)}\) and \(H_\infty(X \mid Y = \perp) = n - 1\).
Average of logs: \(\frac12\cdot0 + \frac12(n - 1) = \frac{n - 1}{2}\).
Smith: \(V(X \mid Y) = \frac12\cdot1 + \frac12\cdot2^{-(n-1)} = \frac12 + 2^{-n}\), so \(H_\infty(X \mid Y) = -\log\big(\tfrac12 + 2^{-n}\big) = n - \log\big(2^{n-1} + 1\big)\), just under 1 bit.




Table 5.2: Smith’s conditional min-entropy against the average of logs for reveal-if-zero(1) on a uniform \(n\)-bit secret. The \(n = 6\) row is computed from the explicit channel matrix and agrees with the closed forms.










\(n\)
Smith \(H_\infty(X \mid Y)\)
Average of \(H_\infty(X \mid Y = y)\)

Table 5.2 shows that the gap grows without bound: about \(\frac{n - 1}{2} - 1\) bits. The average of logs says the secret keeps 31.5 bits of guessing difficulty. But a guesser who sees \(Y\) wins more than half the time, because half the time \(Y\) hands over \(X\), and the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guesser takes that half for free. Smith’s value, about 1 bit, reflects exactly that.
Averaging the logs lets one very uncertain outcome hide an outcome that reveals everything. Smith’s definition keeps the meaning “log of a success probability”.

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
section: 5.7 Fano is tight on the symmetric channel
text:
5.7 Fano is tight on the symmetric channel

Exercise 7. Fano is tight on the symmetric channel. Show that the MAP error of the \(M\)-ary symmetric channel with uniform input is \(\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon \le (M - 1)/M\), and that Equation 5.25 holds with equality. (Fano)







TipSolution





The MAP error.

Joint table. With uniform input, \(p(x, y) = \frac1M C[x, y]\): \(\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{M}\) on the diagonal and \(\frac{\varepsilon}{M(M - 1)}\) off it.
When the diagonal wins. \(1 - \varepsilon \ge \frac{\varepsilon}{M - 1}\) iff \((M - 1)(1 - \varepsilon) \ge \varepsilon\) iff \(M - 1 \ge M\varepsilon\) iff \(\varepsilon \le \frac{M - 1}{M}\). Under this condition the MAP guess on observation \(y\) is \(x = y\).
Success probability by Equation 5.20: \(V(X \mid Y) = \sum_{y=1}^{M}\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{M} = 1 - \varepsilon\). So the MAP error is \(1 - V(X \mid Y) = \varepsilon\).

Fano holds with equality.

The output is uniform. Each column of \(C\) sums to 1 (Exercise 5), so \(p(y) = \frac1M\).
The posterior is a column of \(C\). \(p(x \mid y) = \frac{p(x, y)}{p(y)} = C[x, y]\): \(1 - \varepsilon\) on \(x = y\) and \(\frac{\varepsilon}{M - 1}\) on each of the other \(M - 1\) values.
Its entropy is the row entropy computed in Exercise 5: \(H(X \mid Y = y) = h(\varepsilon) + \varepsilon\log(M - 1)\) for every \(y\). Averaging over \(y\) gives the same value for \(H(X \mid Y)\).
Compare with Equation 5.25 at \(P_e = \varepsilon\). The right side is \(h(\varepsilon) + \varepsilon\log(M - 1)\), the same expression. So Equation 5.25 holds with equality for the MAP estimator.
Why each step of the derivation is tight. Step 3 there, \(H(E \mid \hat X) \le H(E)\), is tight because the error \(E\) has probability \(\varepsilon\) whatever the guess is, so \(E\) is independent of \(\hat X\). Step 4 is tight because, given an error, the true value is uniform over the \(M - 1\) wrong values. Step 6 is tight because the MAP guess is \(\hat X = Y\), so \(\hat X\) and \(Y\) carry the same information.

Since the right side of Equation 5.25 increases in \(P_e\) on \([0, (M - 1)/M]\), the Fano bound obtained by inverting it equals \(\varepsilon\) exactly. Table 5.3 checks this at \(M = 8\).

title: 5  Exercises: Information theory
text:
5.8 A sample-size lower bound

Exercise 8. A sample-size lower bound. In Fano’s method, how many samples must you have before the bound \(P_e \ge 1 - (n\kappa + 1)/\log M\) allows \(P_e \le 0.1\)? Express \(n\) in terms of \(\kappa\) and \(M\). Check: with \(M = 1024\) and \(\kappa = 0.01\) bits, \(n \ge 800\). (Fano’s method)







TipSolution






What “allows” means. The bound rules out \(P_e \le 0.1\) as long as its right side is above 0.1. It stops ruling it out when \[1 - \frac{n\kappa + 1}{\log M} \le 0.1. \tag{5.5}\]
Solve for \(n\). Rearrange to \(\frac{n\kappa + 1}{\log M} \ge 0.9\), then \(n\kappa \ge 0.9\log M - 1\), so \[n \ge \frac{0.9\log M - 1}{\kappa}. \tag{5.6}\] For a general target error \(\delta\), replace 0.9 by \(1 - \delta\).
Check. With \(\log_2 1024 = 10\) and \(\kappa = 0.01\): \(n \ge (9 - 1)/0.01 = 800\). The script gives a bound of 0.1010 at \(n = 799\) and exactly 0.1000 at \(n = 800\).

This is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. With fewer than 800 samples, every estimator has error above 0.1. With 800 or more, Fano no longer forbids it, but that does not mean an estimator reaches it; that depends on the problem. The sample size grows like \(\log M/\kappa\): more candidates, or candidates that are harder to tell apart, push it up.
Fano’s method turns “each sample carries at most \(\kappa\) bits” into a minimum sample size, roughly the number of bits needed to identify the candidate divided by the bits each sample carries.

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
text:
6.1 Constants of regularized logistic regression
Exercises for Optimization, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The solutions use gradient descent (GD), stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) exactly as the chapter defines them. The numbers come from the script code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_optimization.py; run it with uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_optimization.py.

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
text:
Exercise 1. Show that \(\ell(w) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\), with \(\ell\) the logistic loss and \(\|x\| \le 1\), is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex and \((\frac14 + \lambda)\)-smooth on \(\mathbb R^d\), and \((1 + \lambda R)\)-Lipschitz on the ball of radius \(R\). Check: for \(\lambda = 0.1\) and \(R = 5\), the constants are 0.1, 0.35 and 1.5. (Hessian bounds)







TipSolution





Write \(f(w) = \ell(w) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\) with \(m = y\langle w, x\rangle\).

Gradient and Hessian. The chapter’s logistic example gives \(\nabla\ell(w) = -\sigma(-m)\,y\,x\) and \(\nabla^2\ell(w) = \sigma(m)(1 - \sigma(m))\,xx^\top\). The regularizer adds \(\lambda w\) to the gradient and \(\lambda I\) to the Hessian: \[\nabla f(w) = -\sigma(-m)\,y\,x + \lambda w, \qquad \nabla^2 f(w) = \sigma(m)(1 - \sigma(m))\,xx^\top + \lambda I. \tag{6.1}\]
Eigenvalues of the Hessian. \(xx^\top\) has eigenvalue \(\|x\|^2\) along \(x\) and 0 in every direction orthogonal to \(x\). Adding \(\lambda I\) adds \(\lambda\) to each. So the eigenvalues are \(\lambda + \sigma(m)(1 - \sigma(m))\|x\|^2\) (once) and \(\lambda\) (the rest).
Strong convexity. Since \(\sigma(m)(1 - \sigma(m)) \ge 0\), every eigenvalue is at least \(\lambda\), so \(\nabla^2 f \succeq \lambda I\). The same conclusion follows without the Hessian from consequence (b) of the definitions: \(\ell\) is convex, and adding \(\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\) makes it \(\lambda\)-strongly convex.
Smoothness. \(u(1 - u) \le \frac14\) for \(u \in [0, 1]\) and \(\|x\|^2 \le 1\), so every eigenvalue lies in \([\lambda, \frac14 + \lambda] \subset [-(\frac14 + \lambda), \frac14 + \lambda]\). By step 4 of the chapter’s derivation (Hessian bound implies smoothness), \(f\) is \((\frac14 + \lambda)\)-smooth on all of \(\mathbb R^d\).
Gradient on the ball. By the triangle inequality, \(\|\nabla f(w)\| \le \sigma(-m)\|x\| + \lambda\|w\| \le 1 + \lambda R\) when \(\|w\| \le R\), since \(\sigma < 1\), \(|y| = 1\) and \(\|x\| \le 1\).
Lipschitz on the ball. Step 1 of the chapter’s derivation integrates the gradient along the segment from \(w\) to \(w'\). The ball is convex, so for \(w, w'\) in the ball the whole segment stays in it, where step 5 bounds the gradient by \(1 + \lambda R\). So \(|f(w) - f(w')| \le (1 + \lambda R)\|w - w'\|\).

For \(\lambda = 0.1\) and \(R = 5\): strong convexity \(0.1\), smoothness \(\frac14 + 0.1 = 0.35\), and Lipschitz constant \(1 + 0.1 \times 5 = 1.5\), as the check says.
The Lipschitz constant is nearly attained. Take \(\|x\| = 1\), \(y = +1\) and \(w = -Rx\), on the boundary of the ball. Then \(m = -R\) and \(\nabla f(w) = -\sigma(R)x - \lambda Rx\), of norm \(\sigma(R) + \lambda R = 1.4933\) for \(\lambda = 0.1\), \(R = 5\).
The regularizer shifts every curvature up by \(\lambda\), which helps strong convexity and costs smoothness, and its gradient \(\lambda w\) is what limits the Lipschitz constant to a bounded set.

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
section: 6.2 GD on a smooth convex function
text:
6.2 GD on a smooth convex function

Exercise 2. Show that GD with \(\eta = 1/\beta\) on a convex \(\beta\)-smooth \(F\) satisfies \(F(w_{T+1}) - F^* \le \beta\|w_1 - w^*\|^2/(2T)\). Hint: combine the descent lemma with Fact 1 to get \(F(w_{t+1}) - F^* \le \frac\beta2(\|w_t - w^*\|^2 - \|w_{t+1} - w^*\|^2)\), telescope, and use that \(F(w_t)\) decreases. (Descent lemma, telescoping)







TipSolution





Write \(g_t = \nabla F(w_t)\) and \(a_t = \|w_t - w^*\|^2\), so \(w_{t+1} = w_t - g_t/\beta\).

Descent lemma. The chapter showed, from Equation 6.6 with \(w' = w_t - g_t/\beta\), that \(F(w_{t+1}) \le F(w_t) - \frac{1}{2\beta}\|g_t\|^2\).
Convexity (Fact 1, Equation 6.1 with \(w = w_t\), \(w' = w^*\)): \(F(w_t) \le F^* + \langle g_t, w_t - w^*\rangle\). Substitute into step 1: \[F(w_{t+1}) - F^* \le \langle g_t, w_t - w^*\rangle - \frac{1}{2\beta}\|g_t\|^2. \tag{6.2}\]
Recognize a difference of squares (Fact 2). Expand \[a_{t+1} = \Big\|w_t - w^* - \frac{g_t}{\beta}\Big\|^2 = a_t - \frac2\beta\langle g_t, w_t - w^*\rangle + \frac{1}{\beta^2}\|g_t\|^2. \tag{6.3}\] Multiply by \(\beta/2\) and rearrange: \(\frac\beta2(a_t - a_{t+1}) = \langle g_t, w_t - w^*\rangle - \frac{1}{2\beta}\|g_t\|^2\), which is the right side of step 2. So \[F(w_{t+1}) - F^* \le \frac\beta2(a_t - a_{t+1}), \tag{6.4}\] the inequality in the hint.
Telescope over \(t = 1, \dots, T\): \(\sum_{t=1}^T(F(w_{t+1}) - F^*) \le \frac\beta2(a_1 - a_{T+1}) \le \frac\beta2 a_1\).
Monotonicity. By step 1, \(F(w_{t+1}) \le F(w_t)\), so \(F(w_{T+1})\) is the smallest of the \(T\) terms on the left of step 4. Hence \(T(F(w_{T+1}) - F^*) \le \frac\beta2\|w_1 - w^*\|^2\). Divide by \(T\).

Unlike SGD, GD needs no averaging: the last iterate is the best one, because every step decreases \(F\).
How tight is it? The script runs GD with \(\eta = 1/\beta = 4\) on unregularized logistic regression (a fresh dataset with \(n = 1{,}000\), \(d = 5\), drawn the same way as in the chapter; \(\beta = \frac14\) is valid because each example’s loss is \(\frac14\)-smooth). Here \(\|w_1 - w^*\|^2 = \|w^*\|^2 = 10.849\).

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
section: 6.3 The \(1/(\lambda T)\) rate is exact for a noisy quadratic
text:
6.3 The \(1/(\lambda T)\) rate is exact for a noisy quadratic

Exercise 3. Let \(F(w) = \frac\lambda2 w^2\) on \(\mathbb R\) and \(g_t = \lambda w_t + \xi_t\) with independent \(\xi_t\), \(\mathbb E\xi_t = 0\), \(\mathbb E\xi_t^2 = \sigma^2\). With \(\eta_t = 1/(\lambda t)\), show that \(t\,w_{t+1} = (t - 1)w_t - \xi_t/\lambda\), hence \(w_{T+1} = -\frac{1}{\lambda T}\sum_{t\le T}\xi_t\) and \(\mathbb E F(w_{T+1}) = \sigma^2/(2\lambda T)\). Check: \(\lambda = 1\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\), \(T = 100\) gives 0.005. (Strongly convex SGD)







TipSolution






One step. \(w_{t+1} = w_t - \frac{1}{\lambda t}(\lambda w_t + \xi_t) = \big(1 - \frac1t\big)w_t - \frac{\xi_t}{\lambda t}\). Multiply by \(t\): \(t\,w_{t+1} = (t - 1)w_t - \xi_t/\lambda\).
Telescope. Put \(v_t = (t - 1)w_t\). Step 1 says \(v_{t+1} = v_t - \xi_t/\lambda\), and \(v_1 = 0 \cdot w_1 = 0\). So \(v_{T+1} = -\frac1\lambda\sum_{t \le T}\xi_t\), that is \(T w_{T+1} = -\frac1\lambda\sum_{t\le T}\xi_t\). For \(T = 2\): \(w_2 = -\xi_1/\lambda\) and \(2w_3 = w_2 - \xi_2/\lambda = -(\xi_1 + \xi_2)/\lambda\). The start \(w_1\) is forgotten after the first step, whose step size \(1/\lambda\) jumps straight to the minimizer of the noiseless part.
Second moment. The \(\xi_t\) are independent with mean zero, so the cross terms of \((\sum_t\xi_t)^2\) have mean zero and \(\mathbb E(\sum_t\xi_t)^2 = T\sigma^2\). Hence \(\mathbb E w_{T+1}^2 = \frac{T\sigma^2}{\lambda^2T^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{\lambda^2T}\).
Risk. \(\mathbb E F(w_{T+1}) = \frac\lambda2\mathbb E w_{T+1}^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\lambda T}\). Here \(F^* = 0\), so this is the suboptimality.

For \(\lambda = 1\), \(\sigma^2 = 1\), \(T = 100\): \(1/200 = 0.005\). The script runs the recursion from \(w_1 = 5\) with Gaussian noise, 100,000 runs:

Table 6.2 matches the formula within the Monte Carlo error. The SGD iterate is exactly the minimizer of the noiseless part, \(0\), plus the average of \(T\) noise terms scaled by \(1/\lambda\), and an average of \(T\) independent terms has variance \(\sigma^2/T\). No algorithm that only sees these noisy gradients can average the noise away faster.
The \(1/(\lambda T)\) dependence in Equation 6.13 is not slack: on this problem, SGD’s error is exactly of that order.

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
text:
6.4 Smoothness of the sigmoid loss

Exercise 4. Show that \(|\sigma''(s)| \le 1/(6\sqrt3)\) for all \(s\), with equality where \(\sigma(s) = \frac12 \pm \frac{\sqrt3}{6}\). Check: \(1/(6\sqrt3) \approx 0.0962\). (Calculus of \(\sigma\))







TipSolution






First derivative. \(\sigma(s) = (1 + e^{-s})^{-1}\), so \(\sigma'(s) = \frac{e^{-s}}{(1 + e^{-s})^2} = \sigma(s)\cdot\frac{e^{-s}}{1 + e^{-s}} = \sigma(s)(1 - \sigma(s))\).
Second derivative. Differentiate \(\sigma(1 - \sigma)\) by the product rule: \(\sigma'' = \sigma'(1 - \sigma) - \sigma\sigma' = \sigma'(1 - 2\sigma) = \sigma(1 - \sigma)(1 - 2\sigma)\).
Change variable. As \(s\) runs over \(\mathbb R\), \(u = \sigma(s)\) runs over \((0, 1)\). So \(\max_s|\sigma''(s)| = \sup_{u \in (0,1)}|p(u)|\) with \(p(u) = u(1 - u)(1 - 2u) = u - 3u^2 + 2u^3\).
Critical points. \(p'(u) = 1 - 6u + 6u^2 = 0\) at \(u = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 24}}{12} = \frac12 \pm \frac{\sqrt3}{6}\).
Values. At \(u = \frac12 - \frac{\sqrt3}{6}\): \(u(1 - u) = \frac14 - \frac{3}{36} = \frac16\) and \(1 - 2u = \frac{\sqrt3}{3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\), so \(p = \frac{1}{6\sqrt3}\). At \(u = \frac12 + \frac{\sqrt3}{6}\), \(u(1 - u)\) is the same and \(1 - 2u = -\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\), so \(p = -\frac{1}{6\sqrt3}\).
Endpoints. \(p(u) \to 0\) as \(u \to 0\) or \(u \to 1\). A continuous function on \((0, 1)\) that vanishes at both ends attains its largest \(|p|\) at a critical point, so \(|\sigma''| \le \frac{1}{6\sqrt3} = 0.0962\), with equality exactly at \(\sigma(s) = \frac12 \pm \frac{\sqrt3}{6}\).

In terms of \(s\): \(\sigma(s) = u\) means \(s = \ln\frac{u}{1 - u}\), and \(\frac{1/2 + \sqrt3/6}{1/2 - \sqrt3/6} = \frac{3 + \sqrt3}{3 - \sqrt3} = 2 + \sqrt3\). So the extremes are at \(s = \pm\ln(2 + \sqrt3) = \pm1.3170\). A grid search over \([-10, 10]\) in the script finds the maximum \(0.0962\) at \(|s| = 1.3170\). Since the sigmoid-loss Hessian is \(\sigma''(-m)\,xx^\top\) with \(\|x\| \le 1\), this is its smoothness constant \(\beta\).
The sigmoid loss is about 2.6 times smoother than the logistic loss (\(0.0962\) against \(\frac14\)), but non-convex: \(\sigma''\) takes both signs.

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
text:
6.5 Covariance under sampling without replacement

Exercise 5. For a finite population with \(\sum_i u_i = 0\), show that two distinct uniform draws have \(\mathbb E\langle u_{I}, u_{J}\rangle = -\sigma_1^2/(n - 1)\), and verify Equation 6.15 at \(B = n\). Then check it by enumeration on the toy data with \(B = 2\). Check: \(7/6\). (Minibatch variance)







TipSolution





The covariance.

The pair is uniform. Two distinct draws \((I, J)\) are equally likely to be any of the \(n(n - 1)\) ordered pairs of distinct indices, so \(\mathbb E\langle u_I, u_J\rangle = \frac{1}{n(n - 1)}\sum_{i \ne i'}\langle u_i, u_{i'}\rangle\).
Expand the zero sum (Fact 2, applied to \(n\) terms): \(0 = \|\sum_i u_i\|^2 = \sum_i\|u_i\|^2 + \sum_{i \ne i'}\langle u_i, u_{i'}\rangle\). With \(\sum_i\|u_i\|^2 = n\sigma_1^2\), this gives \(\sum_{i \ne i'}\langle u_i, u_{i'}\rangle = -n\sigma_1^2\).
Divide: \(\mathbb E\langle u_I, u_J\rangle = \frac{-n\sigma_1^2}{n(n - 1)} = -\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n - 1}\).

At \(B = n\). The formula gives \(\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n}\cdot\frac{n - n}{n - 1} = 0\). Directly: a batch of \(n\) distinct indices is the whole population, so \(g_B = \frac1n\sum_i\nabla\ell(w, z_i) = \nabla F(w)\) exactly, and the variance is 0. The two agree.
Enumeration on the toy data. In Table 6.2 the deviations are \(u = (2, 1, -3)\), so \(\sigma_1^2 = \frac{4 + 1 + 9}{3} = \frac{14}{3}\).

The covariance. The distinct pairs have products \(u_1u_2 = 2\), \(u_1u_3 = -6\), \(u_2u_3 = -3\), each appearing twice among the 6 ordered pairs, so the mean is \(\frac{2(2 - 6 - 3)}{6} = -\frac73\). The formula gives \(-\frac{14/3}{3 - 1} = -\frac73\).
The batch variance at \(B = 2\). Expand \(\bar u^2 = \frac14(u_I^2 + u_J^2 + 2u_Iu_J)\) and take expectations: \(\frac14\big(2\cdot\frac{14}{3} - 2\cdot\frac73\big) = \frac14\cdot\frac{14}{3} = \frac76\). Listing the three batches, as in Table 6.4, gives \(\frac13(2.25 + 0.25 + 1) = \frac76\) too, and so does Equation 6.15: \(\frac{14/3}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac76\).

The script enumerates every batch in exact fractions:

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
text:
6.6 Critical batch size

Exercise 6. Fix a budget of \(N = TB\) gradient evaluations and put \(\sigma^2/B\) in place of \(\sigma^2\) in Equation 6.17. Show that the optimized bound equals \(2\sqrt{2\beta\Delta\sigma^2/N}\), independent of \(B\), as long as \(B \le \sigma\sqrt{N/(2\beta\Delta)}\), and grows with \(B\) beyond that. Check: for the sigmoid-loss example (\(\beta = 0.0962\), \(\Delta = 0.5\), \(\sigma^2 = 1/16\)) and \(N = 10^4\), the critical batch size is about 81. (Non-convex SGD)







TipSolution






The bound in terms of \(B\). With \(T = N/B\) steps and variance \(\sigma^2/B\), Equation 6.17 reads \[\Phi(\eta) = \frac{2\Delta B}{\eta N} + \frac{\beta\eta\sigma^2}{B}, \qquad 0 < \eta \le \frac1\beta. \tag{6.5}\]
Unconstrained minimum. \(\Phi = a/\eta + b\eta\) with \(a = 2\Delta B/N\) and \(b = \beta\sigma^2/B\). Its derivative \(-a/\eta^2 + b\) vanishes at \(\eta_B = \sqrt{a/b} = B\sqrt{2\Delta/(\beta\sigma^2N)}\), where both terms equal \(\sqrt{ab}\), so \(\Phi(\eta_B) = 2\sqrt{ab} = 2\sqrt{2\beta\Delta\sigma^2/N}\). The \(B\) in \(a\) and the \(1/B\) in \(b\) cancel: the value does not depend on \(B\).
When the constraint is inactive. \(\eta_B \le 1/\beta\) means \(B\sqrt{2\Delta/(\beta\sigma^2N)} \le 1/\beta\), that is \(B \le \frac1\beta\sqrt{\frac{\beta\sigma^2N}{2\Delta}} = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{N}{2\beta\Delta}} = B_{\text{crit}}\). Up to \(B_{\text{crit}}\) the optimized bound is \(2\sqrt{2\beta\Delta\sigma^2/N}\).
Beyond it. For \(B > B_{\text{crit}}\), \(\eta_B > 1/\beta\), and \(\Phi\) decreases on \((0, \eta_B)\), so the best allowed step is \(\eta = 1/\beta\): \[\Phi(1/\beta) = \frac{2\beta\Delta B}{N} + \frac{\sigma^2}{B}. \tag{6.6}\] Its derivative in \(B\) is \(\frac{2\beta\Delta}{N} - \frac{\sigma^2}{B^2}\), which is positive exactly when \(B^2 > \frac{\sigma^2N}{2\beta\Delta} = B_{\text{crit}}^2\). So the bound grows with \(B\). At \(B = B_{\text{crit}}\) both terms equal \(\sigma\sqrt{2\beta\Delta/N}\), so the two pieces join continuously; for \(B \gg B_{\text{crit}}\) the bound is about \(2\beta\Delta B/N = 2\beta\Delta/T\), the noiseless rate with only \(T = N/B\) steps.
The numbers. With \(\beta = 1/(6\sqrt3)\), \(\Delta = 0.5\), \(\sigma = \frac14\), \(N = 10^4\): \(B_{\text{crit}} = \frac14\sqrt{10^4/0.0962} = 80.6\), about 81 as the check says.

Below \(B_{\text{crit}}\) a larger batch reduces the noise by exactly as much as it reduces the number of steps; above it, the step size can no longer grow to use the lower noise, so the extra evaluations are wasted.
Up to the critical batch size, batches trade steps for noise one for one, so they cost nothing per gradient evaluation and pay off through parallelism; beyond it they waste computation.

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
text:
6.7 A sharper sensitivity bound

Exercise 7. Redo the ERM derivation assuming \(J(\cdot; D)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and the two replaced gradients differ by at most \(\Gamma\) at \(w'\). Show that the movement is at most \(\Gamma/(\mu n)\). Using \(\mu \approx \lambda + 0.0233\) and \(\Gamma \approx 1\), predict the ratio observed/bound at \(\lambda = 0.01\) and compare with Table 6.8. (Strong monotonicity)







TipSolution





Use the chapter’s notation: \(J_D = J(\cdot; D)\), \(J_{D'} = J(\cdot; D') = J_D + h\) with \(h(v) = \frac1n(\ell(v, z') - \ell(v, z_i))\), \(w = w^*(D)\), \(w' = w^*(D')\).

The gradient difference at \(w'\). \(\nabla h(w') = \frac1n\big(\nabla\ell(w', z') - \nabla\ell(w', z_i)\big)\), so \(\|\nabla h(w')\| \le \Gamma/n\) by assumption. (The chapter used the triangle inequality to get \(2L/n\); here \(\Gamma\) replaces \(2L\).)
Optimality, as in the chapter: \(\nabla J_D(w) = 0\) and \(\nabla J_D(w') = -\nabla h(w')\).
Strong monotonicity of the \(\mu\)-strongly convex \(J_D\) (Equation 6.7 with \(\mu\) in place of \(\lambda\)): \(\mu\|w' - w\|^2 \le \langle\nabla J_D(w') - \nabla J_D(w), w' - w\rangle = \langle -\nabla h(w'), w' - w\rangle\).
Cauchy–Schwarz (Fact 2) and step 1: \(\mu\|w' - w\|^2 \le \frac\Gamma n\|w' - w\|\).
Divide by \(\mu\|w' - w\|\): \(\|w' - w\| \le \frac{\Gamma}{\mu n}\). With \(\mu = \lambda\) and \(\Gamma = 2L\) this is Equation 6.19.

Prediction. Dividing the sharper bound by the chapter’s, the \(n\) cancels: \[\frac{\Gamma/(\mu n)}{2L/(\lambda n)} = \frac{\lambda\Gamma}{2L\mu} = \frac{0.01 \times 1}{2 \times (0.01 + 0.0233)} = 0.150. \tag{6.7}\] If the sharper bound were nearly attained, the observed/bound ratio at \(\lambda = 0.01\) would be about 0.150. Table 6.8 reports 0.10 to 0.13: the right size, and a little lower.
Why a little lower. The script repeats the experiment at \(n = 1{,}000\), \(\lambda = 0.01\) (20 replacements on a fresh dataset) and measures, for each replacement, \(\Gamma\) at \(w'\) and \(\mu\) as the smallest Hessian eigenvalue of \(J_D\) along the segment from \(w\) to \(w'\) (all the proof needs).

The largest movement is \(2.38\times10^{-2}\), ratio 0.119 to \(2L/(\lambda n)\), inside the chapter’s range.
For that replacement, \(\Gamma = 1.133\) and \(\mu = 0.0404\), so the sharper bound is \(2.81\times10^{-2}\).
Over all 20 replacements, \(\mu\) lies between 0.0402 and 0.0404, larger than \(0.0333\): at the regularized minimizer \(\|w\|\) is smaller than at the unregularized one, and the logistic curvature \(\sigma(m)(1 - \sigma(m))\) is larger at smaller margins. \(\Gamma\) ranges from 0.103 to 1.133, depending on how different the swapped examples are.
The movement is between 0.74 and 0.88 of \(\Gamma/(\mu n)\) for every replacement. The rest of the slack is Cauchy–Schwarz in step 4: \(\nabla h(w')\) is not exactly parallel to \(w' - w\).

Most of the gap between Equation 6.19 and reality is the curvature of the data, which the bound ignores; with the true \(\mu\) and \(\Gamma\) the bound is within a factor of 1.4 of the observed movement.

title: 6  Exercises: Optimization
text:
6.8 The regularized median

Exercise 8. For \(n = 2k + 1\) values, \(k + 1\) zeros and \(k\) ones, minimize \(\frac1n\sum_i|w - z_i| + \frac\lambda2 w^2\) before and after replacing one 0 by a 1. Hint: the subgradient at 0 before the change is \([-1, 1/n]\), which contains 0; after it, the derivative on \((0, 1)\) is \(-1/n + \lambda w\). Check: the move is \(1/(\lambda n)\), half the bound; for \(n = 101\) and \(\lambda = 0.1\), 0.099 against 0.198. (Subgradients, sensitivity)







TipSolution





The objective is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex (consequence (b) of the definitions), so its minimizer is unique, and \(w\) is the minimizer exactly when 0 lies in the subdifferential at \(w\). The subdifferential of \(|w - z|\) is \(\{-1\}\) for \(w < z\), \(\{1\}\) for \(w > z\), and \([-1, 1]\) at \(w = z\).
Before (\(k + 1\) zeros, \(k\) ones). At \(w = 0\):

The \(k + 1\) terms \(|w|\) contribute \(\frac{k + 1}{n}[-1, 1]\).
The \(k\) terms \(|w - 1|\) have derivative \(-1\) at 0 and contribute \(-\frac kn\).
The regularizer has derivative \(\lambda \cdot 0 = 0\).
Total: \(\big[\frac{-(k + 1) - k}{n}, \frac{(k + 1) - k}{n}\big] = [-1, \frac1n]\), using \(n = 2k + 1\). It contains 0, so \(w^*(D) = 0\).

After (\(k\) zeros, \(k + 1\) ones).

On \((0, 1)\) the objective is differentiable. The zeros contribute \(+\frac kn\), the ones \(-\frac{k + 1}{n}\), the regularizer \(\lambda w\): the derivative is \(-\frac1n + \lambda w\). It vanishes at \(w = \frac{1}{\lambda n}\), which lies in \((0, 1)\) when \(\lambda n > 1\).
0 is no longer optimal. At 0 the subdifferential is \(\frac kn[-1, 1] - \frac{k + 1}{n} = [-1, -\frac1n]\), which excludes 0.
The cap. If \(\lambda n \le 1\), the derivative on \((0, 1)\) stays negative, and at \(w = 1\) the subdifferential is \(\frac kn + \frac{k + 1}{n}[-1, 1] + \lambda = [\lambda - \frac1n, 1 + \lambda]\), which contains 0. Then \(w^*(D') = 1\), the unregularized median.

So the minimizer moves by \(\min\big(1, \frac{1}{\lambda n}\big)\). The chapter’s bound with \(L = 1\) is \(\frac{2}{\lambda n}\): when \(\lambda n > 1\) the move is exactly half of it. For \(n = 101\) and \(\lambda = 0.1\), the move is \(\frac{1}{10.1} = 0.0990\) against \(0.1980\). The script minimizes both objectives numerically:

Why half. In step 2 of the chapter’s derivation, the gradient of \(J_D\) at \(w'\) is \(\frac{k + 1}{n} - \frac kn + \lambda w' = \frac2n\) — the full \(2L/n\). But strong monotonicity compares it with the subgradient 0 at \(w = 0\), and the subgradient of \(J_D\) jumps from 0 to \(\frac1n\) at the kink: just to the right of 0 it is already \(\frac1n + \lambda w\). Half of the \(\frac2n\) is absorbed by that jump, and only the other half must be supplied by the regularizer’s slope \(\lambda w'\). The bound assumes all of it is.
Strong convexity turns a jump of 1 into a move of \(1/(\lambda n)\), and the kink of the absolute loss at the old minimizer acts as extra curvature that the bound does not count.

title: 7  Exercises: Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
Exercise 1. Removal against replacement. Define removal stability by \(|\ell(A(S), z) - \ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z)| \le \beta_{\text{remove}}\), where \(S^{\setminus i}\) drops \(z_i\). Show that \(A\) is then \(2\beta_{\text{remove}}\)-uniformly stable in the replace-one sense. Hint: go from \(S\) to \(S^{(i)}\) through \(S^{\setminus i}\). (Triangle inequality)







TipSolution





The key observation is that \(S\) and \(S^{(i)}\) have the same set with \(z_i\) dropped. Take \(n = 3\) and \(i = 2\):

\((z_1, z_3)\)






As Table 7.1 shows, dropping position 2 erases the only place where the two sets differ. In general \((S^{(i)})^{\setminus i} = S^{\setminus i}\).

Insert the midpoint. For any test point \(z\), add and subtract \(\ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z)\): \[\ell(A(S), z) - \ell(A(S^{(i)}), z) = \big[\ell(A(S), z) - \ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z)\big] + \big[\ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z) - \ell(A(S^{(i)}), z)\big]. \tag{7.1}\]
First bracket. Removal stability applied to the training set \(S\) and index \(i\) bounds it by \(\beta_{\text{remove}}\) in absolute value.
Second bracket. Removal stability holds for every training set, so apply it to \(S^{(i)}\) and index \(i\). Since \((S^{(i)})^{\setminus i} = S^{\setminus i}\), it bounds \(|\ell(A(S^{(i)}), z) - \ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z)|\) by \(\beta_{\text{remove}}\).
Triangle inequality. \(|\ell(A(S), z) - \ell(A(S^{(i)}), z)| \le 2\beta_{\text{remove}}\) for every \(S\), \(i\), \(z_i'\) and \(z\). This is Equation 7.9 with \(\beta = 2\beta_{\text{remove}}\).

For a randomized \(A\), the same steps go through with \(\mathbb E_A\) in front of each loss, because the triangle inequality holds for the expected differences too.
Removal and replacement stability are interchangeable up to a factor of 2, which is why the Bousquet–Elisseeff bound can be stated in either form.

title: 7  Exercises: Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.3 The sample mean

Exercise 3. The sample mean. Let \(z_i \in [0, 1]\) with variance \(\sigma^2\), \(A(S) = \frac1n\sum_iz_i\) and \(\ell(w, z) = (w - z)^2\). Show that \(\beta = 2/n\), and that the expected gap is exactly \(2\sigma^2/n\). Check: for fair coins and \(n = 10\), the gap is \(0.05\) and the bound \(0.2\). (Uniform stability, bias of the training loss)







TipSolution





Write \(\bar z = A(S)\) and \(\mu = \mathbb E z_i\).
Stability.

The model moves by at most \(1/n\). \(S\) and \(S^{(i)}\) differ in one term of the average, so \(w - w' = A(S) - A(S^{(i)}) = (z_i - z_i')/n\), and \(|w - w'| \le 1/n\) because \(z_i, z_i' \in [0, 1]\).
Factor the loss difference. \((w - z)^2 - (w' - z)^2 = (w - w')(w + w' - 2z)\).
Bound the second factor. \(w\), \(w'\) and \(z\) all lie in \([0, 1]\), so \(w + w' - 2z \in [-2, 2]\).
Combine. \(|\ell(w, z) - \ell(w', z)| \le \frac1n \cdot 2 = \frac2n\) for every \(S\), \(i\), \(z_i'\) and \(z\). So \(A\) is \(\beta\)-uniformly stable with \(\beta = 2/n\).

The bound is tight up to \(1/n^2\). Steps 1 and 3 cannot be tight at once: \(|w - w'| = 1/n\) forces \(\{z_i, z_i'\} = \{0, 1\}\), so \(w\) and \(w'\) cannot both equal \(z \pm 1\). The best case puts every other point at 1, \(z_i = 0\), \(z_i' = 1\) and \(z = 0\): then \(w = (n-1)/n\), \(w' = 1\), and the loss difference is \(1 - ((n-1)/n)^2 = (2n - 1)/n^2\). The script maximizes over all corner configurations and finds \(0.1900 = 19/100\) at \(n = 10\), against the bound \(0.2000\).
Expected gap.

Expected training loss. Expand around \(\mu\): \(\sum_i(z_i - \bar z)^2 = \sum_i(z_i - \mu)^2 - n(\bar z - \mu)^2\), because the cross term is \(-2(\bar z - \mu)\sum_i(z_i - \mu) = -2n(\bar z - \mu)^2\). Take expectations, using \(\mathbb E(z_i - \mu)^2 = \sigma^2\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar z) = \sigma^2/n\) (independence): \(\mathbb E\sum_i(z_i - \bar z)^2 = n\sigma^2 - \sigma^2\). Divide by \(n\): \[\mathbb E\big[\hat R_S(\bar z)\big] = \frac{n - 1}{n}\sigma^2. \tag{7.2}\]
Expected test loss. A fresh \(z\) is independent of \(\bar z\), so \(\mathbb E(\bar z - z)^2 = \mathrm{Var}(\bar z - z) + (\mathbb E\bar z - \mathbb E z)^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}n + \sigma^2 + 0\): \[\mathbb E\big[R(\bar z)\big] = \frac{n + 1}{n}\sigma^2. \tag{7.3}\]
Gap. Subtract: \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{gap}] = \frac{n + 1 - (n - 1)}{n}\sigma^2 = \frac{2\sigma^2}n\).

Concrete case, \(n = 2\) fair coins (\(\sigma^2 = \frac14\)). The outcomes \((0, 0)\) and \((1, 1)\) have \(\bar z = z_1 = z_2\) and training loss 0. The outcomes \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 0)\) have \(\bar z = \frac12\) and training loss \(\frac14\). So the expected training loss is \(\frac12 \cdot \frac14 = 0.125 = \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\), as step 5 says. The test loss is \(\frac32\sigma^2 = 0.375\), and the gap \(0.25 = 2\sigma^2/2\). The script’s exact enumeration gives train \(0.1250\), test \(0.3750\), gap \(0.2500\).
Check. For fair coins, \(\sigma^2 = \frac14\). At \(n = 10\) the gap is \(2 \cdot \frac14/10 = 0.05\) and the bound \(2/10 = 0.2\). Exact enumeration over the number of ones gives train \(0.2250 = \frac{9}{10}\cdot\frac14\), test \(0.2750 = \frac{11}{10}\cdot\frac14\) and gap \(0.0500\).
The sample mean overfits by \(2\sigma^2/n\), the familiar bias of the uncorrected sample variance counted twice: once because the training points pull \(\bar z\) towards themselves, once because a fresh point does not. Stability gets the \(1/n\) rate right and is loose by the factor \((2/n)/(2\sigma^2/n) = 1/\sigma^2\), which is at least 4 because \(\sigma^2 \le \frac14\) on \([0, 1]\).

text:
7.4 Leave-one-out is unbiased

Exercise 4. Leave-one-out is unbiased. Show that \(\mathbb E[\ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z_i)] = \mathbb E[R(A(S'))]\), where \(S'\) is a training set of size \(n - 1\). Why does this make leave-one-out cross-validation an almost unbiased estimate of the test loss? (Independence, step 1 of the renaming trick)







TipSolution






\(z_i\) is a fresh point for \(A(S^{\setminus i})\). \(S^{\setminus i}\) consists of the \(z_j\) with \(j \ne i\), which are independent of \(z_i\). So \(z_i\) plays the role of \(z_i'\) in step 1 of the renaming trick.
Condition on \(S^{\setminus i}\). The model \(A(S^{\setminus i})\) is then fixed and \(z_i \sim \mathcal D\) is independent of it, so \(\mathbb E[\ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z_i) \mid S^{\setminus i}] = R(A(S^{\setminus i}))\). Take expectations: \(\mathbb E[\ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z_i)] = \mathbb E[R(A(S^{\setminus i}))]\).
\(S^{\setminus i}\) is a training set of size \(n - 1\). It is \(n - 1\) i.i.d. draws from \(\mathcal D\), so it has the same distribution as \(S'\), and \(\mathbb E[R(A(S^{\setminus i}))] = \mathbb E[R(A(S'))]\).

Why leave-one-out is almost unbiased. The leave-one-out estimate is \(\frac1n\sum_i\ell(A(S^{\setminus i}), z_i)\). By linearity and the result above, its expectation is exactly \(\mathbb E[R(A(S'))]\): the expected test loss of the algorithm trained on \(n - 1\) points. The only bias is the difference between training on \(n - 1\) and on \(n\) points. If \(A\) has removal stability \(\beta_{\text{remove}}\) (Exercise 1), apply it to \(S\) and index \(n\): \(|\ell(A(S), z) - \ell(A(S^{\setminus n}), z)| \le \beta_{\text{remove}}\) for every \(z\), so \(|R(A(S)) - R(A(S^{\setminus n}))| \le \beta_{\text{remove}}\), and since \(S^{\setminus n}\) has the law of \(S'\), \[\big|\mathbb E[R(A(S))] - \mathbb E[R(A(S'))]\big| \le \beta_{\text{remove}}. \tag{7.4}\] For a stable algorithm this bias is of order \(1/n\). Compare the training loss: it evaluates \(A(S)\) on points it was fitted to, and its bias is the whole gap.
Concrete case: the sample mean of Exercise 3. The mean of the other \(n - 1\) points has variance \(\sigma^2/(n - 1)\) and is independent of \(z_i\), so the expected leave-one-out loss is \(\sigma^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{n - 1} = \frac{n}{n - 1}\sigma^2\). That is the test loss \(\frac{m + 1}{m}\sigma^2\) of Exercise 3 at size \(m = n - 1\). For fair coins and \(n = 10\), exact enumeration gives:

Leaving the evaluated point out removes the dependence that biases the training loss; what remains is the small cost of training on one fewer example. (Unbiasedness says nothing about variance: the \(n\) terms share most of their training data, so they are correlated.)

section: 7.5 SGD with a strongly convex loss
text:
7.5 SGD with a strongly convex loss

Exercise 5. SGD with a strongly convex loss. If each \(\ell(\cdot, z)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(\rho\)-smooth (on a bounded domain, since a strongly convex function cannot be Lipschitz everywhere), the gradient step with \(\eta \le 2/(\rho + \mu)\) is \((1 - \eta\rho\mu/(\rho + \mu))\)-contractive (Hardt, Recht & Singer 2016, Lemma 3.7). With constant \(\eta\), show that \(\mathbb E\delta_T \le \frac{2L}{n}\cdot\frac{\rho + \mu}{\rho\mu}\) for every \(T\). Check: for \(\mu \ll \rho\) this is about \(2L/(\mu n)\), the ERM bound: with strong convexity, training longer no longer costs stability. (SGD coupling, geometric series)







TipSolution





Run SGD on \(S\) and \(S^{(i)}\) with the same index sequence, as in the chapter, and write \(q = 1 - \eta\rho\mu/(\rho + \mu) < 1\) for the contraction factor and \(\psi_j(w) = w - \eta\nabla\ell(w, z_j)\) for the gradient step on example \(j\).

Same example picked (\(I_t \ne i\), probability \(1 - 1/n\)). Both runs apply the same map \(\psi_{I_t}\), which is \(q\)-contractive: \(\delta_{t+1} \le q\,\delta_t\).
Differing example picked (\(I_t = i\), probability \(1/n\)). Split the difference so that the contraction still applies: \[w_{t+1} - w_{t+1}' = \big[\psi_i(w_t) - \psi_i(w_t')\big] + \eta\big[\nabla\ell(w_t', z_i') - \nabla\ell(w_t', z_i)\big]. \tag{7.5}\] The first bracket has norm at most \(q\,\delta_t\); the second at most \(2\eta L\), since both gradients have norm at most \(L\) on the domain. So \(\delta_{t+1} \le q\,\delta_t + 2\eta L\).
Take expectations over \(I_t\), which is independent of \(\delta_t\): \(\mathbb E\delta_{t+1} \le q\,\mathbb E\delta_t + \frac{2\eta L}n\). (In step 2 of the chapter, without strong convexity, the factor in front of \(\mathbb E\delta_t\) was 1; here it is \(q\) in both cases.)
Unroll from \(\delta_0 = 0\). After one step, \(\mathbb E\delta_1 \le \frac{2\eta L}n\); after two, \(\le \frac{2\eta L}n(1 + q)\); after \(T\), \[\mathbb E\delta_T \le \frac{2\eta L}n\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}q^k = \frac{2\eta L}n\cdot\frac{1 - q^T}{1 - q}. \tag{7.6}\]
Bound the geometric series by its infinite sum, \(\frac{1}{1 - q} = \frac{\rho + \mu}{\eta\rho\mu}\). The step size cancels: \[\mathbb E\delta_T \le \frac{2\eta L}n\cdot\frac{\rho + \mu}{\eta\rho\mu} = \frac{2L}n\cdot\frac{\rho + \mu}{\rho\mu} \quad\text{for every } T. \tag{7.7}\]

Check. If \(\mu \ll \rho\), then \(\frac{\rho + \mu}{\rho\mu} = \frac1\mu + \frac1\rho \approx \frac1\mu\), so \(\mathbb E\delta_T \lesssim \frac{2L}{\mu n}\). That is the weight bound of Equation 7.17 with \(\lambda = \mu\). Multiplying by \(L\) (Fact 1) gives \(\beta \le 2L^2/(\mu n)\), the regularized ERM bound, independent of \(T\).
A numerical check. Take the running example with the regularizer moved into each per-example loss, \(\ell(w, z) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\), with \(\lambda = 0.1\), \(n = 100\) and \(\eta = 0.25\). This loss is \(\mu = \lambda\) strongly convex and \(\rho = \frac14 + \lambda = 0.35\) smooth, and \(\eta \le 2/(\rho + \mu) \approx 4.44\). The logistic part of the gradient has norm at most \(\|x\| = 1\), so, starting from 0 and with \(\eta\lambda \le 1\), an SGD step gives \(\|w_{t+1}\| \le (1 - \eta\lambda)\|w_t\| + \eta\), so the iterates stay in the ball \(\|w\| \le 1/\lambda\), where the gradient norm is at most \(1 + \lambda\cdot\frac1\lambda = 2\): \(L = 2\). Then \(q = 0.98056\) and the bound for every \(T\) is \(\frac{4}{100}\cdot\frac{0.45}{0.035} = 0.5143\). Averaged over 100 coupled pairs of runs, with \(z_1\) replaced by a fresh draw:

7.6 \(k\)-nearest neighbours

Exercise 6. \(k\)-nearest neighbours. Change the script to use \(k = 15\) neighbours with majority vote, and compare its gap with 1-NN for \(n = 200\) and \(n = 1000\). Then show that its worst-case uniform stability is still \(\beta = 1\). What does this say about uniform stability as a measure? (Unstable algorithms, worst case against average case)







TipSolution





The experiment. The solution script replaces the nearest-neighbour search by the \(k\) largest inner products (the features are unit vectors, so these are the \(k\) nearest points) and predicts the sign of the sum of their labels; \(k = 15\) is odd, so there are no ties. A training point counts as one of its own neighbours. Both rules run on the same 10 training sets and the same 2,000 test points:

The 15-NN gap is five to eight times smaller than the 1-NN gap, and it shrinks with \(n\), while the 1-NN gap stays near its limit 0.338 (Table 7.6). The 15-NN training error is close to the Bayes error 0.250, so it is an honest estimate, and its test error is better than 1-NN’s too.
Worst-case stability is still 1. The 0-1 loss lies in \(\{0, 1\}\), so \(\beta \le 1\) always. To show \(\beta = 1\), build one training set where one replacement flips the loss at one test point.

The training set. Fix a test point \(z = (x, +1)\). Put 15 distinct training points close to \(x\), 8 labelled \(+1\) and 7 labelled \(-1\), and put the other \(n - 15\) points far away.
Before. The 15 nearest neighbours of \(x\) are the close points. The vote is \(8 - 7 = +1\), so the prediction is \(+1\) and the loss at \(z\) is 0.
The replacement. Replace one of the \(+1\) close points, \(z_i = (x_i, +1)\), by \(z_i' = (x_i, -1)\), the same point with its label flipped. The neighbours of \(x\) do not change, but the vote becomes \(7 - 8 = -1\).
After. The prediction is \(-1\) and the loss at \(z\) is 1. So \(|\ell(A(S), z) - \ell(A(S^{(i)}), z)| = 1\), and \(\beta = 1\).

The script builds this configuration (15 points near \(e_1\), test point \(e_1\)) and confirms the loss goes from 0 to 1.
What it says about uniform stability. Uniform stability is a worst case over training sets, replacements and test points. It cannot tell 1-NN from 15-NN, although one has a gap of 0.37 and the other of 0.05. The configuration in step 1, a test point with a vote exactly on the edge, is rare under the data distribution; Equation 7.10 says the expected gap is the average replace-one effect, which for 15-NN is small. An average-case notion of stability, which averages over the data instead of taking the worst case, is what explains why \(k\)-NN generalizes.
Uniform stability is sufficient for a small gap but far from necessary: it misses algorithms that are stable on typical data.

title: 7  Exercises: Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.7 The decaying step size

Exercise 7. The decaying step size. For \(\eta_t = c/t\), show that the bound Equation 7.19 is at most \(\frac{2L^2c(1 + \ln T)}{n}\). With \(T = n\) and constant \(\eta = 1/\sqrt n\) instead, show \(\beta \le 2L^2/\sqrt n\), and explain why Equation 7.13 is then vacuous while the bounds of Feldman & Vondrák and of Bousquet, Klochkov & Zhivotovskiy are not. (SGD stability, high-probability rates)







TipSolution





Decaying step. The bound needs \(\eta_t \le 2/\rho\) for every \(t\); the largest step is \(\eta_1 = c\), so take \(c \le 2/\rho\).

Sum the steps. \(\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t = c\sum_{t=1}^T\frac1t\).
Compare with an integral. For \(t \ge 2\), \(\frac1t \le \int_{t-1}^t\frac{ds}s\), because \(1/s \ge 1/t\) on \([t - 1, t]\). Summing, \(\sum_{t=2}^T\frac1t \le \int_1^T\frac{ds}s = \ln T\), so \(\sum_{t=1}^T\frac1t \le 1 + \ln T\).
Substitute into Equation 7.19: \(\beta \le \frac{2L^2}n\cdot c(1 + \ln T) = \frac{2L^2c(1 + \ln T)}n\).

For \(c = 1\) and \(T = n = 10{,}000\), the harmonic sum is \(9.7876\), below \(1 + \ln T = 10.2103\), and the bound is \(0.002042\) (with \(L = 1\)). The step sizes shrink fast enough that \(\beta\) grows only logarithmically in \(T\).
Constant step \(1/\sqrt n\) for \(T = n\) steps. \(\sum_{t=1}^n\eta_t = n\cdot\frac1{\sqrt n} = \sqrt n\), so Equation 7.19 gives \(\beta \le \frac{2L^2}n\sqrt n = \frac{2L^2}{\sqrt n}\).
Why Equation 7.13 is vacuous. Its stability term is \(2n\beta\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/(2n)} = \beta\sqrt{2n\ln(1/\delta)}\). With \(\beta = 2L^2/\sqrt n\) the \(\sqrt n\) cancels and the term is \(2L^2\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\), a constant that does not fall with \(n\). For \(L = 1\) and \(\delta = 0.05\) it is \(4.895\). With \(M = 1\) the gap is at most 1 anyway, so a width near 5 says nothing. This is the \(\beta \sim 1/\sqrt n\) regime of Figure 7.2.
Why the improved bounds are not. Plug \(\beta = 2/\sqrt n\) into their orders (\(L = M = 1\)):

Feldman & Vondrák (2018): \(\sqrt{(\beta + 1/n)\ln(1/\delta)} \approx \sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\,n^{-1/4}\), which goes to zero.
Bousquet, Klochkov & Zhivotovskiy (2020): \(\beta\log n\log(1/\delta) + \sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n} = \frac{2\log n\log(1/\delta)}{\sqrt n} + \sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}n}\), which is \(\tilde O(1/\sqrt n)\).

Both depend on \(\beta\) linearly or through a square root, not through \(n\beta\), so they only need \(\beta \to 0\). Table 7.7 shows the three at \(\delta = 0.05\). The last two columns drop the unknown constants, so they show the rate, not a usable bound.

7.8 Self-influence and label noise

Exercise 8. Self-influence and label noise. Change the label probability to \(\sigma(20x_1)\), which makes labels less noisy, and rerun the self-influence experiment at \(\lambda = 0.01\). Predict before running: does the gap go up or down, and what happens to the share of examples against the trend? (Memorization)







TipSolution





Prediction.

Share against the trend. An example goes against the trend when \(y x_1 < 0\), which happens with probability \(\sigma(-s|x_1|)\) given \(x_1\), for label probability \(\sigma(sx_1)\). That is \(\min(p, 1 - p)\), so the expected share against the trend equals the Bayes error. Raising \(s\) from 5 to 20 makes \(\sigma(-s|x_1|)\) smaller at every \(x_1 \ne 0\), so the share should fall well below a quarter. By quadrature it falls from \(0.250\) to \(0.079\).
Gap. The chapter found that examples against the trend have the largest self-influence, and Equation 7.10 makes the gap the average self-influence. Fewer such examples should mean a smaller gap. Against-trend examples should still be the most memorized ones, since they are still the ones the trend cannot fit.

Result. The solution script repeats the chapter’s experiment (\(n = 40\), \(\lambda = 0.01\), 100 training sets, each example replaced by a fresh draw in turn) with \(\Pr[y = 1 \mid x] = \sigma(20x_1)\):

8.1 Which are negligible?
Exercises for Cryptography basics, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The numbers below, from the total variation (TV) distances of the coin distinguisher to the toy pseudorandom function (PRF) and the learning with errors (LWE) noise budget, come from uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/solutions_crypto_basics.py (seed 0).

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
Exercise 1. Which are negligible? Decide for \(\lambda^{-\log_2\log_2\lambda}\), \(2^{-(\log_2\lambda)^2}\), \(1/\lambda^{100}\) and \(\mu(\lambda) = 2^{-\lambda}\) for even and \(\lambda^{-2}\) for odd \(\lambda\). Check: yes, yes, no, no. (Negligible functions)







TipSolution





Each case compares \(\mu(\lambda)\) with \(\lambda^{-c}\), as Equation 8.5 asks: is \(\mu(\lambda) < \lambda^{-c}\) for all large \(\lambda\), for every \(c > 0\)?
\(\lambda^{-\log_2\log_2\lambda}\): yes.

Both sides are powers of \(\lambda\). For \(\lambda > 1\), \(\lambda^{-a} < \lambda^{-c}\) exactly when \(a > c\).
So the condition is \(\log_2\log_2\lambda > c\), that is \(\lambda > 2^{2^c}\).
For every \(c\) there is such a \(\lambda_0 = 2^{2^c} + 1\), so the function is negligible.

It is negligible only barely. Against \(\lambda^{-10}\) it needs \(\lambda > 2^{1024}\), and at \(\lambda = 128\) it equals \(128^{-\log_2 7} = 2^{-19.65}\), larger than the non-negligible \(\lambda^{-10} = 2^{-70}\).
\(2^{-(\log_2\lambda)^2}\): yes. Write \(2^{-(\log_2\lambda)^2} = (2^{\log_2\lambda})^{-\log_2\lambda} = \lambda^{-\log_2\lambda}\). This is example 2 of the chapter: it is below \(\lambda^{-c}\) for all \(\lambda > 2^c\).
\(1/\lambda^{100}\): no. Take \(c = 101\). Then \(\lambda^{-100} < \lambda^{-101}\) would need \(\lambda < 1\), which never holds for \(\lambda \ge 1\). One exponent \(c\) that fails is enough.
\(2^{-\lambda}\) for even, \(\lambda^{-2}\) for odd \(\lambda\): no.

Take \(c = 3\). The definition needs \(\mu(\lambda) < \lambda^{-3}\) for every \(\lambda \ge \lambda_0\).
For every odd \(\lambda \ge 1\), \(\mu(\lambda) = \lambda^{-2} \ge \lambda^{-3}\).
Odd numbers exceed every \(\lambda_0\), so no \(\lambda_0\) works.

A function is negligible only if it is small for all large \(\lambda\), not just for most of them: one bad subsequence is enough for an adversary to win on those parameters.

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
8.2 Hybrids for TV

Exercise 2. Hybrids for TV. Prove \(\mathrm{TV}(P^{\otimes m}, Q^{\otimes m}) \le m\,\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\) directly with the chain \(H_i\) and Fact 3. Then show that for two coins the true value grows like \(\sqrt m\) when \(\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\) is small. (Hybrid argument)







TipSolution





The bound. \(\mathrm{TV}\) is the TV distance of Fact 2.

Hybrids. Let \(H_i = (Q_1, \dots, Q_i, P_{i+1}, \dots, P_m)\): \(m\) independent entries, the first \(i\) drawn from \(Q\) and the rest from \(P\). Then \(H_0 = P^{\otimes m}\) and \(H_m = Q^{\otimes m}\).
Fix a distinguisher. Let \(A\) be any distinguisher on \(m\)-tuples, randomized or not, with no limit on its running time.
One step changes one entry. \(H_{i-1}\) and \(H_i\) differ only in entry \(i\): \(P\) in \(H_{i-1}\), \(Q\) in \(H_i\). The other \(m - 1\) entries have the same distribution in both, and are independent of entry \(i\). Condition on their values \(w\). Then \(A(\dots)\) becomes a distinguisher \(A_w\) that sees only entry \(i\), so by Fact 2 \[\big|\Pr[A(H_{i-1}) = 1 \mid w] - \Pr[A(H_i) = 1 \mid w]\big| = \mathrm{Adv}_{A_w}(P, Q) \le \mathrm{TV}(P, Q). \tag{8.1}\]
Average over \(w\). The two conditional probabilities are averaged with the same weights in both hybrids, so the triangle inequality gives \(\mathrm{Adv}_A(H_{i-1}, H_i) \le \mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\).
Chain. By Fact 3, \(\mathrm{Adv}_A(H_0, H_m) \le \sum_{i=1}^m\mathrm{Adv}_A(H_{i-1}, H_i) \le m\,\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\).
Take the best \(A\). By Fact 2 the best unbounded distinguisher attains \(\mathrm{TV}(H_0, H_m)\). Step 5 holds for it too, so \(\mathrm{TV}(P^{\otimes m}, Q^{\otimes m}) \le m\,\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\).

The true growth for two coins. Let \(P\) be a coin with heads probability \(\frac12 + \delta\) and \(Q\) a fair coin, so \(\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \delta\).

Only the count matters. A sequence \(\omega\) with \(k\) heads has \(P^{\otimes m}(\omega) = (\frac12 + \delta)^k(\frac12 - \delta)^{m - k}\) and \(Q^{\otimes m}(\omega) = 2^{-m}\), which depend on \(\omega\) only through \(k\). In \(\mathrm{TV} = \frac12\sum_\omega|P^{\otimes m}(\omega) - Q^{\otimes m}(\omega)|\) (Equation 3.20), group the \(\binom mk\) sequences with \(k\) heads. Each group contributes \(\frac12|\mathrm{Bin}(m, \frac12 + \delta)(k) - \mathrm{Bin}(m, \frac12)(k)|\), so the TV distance between the tuples equals the TV distance between the two head counts.
Normal approximation. The biased count has mean \(\frac m2 + m\delta\) and variance \(m(\frac14 - \delta^2) \approx \frac m4\). The fair count has mean \(\frac m2\) and variance \(\frac m4\). For large \(m\) both are close to normal with standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt m/2\).
TV between two normals. In Divergences, two normals with the same \(\sigma\) and means \(s\) apart have \(\mathrm{TV} = 2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\) with \(\mu = s/\sigma\). Here \(s = m\delta\), so \(\mu/2 = m\delta/\sqrt m = \delta\sqrt m\) and \[\mathrm{TV}(P^{\otimes m}, Q^{\otimes m}) \approx 2\Phi(\delta\sqrt m) - 1. \tag{8.2}\]
Small argument. Near 0, \(\Phi(x) \approx \frac12 + x\varphi(0)\) with \(\varphi(0) = 1/\sqrt{2\pi}\). So while \(\delta\sqrt m\) is small, \(\mathrm{TV} \approx \sqrt{2/\pi}\,\delta\sqrt m \approx 0.80\,\delta\sqrt m\): it grows like \(\sqrt m\), not like \(m\).

Table 8.1 compares the exact TV distance with both approximations and with the hybrid bound, for \(\delta = 0.01\).

The normal approximation is poor only at \(m = 1\), where the count is a single coin flip and the bound \(m\delta\) is exact. The linear form overshoots once \(\delta\sqrt m\) is no longer small, because \(2\Phi(x) - 1\) bends over towards 1.

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
8.3 The best threshold

Exercise 3. The best threshold. For \(m\) flips of a \((\frac12 + \delta)\)-coin against a fair coin, show that the likelihood ratio is increasing in the number of heads, so the best test is a threshold, and find where the two binomial probabilities cross. Check: about \(m/2 + m\delta/2\); for \(m = 10{,}000\) and \(\delta = 0.01\) the best advantage is 0.683. (Distinguishers and TV)







TipSolution






Likelihood ratio. For a sequence with \(k\) heads, divide the two probabilities from Exercise 2: \[L(k) = \frac{(\frac12 + \delta)^k(\frac12 - \delta)^{m - k}}{2^{-m}} = (1 + 2\delta)^k(1 - 2\delta)^{m - k}. \tag{8.3}\]
It increases in \(k\). One more head multiplies it by \(L(k + 1)/L(k) = (1 + 2\delta)/(1 - 2\delta) > 1\) for \(\delta > 0\).
The best test is a threshold. By Fact 2, the best distinguisher outputs 1 exactly where the biased coin’s probability is larger, that is where \(L(k) > 1\). Since \(L\) increases, this set is \(\{k > k^*\}\) for the \(k^*\) with \(L(k^*) = 1\).
Where the binomials cross. The binomial probabilities are \(\binom mk\) times the sequence probabilities. The factor \(\binom mk\) is the same for both, so they cross at the same \(k^*\). Take logarithms of \(L(k^*) = 1\): \[k^*\ln(1 + 2\delta) + (m - k^*)\ln(1 - 2\delta) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k^* = m\,\frac{-\ln(1 - 2\delta)}{\ln(1 + 2\delta) - \ln(1 - 2\delta)}. \tag{8.4}\]
Expand for small \(\delta\). With \(u = 2\delta\), \(-\ln(1 - u) = u + \frac{u^2}2 + \frac{u^3}3 + \dots\) and \(\ln(1 + u) - \ln(1 - u) = 2u + \frac{2u^3}3 + \dots\). The ratio is \[\frac{1 + \frac u2 + \frac{u^2}3}{2(1 + \frac{u^2}3)} = \frac12 + \frac u4 + O(u^3) = \frac12 + \frac\delta2 + O(\delta^3). \tag{8.5}\] So \(k^* = \frac m2 + \frac{m\delta}2 + O(m\delta^3)\): halfway between the fair mean \(\frac m2\) and the biased mean \(\frac m2 + m\delta\).
The numbers. For \(m = 10{,}000\) and \(\delta = 0.01\), the exact crossing is \(k^* = 5050.0033\), against \(m/2 + m\delta/2 = 5050\). The test “output 1 iff \(k > k^*\)” has advantage 0.6827, equal to the exact TV distance 0.6827, which rounds to the check value 0.683.
Normal check. The threshold sits \(\frac{m\delta}2 = 50 = 1\cdot\sigma\) from each mean (\(\sigma = \sqrt m/2 = 50\)). So the advantage is about \(\Phi(1) - (1 - \Phi(1)) = 2\Phi(1) - 1 = 0.6827\).

Majority vote is the threshold at \(\frac m2\) instead of \(k^*\). Its exact advantage is 0.4807, which matches the 0.481 simulated in Table 8.4. The fair count lands above \(\frac m2\) almost half the time, so moving the threshold up by one standard deviation gains a lot.
The best distinguisher is a likelihood-ratio test, and for coins that test is a threshold on the head count, placed midway between the two means.

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
8.4 Birthday for 32 bits

Exercise 4. Birthday for 32 bits. How many random 32-bit identifiers can you draw before a collision has probability \(\frac12\)? Check: \(\sqrt{2\cdot2^{32}\ln 2} \approx 77{,}000\). (Birthday bound)







TipSolution






Set up. \(N = 2^{32}\) possible identifiers, \(q\) independent uniform draws.
Use the lower bound as an approximation. By Equation 8.9, \(\Pr[\text{collision}] \ge 1 - e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)}\). For \(q \ll N\) this is close to exact: the only step that lost anything was \(1 - i/N \le e^{-i/N}\), and \(i/N\) is tiny here.
Solve for \(\frac12\). \(1 - e^{-q^2/(2N)} = \frac12\) gives \(q^2/(2N) = \ln 2\), so \[q = \sqrt{2N\ln 2} = \sqrt{2\cdot 2^{32}\cdot 0.6931} = 77{,}162.7. \tag{8.6}\] This is \(1.18\sqrt N\) with \(\sqrt N = 65{,}536\).
Exact check. The script evaluates the exact product \(1 - \prod_{i<q}(1 - i/N)\) and finds that it first reaches \(\frac12\) at \(q = 77{,}164\).

So about 77,000 identifiers, in agreement with the check. A table of 100,000 records with random 32-bit keys is already past this point, which is why Table 8.5 finds a collision probability of 0.688.
Random \(\kappa\)-bit values collide after about \(2^{\kappa/2}\) draws: 32-bit identifiers are safe only for tables of a few thousand rows.

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
8.5 Two-time pad

Exercise 5. Two-time pad. Two messages of English text are encrypted with the same pad. Show what an eavesdropper learns, and why guessing a common word in one message reveals the other at the same position. (Perfect secrecy)







TipSolution





What the eavesdropper learns.

It sees \(c_1 = m_1 \oplus K\) and \(c_2 = m_2 \oplus K\), byte by byte.
Combine them with \(\oplus\). Since \(K \oplus K = 0\), \(c_1 \oplus c_2 = m_1 \oplus m_2\). The pad cancels.
That is all it learns. By Fact 4, \(c_1\) alone is uniform whatever \(m_1\) is. Given \(c_1\), the second ciphertext is \(c_2 = c_1 \oplus (m_1 \oplus m_2)\), fixed. So the pair is \((U, U \oplus (m_1 \oplus m_2))\) with \(U\) uniform. A simulator that receives \(L = m_1 \oplus m_2\) outputs exactly this distribution, so by Equation 8.12 the pair reveals nothing beyond \(m_1 \oplus m_2\).

But \(m_1 \oplus m_2\) is a lot. Perfect secrecy needed a fresh uniform key per message. With the pad reused, the “key” of the second message is the first message, which is English text and far from uniform.
Why a guessed word reveals the other message. Suppose you guess that \(m_1\) contains the word \(w\) at position \(j\). Combine \(w\) with \(c_1 \oplus c_2\) at that position: \[(c_1 \oplus c_2)[j..] \oplus w = m_1[j..] \oplus m_2[j..] \oplus w = m_2[j..] \quad\text{if } m_1[j..] = w. \tag{8.7}\] If the guess is right, you read the other message at the same position. If it is wrong, you get \(m_2 \oplus m_1 \oplus w\), which is usually gibberish. You slide the guess along every position (crib dragging) and keep the positions where readable text comes out. The guess works in both directions: if \(w\) is in \(m_2\) instead, the same step reveals \(m_1\).
The script does this with \(m_1\) set to “meet me at the north gate” and \(m_2\) to “the password is blue fish”, both encrypted under one random pad, and the guess “the” (with its trailing space). Only three positions give lowercase letters and spaces; Table 8.2 lists them.



Table 8.2: Crib dragging the guess “the” across \(c_1 \oplus c_2\) for two 25-byte messages under one pad (seed 0).










Position \(j\)
\((c_1 \oplus c_2)[j..] \oplus\) “the”
Explanation

From “d is” an attacker guesses “password is” and extends both messages a few letters at a time. The false alarm at 17 dies as soon as it is extended, because “jih” does not continue into English.
Perfect secrecy holds for one message per key; reuse leaks \(m_1 \oplus m_2\), and the redundancy of natural language turns that into both plaintexts.

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
8.6 Toy GGM

Exercise 6. Toy GGM. Implement the GGM tree with SHA-256 as a length-doubling generator (\(G_0(s) = \mathrm{SHA256}(s\,\|\,0)\), \(G_1(s) = \mathrm{SHA256}(s\,\|\,1)\)). How many generator calls does one evaluation on \(n\)-bit inputs cost, and what does the proof lose? Check: \(n\) calls; the loss factor is \(nq\). (PRFs)







TipSolution





Implementation. A seed is 32 bytes and each half \(G_b\) returns 32 bytes, so \(G = G_0\,\|\,G_1\) maps 32 bytes to 64: a length-doubling pseudorandom generator (PRG), in the toy model where the hash is treated as one. The tree walk is three lines:
def ggm_eval(gen: CountingGenerator, key: bytes, bits: list[int]) -> bytes:
    node = key
    for b in bits:
        node = gen.half(node, b)  # G_b(node) = SHA256(node || b), counted
    return node
Cost. The walk visits one node per level and computes only the half \(G_{x_i}\) it follows. So one evaluation costs \(n\) generator calls (one hash each). The script counts them: on \(n = 8\) bits, each evaluation makes 8 calls. Evaluating all 256 inputs gives 256 distinct outputs, with a fraction 0.5001 of 1 bits, and re-evaluating an input gives the same output, as a function must.
What the proof loses. Follow the proof sketch in the chapter:

There are \(n + 1\) hybrids \(H_0, \dots, H_n\), where \(H_j\) makes every node at depth \(j\) uniform. \(H_0\) is \(F_k\) and \(H_n\) is a random function.
A \(q\)-query adversary touches at most \(q\) nodes at each depth. Telling \(H_{j-1}\) from \(H_j\) is telling \(q\) outputs of \(G\) from \(q\) uniform strings, which by the hybrid lemma costs at most \(q\cdot\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}\).
Summing the \(n\) steps with Fact 3 gives \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} \le nq\cdot\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}\): a loss factor \(nq\).

Concretely, with \(n = 128\) input bits and \(q = 2^{40}\) queries, \(nq = 2^7\cdot2^{40} = 2^{47}\). For a PRF advantage of at most \(2^{-64}\) the generator must have advantage at most \(2^{-111}\): the reduction costs 47 bits of security.
The GGM tree turns any length-doubling generator into a PRF at \(n\) generator calls per input, but the reduction is loose by \(nq\), so the generator needs a large security margin.

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
8.7 Threshold sharing

Exercise 7. Threshold sharing. In Shamir’s 2-out-of-3 scheme over prime \(\mathbb Z_p\), the dealer picks a uniform \(c\) and gives holder \(i\) the value \(x + ci\). Show by counting that any single share is uniform, and that any two shares determine \(x\). (Simulation by counting)







TipSolution





Holders are numbered \(i = 1, 2, 3\), and \(p > 3\) so that these are distinct and nonzero mod \(p\).
Any single share is uniform.

Fix the secret \(x\) and a holder \(i\). The share \(s_i = x + ci \bmod p\) is a function of the randomness \(c\) alone.
Because \(p\) is prime and \(i \ne 0 \bmod p\), \(i\) has an inverse mod \(p\). For any value \(y\), the equation \(x + ci = y\) has exactly one solution, \(c = (y - x)\,i^{-1}\).
So \(c \mapsto x + ci\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb Z_p\), and by Fact 4 the share is uniform: each value has probability \(1/p\), whatever \(x\) is.
The simulator for one holder, with no leakage, outputs a uniform element of \(\mathbb Z_p\), and Equation 8.12 holds with \(\equiv\).

Table 8.3 walks the count for \(p = 5\) and \(x = 2\): each holder’s column is a permutation of \(\mathbb Z_5\).
