Any two shares determine \(x\).

Holders \(i \ne j\) have \(s_i = x + ci\) and \(s_j = x + cj\). Subtract: \(s_i - s_j = c(i - j)\).
\(i - j \ne 0 \bmod p\), so \(c = (s_i - s_j)(i - j)^{-1}\).
Then \(x = s_i - ci\).

With \(p = 5\), take holders 1 and 3 with \(s_1 = 4\) and \(s_3 = 3\) (the row \(c = 2\)). Then \(s_3 - s_1 = -1 \equiv 4\) and \((3 - 1)^{-1} = 2^{-1} = 3\) (since \(2\cdot3 = 6 \equiv 1\)), so \(c = 4\cdot 3 = 12 \equiv 2\) and \(x = s_1 - c = 4 - 2 = 2\). The script checks exhaustively for \(p = 5\) and \(p = 7\) that every single share is uniform for every \(x\) and that every pair of shares gives back \(x\) for every \(x\) and \(c\).
Geometrically, the shares are points on the line \(y = x + ct\) at \(t = 1, 2, 3\), and \(x\) is its value at \(t = 0\). One point lies on exactly one line through each possible intercept, so it says nothing. Two points fix the line.
Counting shows perfect security for one share; two shares are not uniform on \(\mathbb Z_p^2\), since they lie on a line through the secret.

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
8.8 Regev’s budget

Exercise 8. Regev’s budget. Using the normal approximation, find the \(k\) at which the failure rate for \(p = 4096\), \(B = 32\) reaches 1%. Then change the script’s error distribution to a rounded normal with \(\sigma = 3.2\) and redo it. Check for the first part: \(1024^2/(2.576^2\cdot352) \approx 450\). (Noise growth)







TipSolution





Uniform errors on \(\{-32, \dots, 32\}\).

Variance of one error. \(B(B + 1)/3 = 32\cdot33/3 = 352\), as in the chapter.
Variance of the sum. The \(k\) errors are independent, so their sum has variance \(352k\) and is close to normal.
Failure event. Decryption fails when the summed error leaves \((-p/4, p/4) = (-1024, 1024)\). Ignoring the wrap-around mod \(p\), which only matters near failure rate \(\frac12\), \[\Pr[\text{failure}] \approx \Pr\big[|Z| > 1024/\sqrt{352k}\big], \qquad Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1). \tag{8.8}\]
Set it to 1%. \(\Pr[|Z| > z] = 0.01\) at \(z = 2.576\). So \(1024/\sqrt{352k} = 2.576\), and \[k = \frac{1024^2}{2.576^2\cdot352} = 449.0. \tag{8.9}\] The wrapped approximation used by the chapter’s script, solved over the integers, gives the same \(k = 449\). Adding 449 real toy ciphertexts 20,000 times, the script measures a failure rate of 0.0109, within sampling noise (about 0.0007) of 1%.

Rounded normal errors with \(\sigma = 3.2\). In the solutions script the error sampler is a parameter. The new one rounds \(\mathcal N(0, 3.2^2)\) to the nearest integer.

Variance. Rounding adds roughly \(\frac1{12}\) to the variance. Summing \(j^2\Pr[\mathrm{round}(X) = j]\) exactly gives \(10.3233\), against \(3.2^2 + \frac1{12} = 10.3233\) to this precision.
Same formula. \(k = 1024^2/(2.576^2\cdot10.3233) = 15{,}309\), and the wrapped approximation gives the same integer.
Simulation. Adding 15,309 ciphertexts, 20,000 times, gives a failure rate of 0.0111.

The smaller error buys 34 times as many additions, which is the ratio of the variances, \(352/10.3233\). The budget scales like \((p/\sigma)^2\): halving the error standard deviation buys four times as many additions.
There is no worst-case analogue of Equation 8.16 for a rounded normal, because its support is unbounded; one bounds it by a tail cut instead, such as \(|e| \le 6\sigma\), at a tiny failure probability.
Under random errors the noise budget is set by the variance, not the bound: \(k \approx (p/4)^2/(z^2\sigma^2)\) additions for failure rate \(\Pr[|Z| > z]\).

title: 8  Exercises: Cryptography basics
text:
8.9 Odd modulus

Exercise 9. Odd modulus. Modify the addition experiment to use a prime \(p\) and the encoding \(\lfloor p/2\rfloor\). Measure the extra drift and compare with the prediction of about \(-k/4\). (LWE arithmetic)







TipSolution





Prediction.

Write \(p = 2\Delta + 1\), so the encoding is \(\Delta = \lfloor p/2\rfloor\) and \(2\Delta = p - 1 \equiv -1\).
The sum. As in the derivation of Equation 8.16, the summed ciphertext decrypts to \(v = \sum_i e_i + w\Delta \bmod p\), where \(w = \sum_i m_i\) is the number of 1-bits.
Split \(w\). \(w = (w \bmod 2) + 2\lfloor w/2\rfloor\), so \[w\Delta = (w \bmod 2)\,\Delta + \lfloor w/2\rfloor\cdot 2\Delta \equiv (w \bmod 2)\,\Delta - \lfloor w/2\rfloor. \tag{8.10}\] The first term is the correct encoding of the parity. The second is an extra error of \(-\lfloor w/2\rfloor\): every pair of 1-bits adds \(-1\).
Its mean. For random bits, \(w \sim \mathrm{Bin}(k, \frac12)\), with \(\mathbb E w = k/2\). Also \(\Pr[w \text{ even}] - \Pr[w \text{ odd}] = \mathbb E(-1)^w = (\frac12 - \frac12)^k = 0\) for \(k \ge 1\), so \(\Pr[w \text{ odd}] = \frac12\). Hence \[\mathbb E\lfloor w/2\rfloor = \frac{\mathbb E w - \Pr[w \text{ odd}]}{2} = \frac{k - 1}4, \qquad \text{drift} = -\frac{k - 1}4. \tag{8.11}\] This is the “about \(-k/4\)” of the exercise, exact up to the \(\frac14\).

Measurement. The script repeats the addition experiment with the prime \(p = 4093\) (the largest prime below 4096), errors uniform on \(\{-32, \dots, 32\}\), \(d = 4\) and 20,000 trials. It computes the drift as \(v - \sum_i e_i - (w \bmod 2)\Delta\), centred in \((-p/2, p/2]\), and also reruns \(p = 4096\) for comparison. The normal approximation for the odd modulus shifts the mean of the summed error by the predicted drift. Table 8.4 has the results.

It costs correctness. The drift grows like \(k\), the random part only like \(\sqrt k\). At \(k = 1024\) the drift (\(-256\)) is already 0.43 standard deviations of the random part (\(\sqrt{352\cdot1024} = 600\)), and the failure rate rises from 0.0873 to 0.1167. 9.1 Winning with a prior
Exercises for Threat models and privacy games, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part02-attacks/solutions_threat_models.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/solutions_threat_models.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(b = 1\) is the world where the target is in the data, with view distribution \(Q\); \(b = 0\) is the other world, with view distribution \(P\). An attack’s true positive rate (TPR) is \(\Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 1]\), its false positive rate (FPR) is \(\Pr[b' = 1 \mid b = 0]\), and its advantage is \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\). The total variation (TV) distance and the hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma\) are those of Divergences.
crumbs: 9  Exercises: Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Exercises: Threat models and privacy games
text:
Exercise 1. Winning with a prior. In a two-world game with prior \(\pi_1\) on \(b = 1\), show that no attack wins with probability more than \(\max(\pi_0, \pi_1) + \min(\pi_0, \pi_1)\,\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\). Hint: start from Equation 9.10 and use \(E_\gamma \le E_1\) for \(\gamma \ge 1\). Check: for the noisy count with \(\sigma = 1\) and \(\pi_1 = 0.1\), the bound is \(0.9 + 0.1 \times 0.3829 = 0.9383\), against the exact best 0.9013. (Bayes-optimal guess, hockey-stick)







TipSolution






Case \(\pi_1 \le \frac12\). By Equation 9.10 the best attack wins with probability \(\pi_0 + \pi_1E_\gamma(Q\|P)\) with \(\gamma = \pi_0/\pi_1 \ge 1\).
\(E_\gamma\) is non-increasing in \(\gamma\). For every event \(A\) and \(\gamma \ge 1\), \(Q(A) - \gamma P(A) \le Q(A) - P(A)\), because \(P(A) \ge 0\). Maximizing both sides over \(A\) gives \(E_\gamma(Q\|P) \le E_1(Q\|P) = \mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\).
Combine. The best winning probability is at most \(\pi_0 + \pi_1\mathrm{TV}\), and here \(\pi_0 = \max(\pi_0, \pi_1)\), \(\pi_1 = \min(\pi_0, \pi_1)\).
Case \(\pi_1 > \frac12\). Rename the worlds: call \(b = 0\) the “positive” one. The game is the same, with prior \(\pi_0 < \frac12\) on the renamed positive world and the roles of \(P\) and \(Q\) swapped. TV is symmetric, so step 3 gives \(\pi_1 + \pi_0\mathrm{TV}\), again \(\max + \min\cdot\mathrm{TV}\).
Check. With \(\pi_1 = \frac12\) the bound is \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV} = 0.6915\) for the noisy count, and it is attained. With \(\pi_1 = 0.1\) it is \(0.9 + 0.1 \times 0.3829 = 0.9383\), while the exact best is \(0.9013\).

The bound is loose for skewed priors because it uses the likelihood-ratio threshold 1, while the best attack needs a ratio above 9 before it overrules the prior. Few views carry that much evidence.

title: 9  Exercises: Threat models and privacy games
section: 9.2 The exact count in an unknown crowd
text:
9.2 The exact count in an unknown crowd

Exercise 2. The exact count in an unknown crowd. Show that \(\mathrm{TV}\big(\mathrm{Binomial}(m, \frac12), 1 + \mathrm{Binomial}(m, \frac12)\big) = \binom{m}{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}2^{-m}\), and use Stirling’s formula to show it is about \(\sqrt{2/(\pi m)}\). Hint: write the sum \(\sum_k(q_k - p_k)_+\) with \(q_k = p_{k-1}\), and notice it telescopes. Check: 0.0796 for \(m = 100\), against \(\sqrt{2/(100\pi)} = 0.0798\). (TV, average case)







TipSolution






The two distributions. Let \(p_k = \binom mk2^{-m}\) for \(0 \le k \le m\) and \(p_k = 0\) otherwise. Without the target the count is \(k\) with probability \(p_k\); with it, with probability \(q_k = p_{k-1}\).
Where \(q\) beats \(p\). \(p_k/p_{k-1} = (m - k + 1)/k\), which is below 1 exactly when \(k > (m + 1)/2\). So \(q_k > p_k\) exactly for \(k \ge j := \lfloor (m + 1)/2\rfloor + 1\), up to \(k = m + 1\).
Telescope. \(\mathrm{TV} = \sum_{k \ge j}(p_{k-1} - p_k) = p_{j-1} - p_{m+1} = p_{\lfloor(m+1)/2\rfloor}\).
The central weight. For even \(m\), \(\lfloor (m+1)/2\rfloor = m/2\). For odd \(m\) it is \((m+1)/2 = \lceil m/2\rceil\), and \(\binom{m}{\lceil m/2\rceil} = \binom{m}{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\). Either way \(\mathrm{TV} = \binom{m}{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}2^{-m}\).
Stirling. For \(m = 2j\), \(n! \approx \sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n\) gives \(\binom{2j}{j} \approx \frac{\sqrt{4\pi j}(2j/e)^{2j}}{2\pi j(j/e)^{2j}} = \frac{4^j}{\sqrt{\pi j}}\), so \(\mathrm{TV} \approx 1/\sqrt{\pi j} = \sqrt{2/(\pi m)}\).
Check. Summing \(\frac12\sum_k|p_k - q_k|\) directly and taking the central weight both give 0.2461 for \(m = 10\) and 0.0796 for \(m = 100\). Stirling gives 0.2523 and 0.0798.

Knowing the other records turns this TV from 0.08 into 1: the exact count reveals the target’s presence completely. Only the adversary’s ignorance hides it.

title: 9  Exercises: Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.3 How large a crowd?

Exercise 3. How large a crowd? With \(\sigma = 1\) and \(m\) unknown other bits, how large must \(m\) be for the average-case membership advantage on the noisy count to drop to 0.05? Use the normal approximation, then check with the exact formula. Check: about \(m = 250\). (Mixing, normal approximation)







TipSolution






Normal approximation. The unknown count \(K \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(m, \frac12)\) has variance \(m/4\). Treating it as normal, the release is \(\mathcal N(\frac m2, s^2)\) against \(\mathcal N(\frac m2 + 1, s^2)\) with \(s^2 = m/4 + \sigma^2\), and the TV is \(2\Phi(1/(2s)) - 1\).
Solve for \(s\). \(2\Phi(1/(2s)) - 1 = 0.05\) means \(\Phi(1/(2s)) = 0.525\), so \(1/(2s) = \Phi^{-1}(0.525) = 0.06271\) and \(s = 7.974\), \(s^2 = 63.58\).
Solve for \(m\). \(m = 4(s^2 - \sigma^2) = 4(63.58 - 1) = 250.3\).
Exact check. Computing the exact average-case TV of the chapter for each \(m\), the smallest \(m\) with TV at most 0.05 is \(m = 250\), where TV is 0.0500. The normal approximation also gives 0.0500 there.

To get the same advantage against an adversary who knows the other records, the noise alone would need \(\sigma = s = 7.97\): the 250 unknown records supply the rest of the variance. That protection disappears the moment the adversary learns them.

title: 9  Exercises: Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.4 Reconstruction from one count

Exercise 4. Reconstruction from one count. Prove that the best reconstruction of \(m\) uniform bits from their exact sum recovers an expected fraction \(\mathbb E[\max(K, m - K)]/m\) with \(K \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(m, \frac12)\). Compute it by hand for \(m = 1, 2, 3\). Check: 1, 0.75, 0.75; and 0.6230 for \(m = 10\). (Reconstruction game, posterior)







TipSolution






Score by bits. A reconstruction is a guess \(x'_1, \dots, x'_m\) that may depend on \(K\). Its expected gain is \(\frac1m\sum_i\Pr[x'_i = x_i]\), so each bit can be optimized separately.
Posterior of a bit. Given \(K = k\), all \(\binom mk\) arrangements are equally likely, and bit \(i\) is 1 in \(\binom{m-1}{k-1}\) of them. So \(\Pr[x_i = 1 \mid K = k] = \binom{m-1}{k-1}/\binom mk = k/m\).
Best guess. Guess 1 if \(k/m > \frac12\), else 0 (at \(k = m/2\) both are equally good). The expected number of correct bits given \(K = k\) is \(\max(k, m - k)\). Averaging over \(K\) gives the claim.
By hand.

For \(m = 1\) the count is the record. From \(m = 2\) on, one count says less and less about each bit, and the gain over guessing shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{2\pi m}\).

title: 9  Exercises: Threat models and privacy games
section: 9.5 Releasing a record from a small domain
text:
9.5 Releasing a record from a small domain

Exercise 5. Releasing a record from a small domain. Redo the random-record release when records are uniform on only \(v\) values, so that a non-member can collide with the released record. Find TPR, FPR and the precision at a fair prior. Check: for \(n = v = 1000\), \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.001999\), \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.001\), precision 0.6666. (Membership game, precision)







TipSolution






FPR. If \(z \notin D\), the released record is an independent uniform value, equal to \(z\) with probability \(1/v\).
TPR. If \(z \in D\), the target itself is released with probability \(1/n\). Otherwise (probability \(1 - 1/n\)) another record is released, which equals \(z\) with probability \(1/v\). So \(\mathrm{TPR} = \frac1n + (1 - \frac1n)\frac1v\).
Advantage. \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} = \frac1n - \frac1{nv} = \frac1n(1 - \frac1v)\).
Precision at a fair prior. By Equation 9.13, \(\mathrm{TPR}/(\mathrm{TPR} + \mathrm{FPR})\).
Check. With \(n = v = 1000\): \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.001 + 0.999 \times 0.001 = 0.001999\), \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.001\), advantage 0.000999, precision \(0.001999/0.002999 = 0.6666\). Two million simulated games per world give \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.001945\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.001004\).

Collisions with common values give the target deniability: seeing their value released is now only 2-to-1 evidence. With distinct records (\(v \to \infty\)) the precision is 1.

title: 9  Exercises: Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.6 The inner-product attack

Exercise 6. The inner-product attack. For the centroid detector, the attack “say member when \(\langle z, \theta\rangle\) is large” uses only the inner product. Compute the mean and variance of \(\langle z, \theta\rangle\) in both worlds, approximate both by normals, and show that the best advantage is about \(2\Phi\big(\frac12\sqrt{d/n}\big) - 1\). Check: 0.2763 for \(n = 100\), \(d = 50\); the simulated attack gets 0.2771, and the likelihood-ratio attack of Table 9.4 0.2789. (Gaussian approximation, access levels)







TipSolution






Member world. \(\theta = (z + S)/n\) with \(S \sim \mathcal N(0, (n - 1)I_d)\) independent of \(z \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\), so \(\langle z, \theta\rangle = \|z\|^2/n + \langle z, S\rangle/n\).

Mean: \(\mathbb E\|z\|^2 = d\) and \(\mathbb E\langle z, S\rangle = 0\), so the mean is \(d/n\).
Variance: \(\operatorname{Var}\|z\|^2 = 2d\) (a chi-square with \(d\) degrees of freedom). Given \(z\), \(\langle z, S\rangle \sim \mathcal N(0, (n-1)\|z\|^2)\), so its variance is \((n - 1)d\), and it is uncorrelated with \(\|z\|^2\) because its conditional mean is 0. Total: \((2d + (n-1)d)/n^2\).

Non-member world. \(\theta \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d/n)\) independent of \(z\). Given \(z\), \(\langle z, \theta\rangle \sim \mathcal N(0, \|z\|^2/n)\): mean 0, variance \(d/n\).
Numbers. For \(n = 100\), \(d = 50\): mean 0.5 against 0; standard deviations 0.7106 and 0.7071.
Normal approximation. Both standard deviations are about \(\sqrt{d/n}\) (the member variance is \((n+1)d/n^2 \approx d/n\)). Two normals with equal spread \(\sqrt{d/n}\) and means \(d/n\) apart are a Gaussian pair with standardized shift \(\mu = (d/n)/\sqrt{d/n} = \sqrt{d/n}\), whose TV is \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\) (Divergences). The best threshold attack on the score reaches it.
Check. \(2\Phi(\frac12\sqrt{0.5}) - 1 = 0.2763\). Simulating the attack over 100,000 games per world gives 0.2771. The likelihood-ratio attack (0.2789) also uses \(\|\theta\|^2\) and the target-dependent threshold, which adds a little.

The advantage depends on \(d/n\), the number of parameters per training record. That ratio, not the model’s accuracy, decides how much one record moves the model. Lower bounds in Part 3 turn this attack into a limit on what any defence can achieve.

text:
9.7 Mixing hides

Exercise 7. Mixing hides. One other record with a uniform bit \(\vartheta\); the mechanism releases the exact count \(\vartheta + b\). Compute the best advantage of an adversary who knows \(\vartheta\) and of one who does not, and check them against Equation 9.6. Check: 1 and 0.5. (Fact 3)







TipSolution






Knowing \(\vartheta\). For each \(\vartheta\), the release is \(\vartheta\) when \(b = 0\) and \(\vartheta + 1\) when \(b = 1\): two point masses at different places. \(\mathrm{TV}(P_\vartheta, Q_\vartheta) = 1\), and the attack “say member when the count exceeds \(\vartheta\)” is always right.
Not knowing \(\vartheta\). With \(b = 0\) the count is 0 or 1 with probability \(\frac12\) each; with \(b = 1\) it is 1 or 2.

title: 10  Exercises: Membership inference
text:
10.1 Accuracy with an unbalanced prior
Exercises for Membership inference, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part02-attacks/solutions_membership_inference.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/solutions_membership_inference.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(\phi = y\langle w, x\rangle\) is the logit of the model’s confidence in the true label, IN and OUT are the distributions of a record’s \(\phi\) over models trained with and without it, and an attack’s true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR) are measured over (target model, pool point) pairs of the running example. The likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) is the per-example test of the chapter, and attacks are compared by their receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and the area under the curve (AUC). Exercises 1 and 7 reuse the chapter’s experiment with seed 0, so their numbers match the chapter’s tables; Exercise 6 draws a fresh pool.

title: 10  Exercises: Membership inference
text:
Exercise 1. Accuracy with an unbalanced prior. Suppose a fraction \(\pi_1\) of the queried records are members. Show that “member if correctly classified” has accuracy \(\pi_1(1 - e_{\mathrm{train}}) + (1 - \pi_1)e_{\mathrm{test}}\). With the running example’s errors, compare it with the trivial attack “always non-member” at \(\pi_1 = 0.5\) and \(\pi_1 = 0.1\). Check: 0.5584 against 0.5, and 0.3247 against 0.9. What does this say about reporting accuracy? (Fact 1, Yeom’s attack)







TipSolution






Condition on membership (Fact 1 of Threat models and privacy games): accuracy \(= \pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + (1 - \pi_1)(1 - \mathrm{FPR})\).
The rates of this attack. A member is flagged when it is classified correctly, so \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - e_{\mathrm{train}}\). A non-member is flagged when it is classified correctly, so \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - e_{\mathrm{test}}\) and \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} = e_{\mathrm{test}}\).
Substitute: accuracy \(= \pi_1(1 - e_{\mathrm{train}}) + (1 - \pi_1)e_{\mathrm{test}}\).
The running example has \(e_{\mathrm{train}} = 0.1495\) and \(e_{\mathrm{test}} = 0.2663\).

At \(\pi_1 = 0.5\): \(0.5 \times 0.8505 + 0.5 \times 0.2663 = 0.5584\), against 0.5 for “always non-member”. This is \(\frac12 + \frac12 \times 0.1168\), the advantage of the chapter.
At \(\pi_1 = 0.1\): \(0.1 \times 0.8505 + 0.9 \times 0.2663 = 0.3247\), against 0.9 for “always non-member”.


The attack has the same TPR and FPR in both cases; only the prior changed. At \(\pi_1 = 0.1\) it says “member” to 73% of non-members, and most queries are non-members, so its accuracy collapses below the trivial rule.
Accuracy mixes the attack with the prior. TPR and FPR do not depend on the prior, which is one more reason to report them, and to report them at a low FPR, where a “member” verdict stays reliable even when members are rare.

title: 10  Exercises: Membership inference
text:
10.2 The Gaussian likelihood ratio

Exercise 2. The Gaussian likelihood ratio. For \(H_0: \mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(H_1: \mathcal N(s, 1)\), show \(\ln\Lambda(t) = st - s^2/2\). Use it to find, for the two kinds of record of Table 10.2, the z-score cut that the threshold \(\ln\Lambda \ge 1.497\) puts on each kind, and check that the pooled FPR is \(10^{-3}\). Check: cuts 3.244 (typical) and 2.374 (atypical). (Neyman–Pearson, per-example calibration)







TipSolution






Write the log-densities. \(\ln\mathcal N(t; s, 1) = -\frac12(t - s)^2 - \frac12\ln(2\pi)\) and \(\ln\mathcal N(t; 0, 1) = -\frac12t^2 - \frac12\ln(2\pi)\).
Subtract. The constants cancel: \(\ln\Lambda(t) = -\frac12(t^2 - 2st + s^2) + \frac12t^2 = st - \frac{s^2}2\).
Spot checks (from the script, computing both forms): at \(t = 3.0902\), \(s = 0.5\) gives \(1.4201\) and \(s = 4\) gives \(4.3608\); at \(t = 1\), \(s = 4\) gives \(-4.0000\). The same z-score is strong evidence for a record with a large separation and weak evidence for one with a small separation.
Invert. For \(s > 0\), \(\ln\Lambda \ge c\) is the same as \(t \ge (c + s^2/2)/s\). With \(c = 1.497\):

typical records, \(s = 0.5\): \(t \ge (1.497 + 0.125)/0.5 = 3.244\);
atypical records, \(s = 4\): \(t \ge (1.497 + 8)/4 = 2.374\).

FPR of each kind. Under OUT, \(t \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\), so the FPRs are \(1 - \Phi(3.244) = 5.90\times10^{-4}\) and \(1 - \Phi(2.374) = 0.0088\).
Pool. \(0.95 \times 5.90\times10^{-4} + 0.05 \times 0.0088 = 0.0010\). The TPR is \(0.95\,(1 - \Phi(3.244 - 0.5)) + 0.05\,(1 - \Phi(2.374 - 4)) = 0.0503\), as in the chapter.

A single threshold on the likelihood ratio becomes a different z-score cut for each kind of record: stricter where the separation is small, looser where it is large. That is how the Neyman–Pearson test spends its FPR budget where it buys the most TPR.

title: 10  Exercises: Membership inference
text:
10.3 Same AUC, different exposure

Exercise 3. Same AUC, different exposure. Derive the AUC, best advantage and TPR at FPR \(\alpha\) of attacks A and B in Section 10.6, and repeat the comparison at \(q = 0.01\). Check: AUC 0.5050, \(\mu = 0.0177\), TPR at \(10^{-3}\) 0.01099 for A and 0.00106 for B. (AUC as a ranking probability, Gaussian trade-off)







TipSolution





Attack A.

AUC. The AUC is \(\Pr[\text{member's score} > \text{non-member's score}]\), with ties counted as one half. With probability \(q\) the member is exposed and wins outright; otherwise its score has the same distribution as the non-member’s and it wins half the time. So \(\mathrm{AUC} = q + \frac12(1 - q) = \frac12 + \frac q2\).
TPR. At a threshold with FPR \(\alpha\), the exposed members always pass and the rest pass with probability \(\alpha\): \(\mathrm{TPR} = q + (1 - q)\alpha\).
Best advantage. \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} = q(1 - \alpha)\), largest as \(\alpha \to 0\), where it tends to \(q\).

Attack B.

AUC. A member’s score minus a non-member’s is \(\mathcal N(\mu, 2)\), positive with probability \(\Phi(\mu/\sqrt2)\). Setting this equal to \(\frac12 + \frac q2\) gives \(\mu = \sqrt2\,\Phi^{-1}(\frac12 + \frac q2)\).
TPR is Equation 10.3 with \(s = \mu\), and the best advantage is the total variation between \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\).

Numbers at \(\alpha = 10^{-3}\) (Table 10.1):

title: 10  Exercises: Membership inference
text:
10.4 How many non-members?

Exercise 4. How many non-members? You want to claim, at 95% confidence, that an attack’s FPR is below \(\alpha\), and you see no false positives at all. How many non-members do you need for \(\alpha = 10^{-3}, 10^{-4}, 10^{-5}\)? Check: 2,995, 29,956 and 299,572. Hint: \((1 - \alpha)^n \le 0.05\). (Estimating rates from trials)







TipSolution






The event to rule out. If the true FPR were \(\alpha\) or more, then seeing zero false positives among \(n\) independent non-members would have probability at most \((1 - \alpha)^n\).
Make it unlikely. The one-sided 95% upper bound from zero counts (Hypothesis testing) is below \(\alpha\) exactly when \((1 - \alpha)^n \le 0.05\).
Solve. Take logarithms (both sides negative): \(n \ge \ln 0.05/\ln(1 - \alpha) = \ln 20/(-\ln(1 - \alpha))\).
Plug in. \(\alpha = 10^{-3}\): \(n \ge 2{,}994.2\), so 2,995. \(\alpha = 10^{-4}\): \(n \ge 29{,}955.8\), so 29,956. \(\alpha = 10^{-5}\): \(n \ge 299{,}571.7\), so 299,572. Each is about \(3/\alpha\), the rule of three.

The running example has 64,000 non-member pairs, so a threshold at FPR \(10^{-3}\) leaves about 64 false positives, enough for an interval of about \(\pm 25\%\) on the FPR (the chapter’s \([0.00077, 0.00128]\)). At FPR \(10^{-5}\) the same data could not even certify a bound. The pairs are also not fully independent: the same 1,000 points recur across the 128 target models, which is one more reason the interval is optimistic.
Every factor of ten lower in FPR costs a factor of ten more non-members. Reporting a TPR at FPR \(10^{-5}\) needs hundreds of thousands of non-member evaluations.

title: 10  Exercises: Membership inference
text:
10.5 Membership in a Gaussian mean

Exercise 5. Membership in a Gaussian mean. A “model” is the mean \(\hat\theta\) of \(n\) points drawn from \(\mathcal N(0, I_d)\). The attacker sees \(\hat\theta\) and a target \(z\), and uses \(T = \langle z, \hat\theta\rangle/(\|z\|/\sqrt n)\). Show that \(T \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) when \(z\) is not in the sample, and approximately \(\mathcal N(\sqrt{d/n}, 1)\) when it is. Deduce the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) for \(d = 1{,}000\) and \(n = 100\), and check it by simulation. Check: separation 3.1623, TPR 0.5287. Hint: given \(z\), \(\langle z, \sum_{j \ne i}x_j\rangle \sim \mathcal N(0, (n - 1)\|z\|^2)\), and \(\|z\|^2 \approx d\). (Per-example separation)







TipSolution






OUT. If \(z\) is not in the sample, \(\hat\theta = \frac1n\sum_jx_j\) is independent of \(z\) and \(\hat\theta \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d/n)\). Given \(z\), \(\langle z, \hat\theta\rangle\) is a linear combination of independent Gaussians, so it is \(\mathcal N(0, \|z\|^2/n)\). Dividing by \(\|z\|/\sqrt n\) gives \(T \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\), exactly, whatever \(z\) is.
IN. If \(z = x_i\), then \(\hat\theta = \frac1n\big(z + \sum_{j \ne i}x_j\big)\) and \[\langle z, \hat\theta\rangle = \frac{\|z\|^2}n + \frac1n\Big\langle z, \sum_{j \ne i}x_j\Big\rangle. \tag{10.1}\] Given \(z\), the second term is \(\mathcal N\big(0, (n - 1)\|z\|^2/n^2\big)\) by the hint.
Standardize. Divide by \(\|z\|/\sqrt n\): \(T = \|z\|/\sqrt n + \mathcal N\big(0, (n - 1)/n\big)\).
Approximate. \(\|z\|^2\) is a sum of \(d\) squared standard normals, with mean \(d\) and relative spread \(\sqrt{2/d}\), so \(\|z\|/\sqrt n \approx \sqrt{d/n}\). And \((n - 1)/n \approx 1\). So \(T \approx \mathcal N(\sqrt{d/n}, 1)\).
TPR. By Fact 2 of the chapter with separation \(s = \sqrt{d/n}\), \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - \Phi(3.0902 - s)\).

title: 10  Exercises: Membership inference
text:
10.6 The onion effect

Exercise 6. The onion effect. Remove the 50 outliers from the pool, retrain all target and shadow models, and rerun online LiRA. Before running, predict whether the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) on typical points goes up or down. Then run it (the solutions script does) and explain the result with self-influence. (Self-influence, outliers)







TipSolution






Setup. Draw a new pool as in the chapter (seed 0 stream, after the earlier exercises), train 128 target and 64 shadow models on it, and compute online LiRA with per-example variances. Restrict the evaluation to typical points: build the ROC curve from the (target model, typical point) pairs only and read off the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\). Then delete the 50 outliers, leaving a pool of 950, retrain all 192 models on random halves of it, and repeat.
Result. On typical points the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) goes from 0.0027 with the outliers to 0.0037 without them, with 60,800 typical member pairs behind each number. (The first number differs from the 0.0020 in Table 10.5 because there the threshold was set on all points, outliers included, and the pool is a fresh draw.)
Why it goes up. Each model now trains on 475 points instead of 500, all typical, and the outliers no longer take up the model’s capacity. The typical points that are hardest to predict, those whose labels go against the trend, become the most atypical points in the data. Their self-influence rises, and with it their separation and their exposure. The mean separation of typical points, estimated from the shadow models, goes from 0.502 to 0.621.

Privacy risk is relative to the rest of the dataset. Removing the most exposed records does not make the others safe; it promotes the next layer. Carlini et al. call this the privacy onion effect. A defence has to bound the exposure of every record, not remove the current worst ones.

title: 10  Exercises: Membership inference
section: 10.7 The shadow attack model is a threshold
text:
10.7 The shadow attack model is a threshold

Exercise 7. The shadow attack model is a threshold. Show that if the attack model for class \(c\) is \(\sigma(a_c + b_c\phi)\) with \(b_c > 0\), then within class \(c\) it ranks pairs exactly as the loss does, and it says “member” with probability above \(\frac12\) when \(\phi > -a_c/b_c\). Compute these cut points for the running example. Check: 0.751 for \(y = -1\) and 0.813 for \(y = +1\). (Shadow models, Fact 3)







TipSolution






Monotone in \(\phi\). \(\sigma\) is increasing and \(b_c > 0\), so \(\phi \mapsto \sigma(a_c + b_c\phi)\) is increasing. Within class \(c\), a larger \(\phi\) always gives a larger attack score.
Monotone in the loss. By Fact 3 of the chapter, \(\ell = \ln(1 + e^{-\phi})\) is decreasing in \(\phi\). So within the class, the attack score is a decreasing function of the loss, and it orders pairs exactly as “lower loss means member” does. Any threshold on the score is a threshold on the loss, and the two attacks have the same ROC curve on the pairs of that class.
The cut point. \(\sigma(u) > \frac12\) exactly when \(u > 0\), so the attack model favours “member” when \(a_c + b_c\phi > 0\), that is, \(\phi > -a_c/b_c\).
The running example. The fitted models are \(a_{-1} = -0.179\), \(b_{-1} = 0.238\) and \(a_{+1} = -0.128\), \(b_{+1} = 0.158\). The cut points are \(0.179/0.238 = 0.751\) and \(0.128/0.158 = 0.813\) (computed from the unrounded coefficients).
Across classes. Pooling the two classes with one threshold on the attack score puts slightly different thresholds on \(\phi\) in each class, so the pooled ROC differs from the loss attack’s only through that offset. The chapter’s Table 10.4 shows how little that buys: AUC 0.577 for both, and TPR at FPR 1% of 0.0104 against 0.0103 for the loss attack.

An attack model that sees only the record-blind output \((y, \phi)\) can do no more than choose a loss threshold per class. Its value is calibration, not power.

title: 11  Exercises: Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.1 A balanced prior
Exercises for Attribute inference and model inversion, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part02-attacks/solutions_attribute_inference.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/solutions_attribute_inference.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. A record is \((s, x, y)\), \(f_y(x, s)\) is the model’s confidence in label \(y\), and \(V(S \mid O) = \sum_o\max_s p(s, o)\) is the success of the best guess of \(s\) from \(O\), the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess. A membership test has a true positive rate (TPR) on members and a false positive rate (FPR) on non-members. In the smoking table of the chapter, \(s = 1\) is “smoker”, \(x\) the age band and \(y = 1\) “has the disease”.

title: 11  Exercises: Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
Exercise 1. A balanced prior. Redo the smoking table with \(\Pr[\text{smoker}] = 0.5\) and everything else unchanged. Compute \(V(S)\), \(V(S \mid X)\), \(V(S \mid X, Y)\) and the two leakages. Check: \(V(S \mid X) = 0.6\), \(V(S \mid X, Y) = 0.7\). Why does age now change the guess when it did not before? (MAP guess, vulnerability)







TipSolution






The joint table. Multiply \(\Pr[s] = 0.5\) by \(\Pr[x \mid s]\) and \(\Pr[y \mid x, s]\). For example, \(p(\text{smoker}, \text{old}, \text{disease}) = 0.5 \times 0.6 \times 0.7 = 0.21\).

No observation. Both values have probability 0.5, so \(V(S) = 0.5\).
Age alone. Young: non-smoker \(0.27 + 0.03 = 0.3\) against smoker \(0.12 + 0.08 = 0.2\). Old: non-smoker \(0.2\) against smoker \(0.3\). The best guess is “non-smoker” for the young and “smoker” for the old, and \(V(S \mid X) = 0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6\).
Age and disease. The bold column maxima add up to \(V(S \mid X, Y) = 0.27 + 0.08 + 0.14 + 0.21 = 0.7\). Both check values are right.
Leakages. From age: \(\log_2(0.6/0.5) = 0.2630\) bits. From age and disease: \(\log_2(0.7/0.5) = 0.4854\) bits.

Why age now matters. Being old multiplies the odds of smoking by \(\Pr[\text{old} \mid \text{smoker}]/\Pr[\text{old} \mid \text{non-smoker}] = 0.6/0.4 = 1.5\). With prior odds \(0.3/0.7\), the posterior odds for an old person are \(\frac37 \times 1.5 = 0.643 < 1\), so the guess stays “non-smoker”. With prior odds 1 they are \(1.5 > 1\), and the guess flips.
Whether a piece of evidence changes the best guess depends on the prior as much as on the evidence: a skewed prior absorbs weak evidence.

title: 11  Exercises: Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.2 The marginal prior

Exercise 2. The marginal prior. Fredrikson et al.’s attack uses \(p(s)\) in place of \(p(s \mid x)\). On the smoking table, with a calibrated model, compute the success of \(\arg\max_s p(s)\,f_y(x, s)\), breaking ties towards “non-smoker”. Check: 0.706, against 0.748 for imputation. Which cell causes the loss? (Bayes’ rule, Fact 1)







TipSolution






Scores. With a calibrated model, \(f_y(x, s) = \Pr[y \mid x, s]\). The scores \(p(s)\Pr[y \mid x, s]\) for (non-smoker, smoker) in each cell are:

young, no disease: \(0.7 \times 0.9 = 0.63\) against \(0.3 \times 0.6 = 0.18\), guess non-smoker;
young, disease: \(0.7 \times 0.1 = 0.07\) against \(0.3 \times 0.4 = 0.12\), guess smoker;
old, no disease: \(0.7 \times 0.7 = 0.49\) against \(0.3 \times 0.3 = 0.09\), guess non-smoker;
old, disease: \(0.7 \times 0.3 = 0.21\) against \(0.3 \times 0.7 = 0.21\), a tie, broken towards non-smoker.

Success. Add the mass of the guessed value in each cell of the smoking table: \(0.378 + 0.048 + 0.196 + 0.084 = 0.706\). The check value is right.
Where the loss is. Only the last cell differs from imputation, which guesses “smoker” there and gets \(0.126\) instead of \(0.084\). The loss is \(0.748 - 0.706 = 0.042\).
Why. Bayes’ rule needs \(p(s \mid x)\): an old person is a smoker with probability \(0.3913\), not \(0.3\). With it the scores are \(0.3913 \times 0.7 = 0.2739\) against \(0.6087 \times 0.3 = 0.1826\), and the tie is broken the right way. Dropping the dependence of \(s\) on \(x\) throws that evidence away. By Fact 1, any rule other than the MAP guess can only do worse.

An inversion attack is only as good as the adversary’s model of how the sensitive attribute relates to what it already knows.

title: 11  Exercises: Attribute inference and model inversion
section: 11.3 The reduction at low false positive rate
text:
11.3 The reduction at low false positive rate

Exercise 3. The reduction at low false positive rate. The membership test \(\mathcal B\) built from the toy attack has TPR 0.7832 at FPR 0.7262. Using the mixing of tests in Hypothesis testing, find the best TPR it can reach at FPR \(10^{-3}\). Check: \(0.00108\). Why can it not do better? Hint: its only output is one bit. (Neyman–Pearson, mixing tests)







TipSolution






What the test sees. \(\mathcal B\) observes one bit: whether the attribute guess was right. “Right” happens with probability 0.7832 for members and 0.7262 for non-members; “wrong” with 0.2168 and 0.2738.
Every test on that bit. A test fires with probability \(\phi_1\) on “right” and \(\phi_0\) on “wrong”. Its rates are \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.7262\,\phi_1 + 0.2738\,\phi_0\) and \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.7832\,\phi_1 + 0.2168\,\phi_0\).
Neyman–Pearson. The likelihood ratio of “right” is \(0.7832/0.7262 = 1.0785\), and of “wrong” \(0.2168/0.2738 = 0.7918\). The most powerful test spends its false positive budget on the outcome with the larger ratio first: \(\phi_0 = 0\) and \(\phi_1 = 10^{-3}/0.7262\).
The result. \(\mathrm{TPR} = 0.7832 \times 10^{-3}/0.7262 = 0.00108\). At FPR 0.1 the same calculation gives 0.10785.

Why not better. Every test on one bit is a mix of the four deterministic tests “never”, “on right”, “on wrong” and “always”, so its trade-off curve consists of two straight segments. Near the origin the slope is the largest likelihood ratio, 1.0785, so at low FPR the TPR is at most 1.0785 times the FPR. A dedicated membership attack looks at the whole confidence vector and can have a far steeper curve near zero.
An attribute attack is a membership test that has thrown away everything but one bit, so its power at low false positive rate is barely above chance.

title: 11  Exercises: Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.4 Label-only inversion

Exercise 4. Label-only inversion. The hospital releases only a label: “disease” when \(\Pr[y = 1 \mid x, s] > \frac12\). On the smoking table, the adversary queries the label at both values of \(s\), scores \(p(s \mid x)\,\mathbf 1[\mathrm{label}(x, s) = y]\), and breaks ties with \(p(s \mid x)\). Compute its success. Check: 0.742, a loss of 0.006 against imputation. (Fact 3, MAP guess)







TipSolution






The labels. Only the old smoker has disease probability above \(\frac12\) (0.7). So the label is “disease” at (old, smoker) and “no disease” at the other three inputs.
Cell by cell. \(p(\text{smoker} \mid \text{young}) = 0.2222\) and \(p(\text{smoker} \mid \text{old}) = 0.3913\), so ties go to “non-smoker”.

young, no disease: both labels match \(y\), a tie, guess non-smoker, right on \(0.378\);
young, disease: neither label matches, a tie, guess non-smoker, right on \(0.042\);
old, no disease: only the non-smoker label matches, guess non-smoker, right on \(0.196\);
old, disease: only the smoker label matches, guess smoker, right on \(0.126\).

Success. \(0.378 + 0.042 + 0.196 + 0.126 = 0.742\). The check value is right.
The loss. Imputation guesses “smoker” for young people with the disease and gets \(0.048\) there instead of \(0.042\): a loss of \(0.006\). The label is a function of the confidences, so by Fact 3 a loss, not a gain, was the only possibility.

A coarse output costs the attacker only in the cells where the coarse answer cannot tell the candidates apart; everywhere else it is as good as the full confidence.

title: 11  Exercises: Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.5 Two independent clues

Exercise 5. Two independent clues. Let \(s \in \{-1, +1\}\) be uniform, and let \(u \sim \mathcal N(as, 1)\) and \(v \sim \mathcal N(bs, 1)\) be independent given \(s\). Show that the imputation success from \((u, v)\) is \(\Phi\big(\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\big)\). Check: with \(a = 0.5\) and \(b = 1\), \(\Phi(1.1180) = 0.8682\), against \(\Phi(0.5) = 0.6915\) from \(u\) alone. Hint: the log-likelihood ratios add. (Likelihood ratios, Gaussian tails)







TipSolution






Log-likelihood ratio of one clue. \(\ln\frac{\mathcal N(u; a, 1)}{\mathcal N(u; -a, 1)} = \frac{-(u - a)^2 + (u + a)^2}{2} = 2au\). Likewise \(2bv\) for \(v\).
They add. Given \(s\), the clues are independent, so the joint density is the product and the log-likelihood ratio is \(L = 2au + 2bv\).
The MAP guess. With a uniform prior the posterior odds equal the likelihood ratio, so the MAP guess is \(+1\) when \(L > 0\) and \(-1\) when \(L < 0\).
Distribution of \(L\) given \(s = +1\). \(u\) has mean \(a\) and \(v\) mean \(b\), both with variance 1. So \(L\) is normal with mean \(2a^2 + 2b^2\) and variance \(4a^2 + 4b^2\).
Success. \(\Pr[L > 0 \mid s = +1] = \Phi\Big(\frac{2(a^2 + b^2)}{2\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}\Big) = \Phi\big(\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\big)\). By symmetry the same holds for \(s = -1\), so this is the overall success.
Numbers. \(\sqrt{0.25 + 1} = 1.1180\) and \(\Phi(1.1180) = 0.8682\). A million simulated draws give 0.8686. From \(u\) alone (\(b = 0\)) the success is \(\Phi(0.5) = 0.6915\), and from \(v\) alone \(\Phi(1) = 0.8413\).

Independent clues add in squared separation, not in success probability: a weak public feature and a strong label combine to more than either, but much less than their sum.

11.6 A model that memorizes

Exercise 6. A model that memorizes. A lookup model stores each training record under a unique record identifier, such as a patient number. Queried with a person’s identifier and a candidate \((x, s, y)\), it returns \(f_y(x, s) = 1\) when that person is a training member and the candidate is their stored record, and the population’s \(p(y \mid x, s)\) for every other query. The lookup is keyed on the identifier, not on the values, because the smoking table has only eight kinds of record and many people share each one. So a non-member’s query never hits a stored record, and a member’s query hits only at the member’s own true values. On the smoking table, compute the success of MAP inversion on members and on non-members. Check: 0.874 on members, 0.748 on non-members, an advantage of 0.126. Non-members. None of their queries is stored, so the model answers with \(p(y \mid x, s)\) at both candidates. It is calibrated, so MAP inversion is imputation and succeeds with \(V(S \mid X, Y) = 0.748\).

title: 12  Exercises: Property inference
text:
12.1 Shifting a unimodal pmf
Exercises for Property inference, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part02-attacks/solutions_property_inference.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/solutions_property_inference.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(\pi_t\) mixes a majority group and a subgroup of share \(t\), a dataset is \(n\) independent records from \(\pi_t\), and the attacker must tell \(t_0\) from \(t_1\), with \(\bar t = \frac{t_0 + t_1}2\). Its advantage is the true positive rate minus the false positive rate, its accuracy with a fair bit is \(\frac12(1 + \text{advantage})\), and the best advantage is the total variation (TV) distance between the two laws of what it sees. \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function.

title: 12  Exercises: Property inference
text:
Exercise 1. Shifting a unimodal pmf. Prove that \(\mathrm{TV}(\mathcal L(X), \mathcal L(X + 1)) = \max_k\Pr[X = k]\) for any integer-valued \(X\) whose pmf rises to a mode and then falls, and deduce Equation 12.9. Check: for \(X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(99, \frac12)\) both sides are 0.0796, and the membership advantage at \(n = 100\) is half of that, 0.0398. Find a pmf for which the identity fails. (Total variation, membership)







TipSolution





Write \(p_k = \Pr[X = k]\), and let \(k^*\) be a mode: \(p_k\) is non-decreasing for \(k \le k^*\) and non-increasing for \(k \ge k^*\).

TV as a sum of differences. \(X + 1\) takes the value \(k\) with probability \(p_{k-1}\). So \[\mathrm{TV}(\mathcal L(X), \mathcal L(X + 1)) = \frac12\sum_k|p_k - p_{k-1}|, \tag{12.1}\] with \(p_k = 0\) outside the support.
The climb telescopes. For \(k \le k^*\) the differences are non-negative, so \(\sum_{k \le k^*}|p_k - p_{k-1}| = \sum_{k \le k^*}(p_k - p_{k-1}) = p_{k^*}\). All terms cancel except the last, and the pmf starts from 0.
The descent telescopes. For \(k > k^*\) the differences are non-positive, so \(\sum_{k > k^*}|p_k - p_{k-1}| = \sum_{k > k^*}(p_{k-1} - p_k) = p_{k^*}\), since the pmf ends at 0.
Add and halve. The total is \(2p_{k^*}\), and half of it is \(p_{k^*} = \max_kp_k\).
Membership. Step 3 of the chapter’s membership derivation reduced the membership advantage to \((1 - t)\,\mathrm{TV}(\mathcal L(X + 1), \mathcal L(X))\) with \(X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, t)\). A binomial pmf is unimodal: the ratio \(p_{k+1}/p_k = \frac{(n - 1 - k)t}{(k + 1)(1 - t)}\) decreases in \(k\), so it crosses 1 at most once. Steps 1–4 give \((1 - t)\max_kp_k\), which is Equation 12.9.
Check. For \(X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(99, \frac12)\) the script finds \(\mathrm{TV}(X, X + 1) = 0.0796 = \max_kp_k\). With \(1 - t = \frac12\), the membership advantage at \(n = 100\) is \(0.0398\), which matches the game computed directly.

A pmf where it fails. Let \(X\) be uniform on \(\{0, 2\}\). Then \(X + 1\) is uniform on \(\{1, 3\}\), the two supports are disjoint, and the TV is 1. The largest probability is \(\frac12\). The pmf goes up, down, up and down again, so the climbs and descents in steps 2 and 3 add up to \(4 \times \frac12 = 2\), not \(2\max_kp_k = 1\).
A shift by one record is invisible exactly to the extent that the distribution is spread out; for a unimodal count, the height of the mode measures how spread out it is.

title: 12  Exercises: Property inference
section: 12.2 How much data does the property attacker need?
text:
12.2 How much data does the property attacker need?

Exercise 2. How much data does the property attacker need? With \(t_0 = 0.45\) and \(t_1 = 0.55\), use Equation 12.10 to find the \(n\) at which the best attacker on the released count reaches accuracy 0.95. Then find the smallest such \(n\) exactly. Check: the approximation gives \(n = 270.6\); the exact answer is 269. (Normal approximation)







TipSolution






Accuracy from advantage. By Equation 12.10, the best accuracy is approximately \[\frac12 + \frac12\Big(2\Phi\Big(\frac{\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|}{2\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}}\Big) - 1\Big) = \Phi\Big(\frac{\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|}{2\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}}\Big). \tag{12.2}\]
Invert \(\Phi\). Setting it to 0.95 gives \(\sqrt n = 2\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}\,\Phi^{-1}(0.95)/|t_1 - t_0|\). Here \(\bar t = 0.5\), \(\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)} = 0.5\), \(\Phi^{-1}(0.95) = 1.6449\) and \(|t_1 - t_0| = 0.1\), so \(\sqrt n = 2 \times 0.5 \times 1.6449/0.1 = 16.449\).
Square. \(n = 270.6\), so the approximation says 271 records.
Exact. The script computes \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}(\mathrm{Bin}(n, 0.45), \mathrm{Bin}(n, 0.55))\) for each \(n\). The smallest \(n\) with accuracy at least 0.95 is 269, where the accuracy is 0.9501; at \(n = 268\) it is 0.9495.

The approximation is off by two records. It uses the variance at the midpoint, \(0.25\), for both hypotheses, while the true variances are \(0.45 \times 0.55 = 0.2475\), slightly smaller, and it smooths over the integer steps of the count.
A few hundred records suffice to tell a 45% share from a 55% share with 95% accuracy. A dataset of that size is small by any standard.

title: 12  Exercises: Property inference
text:
12.3 Leakage in records

Exercise 3. Leakage in records. Suri & Evans measure a model’s leakage by the number \(k\) of records, with their groups visible, that an attacker would need to see to match the model’s accuracy. Show that for a small gap, \(k \approx n(\kappa\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)})^2\), which is \(n(\kappa/2)^2\) at \(\bar t = \frac12\). Check: for the logistic regression at \(n = 1{,}000\) and gap 0.1, the predicted accuracy is 0.8467 and the exact \(k\) is 105, against \(n(\kappa/2)^2 = 104.6\). (Scaling law)







TipSolution






The records attacker. With \(k\) records and their groups, the count of subgroup records is sufficient (the game section of the chapter), so the best accuracy is that of the count. By Exercise 2, step 1, it is approximately \(\Phi\big(\sqrt k\,|t_1 - t_0|/(2\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)})\big)\).
The model attacker. By Equation 12.13 and Equation 12.5, the best accuracy from a model trained on \(n\) records is approximately \(\Phi\big(\kappa\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|/2\big)\).
Equate the arguments. \(\Phi\) is increasing, so the accuracies match when \(\sqrt k/\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)} = \kappa\sqrt n\). The gap cancels, and \[k = n\,\kappa^2\,\bar t(1 - \bar t). \tag{12.3}\]
At \(\bar t = \frac12\): \(\bar t(1 - \bar t) = \frac14\), so \(k = n(\kappa/2)^2\).
Check. For the logistic regression, \(\kappa = 0.647\) and \((\kappa/2)^2 = 0.105\). At \(n = 1{,}000\) and \(t_0, t_1 = 0.45, 0.55\), Equation 12.12 predicts accuracy 0.8467. The smallest \(k\) for which the exact binomial attacker reaches 0.8467 is 105, and the formula gives \(1000 \times 0.1046 = 104.6\). At \(n = 200\) the prediction is 0.6763, matched by 21 records, against \(20.9\) from the formula.

The logistic regression, which never sees the group, gives the property away as well as one record in ten would with its group label attached.

title: 12  Exercises: Property inference
text:
12.4 Symmetries of a tanh network

Exercise 4. Symmetries of a tanh network. Show that \(h!\,2^h\) parameter vectors represent the same generic network, and evaluate it for \(h = 8\) and \(h = 100\). Verify that \(\sum_ju_ju_j^\top\) is invariant and that \(\sum_ju_j\) is not invariant under sign flips. Check: \(h = 8\) gives 10,321,920. (Symmetry)







TipSolution






Every \(g = S\Pi\) preserves the function. This is Equation 12.15: \(\tanh(gz) = g\tanh(z)\), and \(g^\top g = I\).
Count the \(g\). There are \(h!\) permutations \(\Pi\) and \(2^h\) sign patterns \(S\). Each pair gives a different matrix \(g\), because \(g\) sends the \(j\)-th basis vector to \(\pm\) the \(\pi(j)\)-th, which determines both \(\pi\) and the sign.
Distinct \(g\) give distinct parameters, for a generic network. Suppose \(g\theta = g'\theta\). Then \(r = g'^{-1}g\) fixes \(\theta\): it sends each unit \(u_j\) to \(\pm u_{\pi(j)}\) and gets \(u_j\) back. If no two units are equal or opposite, this forces \(\pi(j) = j\). And if no unit is 0, the sign must be \(+\), since \(u_j = -u_j\) would mean \(u_j = 0\). So \(r = I\), and \(g = g'\). Generic parameters (drawn from a density) have distinct, non-opposite, non-zero units with probability 1.
Evaluate. \(h = 4\): \(24 \times 16 = 384\). \(h = 8\): \(40{,}320 \times 256 = 10{,}321{,}920\). \(h = 100\): \(100! \times 2^{100} = 1.1831\times10^{188}\).
Second moments are invariant. \(\sum_j(gu)_j(gu)_j^\top\): a permutation reorders the terms of the sum, and a sign flip replaces \(u_ju_j^\top\) by \((-u_j)(-u_j)^\top = u_ju_j^\top\).
The plain sum is not. Flipping unit 1 changes \(\sum_ju_j\) by \(-2u_1 \ne 0\). It is invariant under permutations only.
Numerical check. The script draws a random network with \(h = 4\), applies the permutation \((3, 1, 4, 2)\) and flips units 2 and 3. The logits on 500 inputs agree to \(10^{-12}\), the second-moment features agree to \(10^{-12}\), and the raw weights differ by more than 0.1.

For a network of realistic width, the number of equivalent parameter vectors is astronomically larger than any number of shadow models, so a meta-classifier cannot learn the symmetry from examples; it has to be built in.

title: 12  Exercises: Property inference
text:
12.5 Several released models

Exercise 5. Several released models. The victim releases \(k\) models, each trained on its own dataset of \(n\) records from the same \(\pi_t\). Show that the best attack sums the \(k\) linear scores, and that its accuracy is \(\Phi(\sqrt k\,\Delta/2)\), where \(\Delta\) is the Mahalanobis distance of Equation 12.12 for one model. Compare with one model trained on \(kn\) records. Check: for the logistic regression at \(n = 200\) and gap 0.2, \(\Delta = 1.827\); with \(k = 4\) the predicted accuracy is 0.966. (Fact 3, additivity)







TipSolution






The models are independent given \(b\). Each is trained on its own dataset, so under hypothesis \(b\) the models \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_k\) are independent, each approximately \(\mathcal N(m_b, \Sigma)\) with \(m_b = \theta(t_b)\) and \(\Sigma = \bar\Sigma_1/n\).
Log-likelihood ratios add. The joint density is a product, so the joint log-likelihood ratio is \(\sum_iL(\theta_i)\), with \(L(\theta) = w^\top(\theta - \frac{m_0 + m_1}2)\) from Fact 3. The best attack thresholds this sum at 0: it adds the linear scores.
Its distribution. Each \(L(\theta_i)\) has mean \(\pm\Delta^2/2\) and variance \(\Delta^2\) (Fact 3, step 3). The sum of \(k\) independent copies has mean \(\pm k\Delta^2/2\) and variance \(k\Delta^2\).
Accuracy. Under hypothesis 1 the attack is right when the sum is positive, with probability \(\Phi\big((k\Delta^2/2)/(\sqrt k\,\Delta)\big) = \Phi(\sqrt k\,\Delta/2)\). Hypothesis 0 is symmetric.
One model on \(kn\) records. By Equation 12.12, \(\Delta\) grows like \(\sqrt n\), so a single model trained on \(kn\) records has Mahalanobis distance \(\sqrt k\,\Delta\): the same accuracy.
Check. At \(n = 200\) and \(t_0, t_1 = 0.4, 0.6\), Equation 12.12 gives \(\Delta = 1.827\), so one model gives \(\Phi(0.913) = 0.819\). Four models give \(\Delta\sqrt4 = 3.653\) and accuracy \(\Phi(1.827) = 0.966\), and one model on 800 records also has \(\Delta = 3.653\). Simulation, with the meta-classifier fitted on 150 shadow models per side and scores summed over groups of 4 target models: accuracy 0.817 for one model and 0.970 for four.

Every release adds evidence. A victim who retrains and republishes a model on fresh data from the same population leaks the property as if it had trained one model on all of the data.

title: 12  Exercises: Property inference
text:
12.6 Noise sized for one record

Exercise 6. Noise sized for one record. The hospital adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) noise to the released count, with \(n = 10{,}000\), \(t_0 = 0.45\), \(t_1 = 0.55\). Using normal approximations, find the property and membership advantages at \(\sigma = 10\), and the \(\sigma\) at which the property advantage falls to 0.1. Check: at \(\sigma = 10\) the property advantage is still 1.0000; hiding the property needs \(\sigma \approx 3{,}979\). (Normal approximation, group size)







TipSolution






The released value. \(S + N\) is approximately normal, with variance \(n\bar t(1 - \bar t) + \sigma^2 = 2{,}500 + \sigma^2\) under both hypotheses (variance at the midpoint, as in Equation 12.10). Write \(s = \sqrt{2500 + \sigma^2}\).
Property. The means differ by \(n|t_1 - t_0| = 1{,}000\). The Gaussian pair has standardized shift \(1000/s\), so the advantage is \(2\Phi(1000/(2s)) - 1\). At \(\sigma = 10\), \(s = 50.99\) and the argument of \(\Phi\) is 9.81: the advantage is 1.0000.
Membership. The target shifts \(S\) by 1 with probability \(1 - \bar t\) (step 2 of the chapter’s membership derivation), so the advantage is \((1 - \bar t)(2\Phi(1/(2s)) - 1)\). Without noise this is 0.0040, and at \(\sigma = 10\) it is 0.0039.
Noise that hides the property. Set \(2\Phi(1000/(2s)) - 1 = 0.1\), so \(\Phi(1000/(2s)) = 0.55\) and \(1000/(2s) = \Phi^{-1}(0.55) = 0.1257\). Then \(s = 3{,}979\), and \(\sigma = \sqrt{s^2 - 2500} = 3{,}979\) to the nearest unit.
What that noise costs. The count is about 5,000, and the noise now has standard deviation about 4,000. The release says almost nothing about anything. The membership advantage has dropped to 0.000050, far below anything a membership attacker would care about.

Noise of size 10 hides one record and leaves the property in plain view. To hide a property carried by 1,000 records, the noise must be on the scale of 1,000 records, a group-sized defence with a group-sized cost.

title: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Expected exposure of a small space
Exercises for Memorization and training-data extraction, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part02-attacks/solutions_memorization.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/solutions_memorization.py. With the default seed it rebuilds the chapter’s contact list and its canary “my pin is 58745”.
The notation is the chapter’s: \(\mathcal R\) is the canary’s randomness space, the rank of a candidate counts the candidates at least as likely (itself included), and exposure is \(\log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}\). \(N(c, w)\) are the counts of an \(n\)-gram model, \(\alpha = 0.1\) its smoothing constant and \(V = 39\) its alphabet size. In a written-out context, _ stands for a space.
crumbs: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction

title: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
Exercise 1. Expected exposure of a small space. For \(|\mathcal R| = 10\) and a canary that was not inserted (no ties), compute \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{exposure}]\) from Equation 13.11 and \(\Pr[\mathrm{exposure} \ge 2]\) exactly. Check: 1.1428 bits and 0.2. (Null distribution of exposure)







TipSolution






The rank is uniform. The canary was not inserted, so the model does not depend on it, and with no ties its rank is uniform on \(\{1, \dots, 10\}\) (step 2 of the null-distribution derivation).
The mean. \(\mathbb E[\log_2\operatorname{rank}] = \frac{1}{10}\sum_{i=1}^{10}\log_2i = \frac{\log_2(10!)}{10} = \frac{\log_2 3{,}628{,}800}{10} = \frac{21.791}{10} = 2.1791\).
Subtract from \(\log_2 10 = 3.3219\): \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{exposure}] = 3.3219 - 2.1791 = 1.1428\) bits. It is below the limit \(\log_2e = 1.4427\): the \(O(\ln N/N)\) correction in Stirling’s formula is still large at \(N = 10\).
The tail. Exposure \(\ge 2\) means \(\log_2\operatorname{rank} \le \log_210 - 2\), that is \(\operatorname{rank} \le 10/4 = 2.5\). Ranks 1 and 2 qualify, so the probability is \(2/10 = 0.2\), below the bound \(2^{-2} = 0.25\). The bound is loose here because \(10 \cdot 2^{-2}\) is not an integer.

Exposure has the same law for every model when the canary is absent and there are no ties: it depends only on \(|\mathcal R|\).
crumbs: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction

title: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.2 Samples for extraction

Exercise 2. Samples for extraction. A secret has probability \(p = 0.0442\) after its prefix. How many samples does the bound Equation 13.6 ask for to extract it with probability 99%, and how many does the exact condition \((1 - p)^m \le 0.01\) ask for? Check: 105 and 102. (Samples needed)







TipSolution






The bound. \(m \ge \ln(1/0.01)/p = 4.6052/0.0442 = 104.19\), so \(m = 105\).
The exact condition. \((1 - p)^m \le 0.01\) is \(m\ln(1 - p) \le \ln 0.01\). Dividing by the negative \(\ln(1 - p) = -0.04521\) flips the inequality: \(m \ge 4.6052/0.04521 = 101.9\), so \(m = 102\).
Check. With 102 samples the success probability is \(1 - 0.9558^{102} = 0.9901\); with 101 it is 0.9896, just short of 99%.
Why the bound is close. \(1 - p \le e^{-p}\) loses only a factor \(e^{-p^2/2}\) per sample for small \(p\) (\(\ln(1 - p) = -p - p^2/2 - \dots\)). The relative error of the bound is about \(p/2 = 2\%\), which is the gap between 104.2 and 101.9.

For rare strings the bound and the exact count agree; the useful rule is “about \(4.6/p\) samples for 99%”.

title: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.3 A canary in unique contexts has maximal exposure
text:
13.3 A canary in unique contexts has maximal exposure

Exercise 3. A canary in unique contexts has maximal exposure. Suppose the order \(n\) is large enough that every context met while scoring a pin after “my pin is” contains at least the prefix’s last two characters, the “s” and the space after it (for five digits and the end-of-line symbol, \(n \ge 8\)), and that these contexts, each a stretch of the prefix ending in “s” followed by the digits scored so far, occur in the training data only in the \(k \ge 1\) copies of the canary. (A context that held only the space would not do: a space followed by digits can also occur in the background text.) Show that the canary is the unique most likely pin, so its exposure is \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\). Hint: compare the canary with a pin that first differs at position \(j\); after position \(j\) that pin’s contexts were never seen, so each of its later symbols has probability \(1/V\), and use Equation 13.3. Check: the order-8 model of the script gives the canary of Table 13.5 exposure 16.61 at \(k = 1\). (Fact 2, rank)







TipSolution





Write the canary as \(\hat r = \hat r_1\dots\hat r_5\) and let \(\hat r_6\) be the end-of-line symbol; a candidate \(r\) is scored on the same six steps (Equation 13.1).

Which contexts have counts. Every context met while scoring contains the “s” that ends the prefix, so by assumption it can only have been seen in the canary’s copies. The canary’s own contexts were seen exactly \(k\) times each, always followed by the canary’s next symbol. A context that is not on the canary’s path was never seen.
Take a candidate \(r \ne \hat r\) and let \(j\) be the first position where \(r_j \ne \hat r_j\). Positions before \(j\) contribute the same factors to both scores, so only positions \(j, \dots, 6\) matter.
Position \(j\). Both are scored in the canary’s context \(c_j\). By Equation 13.3 the canary gets \(\frac{k + \alpha}{k + \alpha V}\) and \(r\) gets \(\frac{\alpha}{k + \alpha V}\), strictly less.
Positions after \(j\). The candidate’s context now contains \(r_j \ne \hat r_j\), so it is not on the canary’s path and was never seen: \(N(c) = 0\) and Equation 13.2 gives \(\alpha/(\alpha V) = 1/V\) for every symbol. The canary keeps getting \(\frac{k + \alpha}{k + \alpha V}\).
Compare the factors. \(\frac{k + \alpha}{k + \alpha V} \ge \frac1V\) is equivalent to \(V(k + \alpha) \ge k + \alpha V\), that is \(Vk \ge k\), which holds. At \(k = 1\): \(0.2245 \ge 1/39 = 0.0256\).
Conclude. Every factor of the canary is at least the candidate’s, and the one at position \(j\) is strictly larger, so \(p(\hat r) > p(r)\). This holds for every \(r \ne \hat r\), so the canary has rank 1 and exposure \(\log_2|\mathcal R| = \log_2 10^5 = 16.61\).

On the chapter’s corpus. No background line contains s_, because names end in a vowel, so the contexts of the order-8 model after “my pin is” all contain s_ and the assumptions hold. The script gives exposure 16.61 at \(k = 1\) for order 8, and also for order 6, where the assumption fails at the last steps but the canary still wins.
A model with enough context to give a secret its own path memorizes it completely from one copy. Exposure saturates, and the only remaining question is whether an attacker can find the prefix.
crumbs: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction

title: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.4 Copies needed by hand

Exercise 4. Copies needed by hand. A secret’s five steps have counts (true digit, strongest rival) without the secret of \((1, 2), (0, 2), (0, 5), (0, 1), (0, 1)\), and every rival has a lower code than the true digit. What is \(k^*\)? Which step decides it? If a larger model split that context so that the rival count at the third step fell from 5 to 2, what would \(k^*\) become? Check: 6, then 3. (Equation 13.7)







TipSolution






Ties go to the rival. Greedy decoding breaks ties toward the lowest code, and every rival has a lower code, so the true digit must win strictly at every step: \(k \ge \text{rival} - \text{true} + 1\).
Per step. \(2 - 1 + 1 = 2\), \(2 - 0 + 1 = 3\), \(5 - 0 + 1 = 6\), \(1 - 0 + 1 = 2\), \(1 - 0 + 1 = 2\).
The maximum is \(k^* = 6\), set by the third step. With 5 copies the first two digits come out right, the third goes to the rival, and decoding leaves the secret’s path.
After the split the third step needs \(2 - 0 + 1 = 3\), so the steps need \(2, 3, 3, 2, 2\) and \(k^* = 3\). The bottleneck is now shared by the second and third steps.
If ties went the other way (rivals with higher codes), every requirement would drop by one and \(k^*\) would be 5 before the split.

A larger model helps the secret only where it splits the bottleneck context. Splitting an easy context changes nothing.
crumbs: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction

title: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.5 Exposure as a membership test over many canaries
text:
13.5 Exposure as a membership test over many canaries

Exercise 5. Exposure as a membership test over many canaries. Plant 20 canaries “my pin is \(r_i\)”, one copy each, in the training set of the order-3 model of the chapter, and draw 20 more pins that you do not plant. Declare “planted” when the exposure is at least 3 bits. Use Equation 13.10 to bound the false positive rate, then measure both rates. Why is the detection so much weaker than for the single canary of Table 13.5, which reached 4.05 bits with one copy? Check: the bound is \(2^{-3} = 0.125\); the script measures a true positive rate of 0.25 and a false positive rate of 0.15 on the 20 unplanted pins, and 0.1250 over all 99,980 unplanted pins. (Exposure, hypothesis testing)







TipSolution






The bound. An unplanted pin is independent of the model, so by Equation 13.10 its exposure is at least 3 with probability at most \(2^{-3} = 0.125\). That is the false positive rate of the test “exposure \(\ge 3\)”.
Measured. All 40 exposures come from one model trained with the 20 planted canaries. Planted pins: 5 of 20 reach 3 bits, a true positive rate of 0.25, and their mean exposure is 1.82 bits. Unplanted pins: 3 of 20 reach it, 0.15, with mean exposure 1.64. Twenty pins is a small sample: over all 99,980 unplanted pins the fraction is exactly 0.1250, on the bound, because the scores have no ties and the rank of a random pin is uniform.
Why the test is weak. At order 3 only the first digit of a canary has a context that the background never uses, s_. With one canary, that context sends its whole count to the canary’s first digit, worth 3.46 bits (Table 13.2). With 20 canaries, the context s_ is followed 20 times by 20 first digits spread over 10 values. Each canary’s first digit gets about 2 of the 20 counts, and it competes with the first digits of the other 19 canaries instead of with nothing. Its advantage over a random first digit shrinks from a factor of 11 to about \((2 + \alpha)/(\text{average count} + \alpha) \approx 1\). The remaining digits share their contexts with 5,000 background pins, where one copy is a negligible vote.
Reading it as a test. At false positive rate 0.125 the test finds a quarter of the planted canaries: barely better than chance. Auditing with many canaries needs either canaries that do not share contexts (different prefixes) or more copies.

Canaries planted with the same prefix compete for the same contexts. Their exposures measure memorization of the set, not of each one.
crumbs: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction

title: 13  Exercises: Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.6 Which secrets an unprompted sampler finds
text:
13.6 Which secrets an unprompted sampler finds

Exercise 6. Which secrets an unprompted sampler finds. By the chain rule, one sample from the start of a line equals a given training line with probability \(p(\text{line})\). Predict the fraction of the secrets of each duplication group that appear at least once among 20,000 samples from the order-6 model (trained without the public lines), and compare with a simulation. Check: for the secrets with 16 copies the mean \(p(\text{line})\) is \(1.34 \times 10^{-4}\), the predicted fraction 0.91 and the simulated one 0.96; for 4 copies, 0.01 and 0.02. (Chain rule, samples needed)







TipSolution






One sample. A temperature-1 sample draws each symbol from \(p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\) and stops at the end-of-line symbol, so it equals a given line, end of line included, with probability \(p(\text{line})\) (Equation 13.1).
Many samples. The samples are independent, so a line with probability \(p\) appears at least once among \(m\) of them with probability \(1 - (1 - p)^m\), as in the derivation of Equation 13.6.
Average over each group. For each secret compute \(p\) under the model and average \(1 - (1 - p)^{20{,}000}\) over the 100 secrets of the group. Averaging the probabilities, not plugging in the mean \(p\), matters: the per-secret probabilities differ by orders of magnitude.

Why the probability climbs so fast with \(k\). The line’s probability is a product over its 13 symbols. The name’s first symbols are drawn in contexts shared with every line (the start of a line, then one or two letters). Each copy is one vote in each of those contexts, so each factor grows with \(k\), and the product of several growing factors grows faster than \(k\): from 4 to 16 copies the mean probability rises by a factor of 280. Once the name reaches contexts of its own, the remaining factors approach 1 (Table 13.2).

The predictions agree with the simulation within the sampling error of 100 secrets per group. They also explain the chapter’s attack: the 4-copy secrets have a 1 in 100 chance each, so almost none appear, although 76% of them are discoverably memorized at order 6.
An unprompted attacker meets a secret at the rate \(p(\text{line})\), which is the product of every vote along its path, prefix included. Holding the prefix removes most of that product.
