title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.6 A preview of advanced composition

Exercise 6. A preview of advanced composition. Show that if \(\Pr_{y \sim M(D)}[L_{D,D'}(y) > \varepsilon] \le \delta\) for every ordered neighbouring pair, then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. For \(k\) randomized-response answers at \(\varepsilon_0\), use Hoeffding’s inequality on \(L\) to show that \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon = k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) + \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}\). Check: for \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), \(k = 1000\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) this gives \(21.62\), against 100 for basic composition and the exact 19.345. (Composition, concentration)







TipSolution





A tail bound on the loss gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).

The worst event for \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\) is \(B = \{y : p(y) > e^\varepsilon q(y)\} = \{L > \varepsilon\}\) (Fact 3 of Divergences).
Drop the negative term: \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = P(B) - e^\varepsilon Q(B) \le P(B) = \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\).
This holds for every ordered pair, which is the hockey-stick form of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.

The mean of the loss. For one answer under \(D\) (bit 1), the loss is \(+\varepsilon_0\) with probability \(t = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0}}{1 + e^{\varepsilon_0}}\) and \(-\varepsilon_0\) with probability \(1 - t\). Its mean is \(\varepsilon_0(2t - 1)\), and \[2t - 1 = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} = \tanh(\varepsilon_0/2). \tag{19.4}\] For \(k\) independent answers (Fact 3 of the chapter) the mean is \(k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). At \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), \(t = 0.5250\) and \(2t - 1 = \tanh(0.05) = 0.04996\), so for \(k = 1000\) the mean is 4.996.
Hoeffding.

\(L = \sum_{i=1}^kL_i\) with independent \(L_i \in [-\varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_0]\), each of range \(2\varepsilon_0\). Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration) gives, for \(s > 0\), \[\Pr[L - \mathbb E L \ge s] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2s^2}{k(2\varepsilon_0)^2}\Big) = \exp\Big(-\frac{s^2}{2k\varepsilon_0^2}\Big). \tag{19.5}\]
Set the right side to \(\delta\): \(s = \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}\).
Combine with the first part: with \(\varepsilon = \mathbb E L + s\), \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\). Randomized response is symmetric in the two bits, so the same holds for the reversed pair, and \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.

The check. For \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), \(k = 1000\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\): \(s = 0.1\sqrt{2000 \ln 10^6} = 16.623\), so \(\varepsilon = 4.996 + 16.623 = 21.62\). The exact tail at that point is \(\Pr_D[L > 21.62] = 5.319 \times 10^{-8}\), well below \(10^{-6}\), which shows how much Hoeffding gives away. The exact \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) is 19.345 and basic composition gives 100.
The bound grows like \(\sqrt k\), not \(k\): the mean grows like \(k\varepsilon_0^2/2\), small when \(\varepsilon_0\) is small, and the fluctuations like \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt k\). Advanced composition proves the same shape for any \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP mechanisms.

title: 19  Exercises: Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.7 Ask until yes

Exercise 7. Ask until yes. A survey asks a person for randomized-response answers at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), one at a time, and stops at the first answer 1 or after 3 answers. Only the number of answers asked is published (1, 2, 3, or “3 and no 1”). Show it is \(3\ln 3\)-DP by adaptive composition, then compute its exact \(\varepsilon\). Check: the exact \(\varepsilon\) is \(\ln 27 = 3.2958\): the basic bound is attained. (Adaptive composition, post-processing)







TipSolution





The bound.

Write it as an adaptive composition of three steps. Step \(i\) looks at the previous answers. If one of them is 1, it outputs “stopped”, which does not depend on the data (0-DP). Otherwise it asks a fresh randomized-response question (\(\ln 3\)-DP). For every fixed previous output, step \(i\) is at most \(\ln 3\)-DP.
Adaptive composition gives \(3\ln 3\) for the transcript of three steps.
The published count is a function of the transcript, so post-processing keeps \(3\ln 3\).

The exact \(\varepsilon\). Let \(s\) be the probability that one answer is 1: \(s = \frac34\) under bit 1 and \(\frac14\) under bit 0. Stopping after answer \(i\) means \(i - 1\) zeros and then a 1, with probability \((1 - s)^{i-1}s\); no 1 in three answers has probability \((1 - s)^3\). Table 19.1 lists the four outputs.

20.1 A private mean under add/remove
Exercises for The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_laplace_gaussian.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_laplace_gaussian.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Guarantees are differential privacy (DP) guarantees; \(\Delta_1\) and \(\Delta_2\) are the \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) sensitivities; \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\) for the Gaussian mechanism; \(\Phi\) and \(\varphi\) are the standard normal distribution function and density; and \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) - e^\varepsilon\Phi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\) is the exact privacy curve of the Gaussian mechanism (Equation 20.17).

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
Exercise 1. A private mean under add/remove. Records lie in \([0, 1]\) and neighbours differ by adding or removing a record, so \(n\) is private. Release the sum \(S\) and the count \(n\), each with the Laplace mechanism at \(\varepsilon/2\), and estimate the mean as \((S + Z_s)/(n + Z_c)\). Show that the release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP and that the root-mean-square error is approximately \(\frac{2\sqrt2}{n\varepsilon}\sqrt{1 + m^2}\) for true mean \(m\). Check: at \(n = 1000\), \(m = 0.3\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) this is 0.00295 (simulated 0.00296), against 0.00141 for the replace-neighbour mean with \(n\) public. (Sensitivity, basic composition, first-order error)







TipSolution





Privacy.

Sensitivities. Adding or removing a record \(x \in [0, 1]\) changes the count by 1 and the sum by \(x \le 1\). So each query has \(\Delta_1 = 1\).
Each release. \(S + Z_s\) with \(Z_s \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) is the Laplace mechanism with scale \(\Delta_1/(\varepsilon/2)\), so it is \(\frac\varepsilon2\)-DP. The same holds for \(n + Z_c\).
Together. By basic composition (Post-processing, group privacy and composition) the pair is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Equivalently, the vector \((S, n)\) has \(\Delta_1 = 1 + 1 = 2\), and independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) noise on both coordinates is exactly the Laplace mechanism for it.
The estimate. Dividing the two noisy numbers is post-processing, so it costs nothing more.

Error.

Write the error. With \(S = nm\), \[\frac{nm + Z_s}{n + Z_c} - m = \frac{Z_s - mZ_c}{n + Z_c}. \tag{20.1}\]
First order. The noise has scale \(b = 2/\varepsilon\), tiny next to \(n\), so \(n + Z_c \approx n\) and the error is \(\approx (Z_s - mZ_c)/n\).
Variance. \(Z_s\) and \(Z_c\) are independent with variance \(2b^2\) each, so the variance is \(2b^2(1 + m^2)/n^2\). Take the square root and substitute \(b = 2/\varepsilon\): \(\frac{\sqrt2\cdot2}{n\varepsilon}\sqrt{1 + m^2} = \frac{2\sqrt2}{n\varepsilon}\sqrt{1 + m^2}\).
Check. At \(n = 1000\), \(m = 0.3\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(\frac{2\sqrt2}{1000}\sqrt{1.09} = 0.00295\). A million simulated releases give 0.00296.
Compare. Under replace neighbours with \(n\) public, the mean has \(\Delta_1 = 1/n\) and needs only \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/(n\varepsilon))\) noise, with root-mean-square error \(\sqrt2/(n\varepsilon) = 0.00141\). Hiding \(n\) and splitting the budget costs a factor of about 2.

A caveat. Strictly, the ratio has no finite variance: \(n + Z_c\) has a positive density at 0, so the error can be arbitrarily large with probability of order \(e^{-n\varepsilon/2}\), which is \(e^{-500}\) here and never shows up in a simulation. In practice you replace the denominator by \(\max(n + Z_c, 1)\), which is post-processing and removes the problem.
Under add/remove the size of the dataset is itself private, and releasing it costs part of the budget.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
section: 20.2 The Laplace scale cannot be smaller
text:
20.2 The Laplace scale cannot be smaller

Exercise 2. The Laplace scale cannot be smaller. For a count, show that \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise with \(b < 1/\varepsilon\) is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP, by exhibiting an event. Then show that \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) noise is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP for \(\varepsilon' < \varepsilon\) with \(\delta = 1 - e^{-(\varepsilon - \varepsilon')/2}\). Check: \(b = 0.9\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) gives the ratio \(e^{1/0.9} = 3.0377 > e\); with \(b = 1\), \(\delta(0.5) = 0.2212\). (Tightness, hockey-stick of a Laplace pair)







TipSolution





The violating event.

A neighbouring pair. Take datasets with counts \(f(D) = 0\) and \(f(D') = 1\).
The event \(S = \{y \le 0\}\). Under \(M(D) = \mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\), \(\Pr[S] = \frac12\). Under \(M(D') = \mathrm{Lap}(1, b)\), \(\Pr[S] = \frac12e^{-1/b}\), from the Laplace distribution function.
The ratio is \(e^{1/b}\). If \(b < 1/\varepsilon\), then \(1/b > \varepsilon\) and \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] > e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S]\), which pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP forbids.
Check. \(b = 0.9\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(e^{1/0.9} = 3.0377 > e = 2.7183\).

The \(\delta\) curve. Work in units of \(b = 1/\varepsilon\), so the shift is \(t = 1/b = \varepsilon\). Let \(P = \mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) and \(Q = \mathrm{Lap}(t, 1)\).

The privacy loss. \(L(y) = |y - t| - |y|\), which is \(t\) for \(y \le 0\), \(t - 2y\) for \(0 \le y \le t\), and \(-t\) for \(y \ge t\).
The bad event. For \(0 \le \varepsilon' < t\), \(L(y) > \varepsilon'\) exactly when \(y < c\) with \(c = (t - \varepsilon')/2 \in (0, t/2]\).
Its two probabilities. \(P[y < c] = 1 - \frac12e^{-c}\) and \(Q[y < c] = \frac12e^{-(t - c)}\).
The hockey-stick (Fact 3 of the chapter): \(\delta = P(B) - e^{\varepsilon'}Q(B) = 1 - \frac12e^{-c} - \frac12e^{\varepsilon' - t + c}\). Since \(\varepsilon' - t = -2c\), the last exponent is \(-c\), and \(\delta = 1 - e^{-c} = 1 - e^{-(\varepsilon - \varepsilon')/2}\).
Check. \(b = 1\) (\(\varepsilon = 1\)) at \(\varepsilon' = 0.5\): \(1 - e^{-0.25} = 0.2212\). At \(\varepsilon' = 0\) the formula gives \(1 - e^{-1/2} = 0.3935\), the total variation distance of the pair, and at \(\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\) it gives 0.

The Laplace mechanism is exactly \(\varepsilon\)-DP and no better: below \(\varepsilon\) you must pay a \(\delta\) that is not small.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
section: 20.3 The slope of the privacy curve
text:
20.3 The slope of the privacy curve

Exercise 3. The slope of the privacy curve. Show that \(\varphi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) = e^\varepsilon\varphi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\), and deduce \(\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = -e^\varepsilon\Phi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\). Conclude that \(\delta_\mu\) is strictly decreasing in \(\varepsilon\), and show in the same way that \(\frac{d}{d\mu}\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \varphi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) > 0\). Check: at \(\mu = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) the slope is \(-0.1816\), matching a finite difference. (Differentiating Equation 20.17)







TipSolution





Write \(a = \frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\) and \(c = -\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\), so \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi(a) - e^\varepsilon\Phi(c)\).

The density identity. \(a^2 - c^2 = (a - c)(a + c) = \mu\cdot\big(-\frac{2\varepsilon}\mu\big) = -2\varepsilon\). So \(\varphi(a)/\varphi(c) = e^{-(a^2 - c^2)/2} = e^\varepsilon\). This is the statement that the likelihood ratio at the boundary of the bad event is exactly \(e^\varepsilon\).
Differentiate in \(\varepsilon\). \(\frac{da}{d\varepsilon} = \frac{dc}{d\varepsilon} = -\frac1\mu\). By the product and chain rules, \[\frac{d\delta_\mu}{d\varepsilon} = -\frac{\varphi(a)}\mu - e^\varepsilon\Phi(c) + \frac{e^\varepsilon\varphi(c)}\mu. \tag{20.2}\]
Cancel. By step 1 the first and last terms cancel, leaving \(-e^\varepsilon\Phi(c) < 0\). So \(\delta_\mu\) is strictly decreasing in \(\varepsilon\).
Differentiate in \(\mu\). \(\frac{da}{d\mu} = \frac12 + \frac\varepsilon{\mu^2}\) and \(\frac{dc}{d\mu} = -\frac12 + \frac\varepsilon{\mu^2}\), so \(\frac{d\delta_\mu}{d\mu} = \varphi(a)\big(\frac12 + \frac\varepsilon{\mu^2}\big) - e^\varepsilon\varphi(c)\big(-\frac12 + \frac\varepsilon{\mu^2}\big)\). Replace \(e^\varepsilon\varphi(c)\) by \(\varphi(a)\) (step 1): the \(\varepsilon/\mu^2\) terms cancel and the result is \(\varphi(a) > 0\).
Check. At \(\mu = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(c = -1.5\) and the slope is \(-e\,\Phi(-1.5) = -0.1816\). A central finite difference with step \(10^{-6}\) gives \(-0.1816\) too, and the script evaluates the identity of step 1 to \(0.0\) in floating point. At \(\varepsilon = 0\), \(\delta_1(0) = \Phi(\frac12) - \Phi(-\frac12) = 2\Phi(\frac12) - 1 = 0.3829\), the total variation distance.

The slope \(-e^\varepsilon\Phi(c)\) is the correction term of the bad-event bound, \(e^\varepsilon Q(B)\), so the two terms of the exact \(\delta\) are tied together by one derivative.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.4 Calibrate by hand

Exercise 4. Calibrate by hand. Run bisection on \(\ln\mu\) over \([10^{-3}, 100]\) for \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), and compare the result with the classic formula. Check: \(\mu^* = 0.124106\), so \(\sigma^* = 8.0576\,\Delta_2f\), against the classic 10.5976 (a ratio of 1.315). (Analytic calibration)







TipSolution






Why bisection works. By Exercise 3, \(\delta_\mu(0.5)\) is strictly increasing in \(\mu\), so \(\delta_\mu(0.5) = 10^{-6}\) has exactly one root, and at any trial \(\mu\) the sign of \(\delta_\mu(0.5) - 10^{-6}\) says on which side of it you are.
The steps. Take the midpoint in \(\ln\mu\), \(\sqrt{\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\mu_{\mathrm{hi}}}\). If \(\delta_\mu(0.5) > 10^{-6}\) the noise is too small, so the root is below and \(\mu_{\mathrm{hi}}\) moves down; otherwise \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\) moves up. The first midpoint is \(\sqrt{10^{-3}\times100} = 0.316228\), where \(\delta\) is too large. Table 20.1 shows the interval after selected steps.

The classic formula. \(\sigma = \Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25\times10^6)}/0.5 = 10.5976\,\Delta_2f\), a factor of 1.315 more, or 73% more variance.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.5 Composing Gaussian mechanisms exactly

Exercise 5. Composing Gaussian mechanisms exactly. You answer \(k\) queries, each with \(\Delta_2 = 1\), by adding independent \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) noise to each. Show that the \(k\) answers together are one Gaussian mechanism with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt k\), so their exact privacy curve is \(\delta_{\sqrt k/\sigma}(\varepsilon)\). Compare with basic composition. Check: \(k = 16\), \(\sigma = 4\) gives \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); basic composition with \(\delta/16\) per query gives \(\varepsilon = 16 \times 1.0864 = 17.3818\). (Fact 1, sensitivity of a concatenation)







TipSolution






Stack the queries. Let \(F(D) = (f_1(D), \dots, f_k(D)) \in \mathbb R^k\) (each \(f_i\) real-valued, or stack the coordinates if they are vectors). The release is \(F(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_k)\), because the noises are independent with the same variance.
Its sensitivity. \(\|F(D) - F(D')\|_2^2 = \sum_i|f_i(D) - f_i(D')|^2 \le k\), so \(\Delta_2F \le \sqrt k\).
Its privacy curve. By the chapter’s analytic result, the release is \((\varepsilon, \delta_\mu(\varepsilon))\)-DP with \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\) for every \(\varepsilon\), and exactly that when some pair reaches \(\Delta_2F = \sqrt k\).
Check. \(k = 16\), \(\sigma = 4\): \(\mu = 4/4 = 1\). Solving \(\delta_1(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) gives \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\), the value read off Figure 20.2 for \(\sigma/\Delta_2 = 1\).
Basic composition. Each query alone has \(\mu = 1/4\). Spend \(\delta/16 = 6.25\times10^{-7}\) on each: solving \(\delta_{1/4}(\varepsilon) = 6.25\times10^{-7}\) gives \(\varepsilon = 1.0864\) per query, and basic composition adds them to \(\varepsilon = 17.3818\) at total \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). That is four times the exact value.

Why. Basic composition adds \(\varepsilon\)’s, so it grows like \(k\). The exact curve depends on \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\), which grows like \(\sqrt k\): sixteen queries cost as much as one query with a quarter of the noise. The same argument holds for adaptively chosen queries, with more care; Advanced and optimal composition and Part 4 develop it.
Gaussian noise composes into Gaussian noise, so for Gaussian mechanisms the exact composed guarantee is a one-line formula.

title: 20  Exercises: The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.6 A private mean of vectors

Exercise 6. A private mean of vectors. Each of \(n\) records is a vector in \(\mathbb R^d\) with \(\|x\|_2 \le 1\), and neighbours replace one record. Find \(\Delta_2\) and an upper bound on \(\Delta_1\) for the mean, and compare the expected squared \(\ell_2\) error of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. Check: at \(d = 100\), \(n = 10{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the root-mean-square \(\ell_2\) errors are 0.02828 (Laplace) and 0.00746 (Gaussian). (Equation 20.8, dense queries)







TipSolution






\(\ell_2\) sensitivity. Replacing \(x\) by \(x'\) moves the mean by \((x' - x)/n\), and \(\|x' - x\|_2 \le \|x\|_2 + \|x'\|_2 \le 2\). So \(\Delta_2 = 2/n\), reached by \(x' = -x\).
\(\ell_1\) sensitivity. By Equation 20.8, \(\Delta_1 \le \sqrt d\,\Delta_2 = 2\sqrt d/n\), reached when \(x\) and \(x'\) are opposite vectors with all coordinates \(\pm1/\sqrt d\).
Laplace error. Each of the \(d\) coordinates has variance \(2b^2\) with \(b = \Delta_1/\varepsilon\), so \(\mathbb E\|Z\|_2^2 = 2db^2\) and the root-mean-square \(\ell_2\) error is \(\sqrt{2d}\cdot\frac{2\sqrt d}{n\varepsilon} = \frac{2\sqrt2\,d}{n\varepsilon}\).
Gaussian error. \(\mathbb E\|Z\|_2^2 = d\sigma^2\) with \(\sigma = \Delta_2\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\), so the root-mean-square error is \(\sqrt d\cdot\frac2n\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\).
Check. At \(d = 100\), \(n = 10{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): Laplace gives \(2\sqrt2\times100/10^4 = 0.02828\). With \(\sigma_1(1, 10^{-5}) = 3.7306\), Gaussian gives \(10\times2\times10^{-4}\times3.7306 = 0.00746\). The ratio is 3.79, and it grows like \(\sqrt d\).

Bounding a vector’s \(\ell_2\) norm makes its \(\ell_1\) sensitivity grow like \(\sqrt d\), so for norm-bounded data, such as clipped gradients, Gaussian noise is the right choice.

The solutions use the chapter’s notation and its abbreviation for differential privacy (DP). \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), \(L = \ln(p/q)\) is the privacy loss with \(Y \sim P\), \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\), and randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) is truthful with probability \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\).

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
Exercise 1. The sharp mean loss. Show that \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le \varepsilon^2/2\) and \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le \varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) for every \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), and that the ratio of the two mean bounds tends to \(\frac12\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the three values are 0.4621, 0.5 and 1.7183. (Fact 3, Taylor expansion)







TipSolution






\(\tanh u \le u\) for \(u \ge 0\). Both sides are 0 at \(u = 0\), and the derivative of \(\tanh\) is \(1 - \tanh^2 u \le 1\), the derivative of \(u\). So \(\tanh u\) never catches up. With \(u = \varepsilon/2\): \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le \varepsilon\cdot\varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon^2/2\).
Against \(\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\). Write \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon/2} - e^{-\varepsilon/2}}{e^{\varepsilon/2} + e^{-\varepsilon/2}} = \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1}{e^\varepsilon + 1}\) (multiply numerator and denominator by \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\)). The denominator \(e^\varepsilon + 1\) is at least 2, so \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le \frac12(e^\varepsilon - 1) \le e^\varepsilon - 1\).
The ratio. By step 2, \(\frac{\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)}{\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)} = \frac{1}{e^\varepsilon + 1}\), which tends to \(\frac12\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\) and decreases as \(\varepsilon\) grows.
Check. Table 21.1 lists the three values.

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.2 When does advanced composition pay?

Exercise 2. When does advanced composition pay? Show that Equation 21.7 is below \(k\varepsilon\) exactly when \(k > 2\ln(1/\delta')/(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2\), for \(\varepsilon < \ln 2\). Check: for \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\) the threshold is 28.8, so advanced composition wins from \(k = 29\). (Advanced composition)







TipSolution






Write the inequality. \(\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1) < k\varepsilon\).
Divide by \(\varepsilon > 0\) and collect the \(k\) terms: \(\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} < k(2 - e^\varepsilon)\).
Sign. For \(\varepsilon < \ln 2\), \(2 - e^\varepsilon > 0\), so both sides are positive and squaring keeps the inequality: \(2k\ln(1/\delta') < k^2(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2\).
Divide by \(k(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2 > 0\): \(k > 2\ln(1/\delta')/(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2\). (For \(\varepsilon \ge \ln 2\) the right side of step 2 is not positive, and advanced composition never wins.)
Check. \(2\ln 10^5 = 23.03\) and \((2 - e^{0.1})^2 = 0.8948^2 = 0.8007\), so the threshold is 28.8. The script confirms: advanced composition gives 2.8336 at \(k = 28\) (above \(2.8\)) and 2.8891 at \(k = 29\) (below \(2.9\)).

With the \(\tanh\) mean term, the same steps give \(k > 2\ln(1/\delta')/(1 - \tanh(\varepsilon/2))^2\), which is 25.5 at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), so that form wins from \(k = 26\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the original form needs \(k > 186.6\).
Advanced composition is a large-\(k\) tool: below about \(2\ln(1/\delta')\) steps, the \(\delta'\) it spends buys nothing.

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.3 Two rounds by hand

Exercise 3. Two rounds by hand. From Table 21.2, compute \(\delta(\varepsilon')\) for two rounds of randomized response at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\), for all \(\varepsilon' \in [0, 2\ln 3]\). Check: \(\delta(0) = \frac12\), \(\delta(\ln 3) = \frac38\), \(\delta(2\ln 3) = 0\). Compare with what basic composition says. (Fact 1, optimal composition)







TipSolution






Which outputs count. By Fact 1, \(\delta(\varepsilon') = \sum_y p(y)(1 - e^{\varepsilon' - L(y)})_+\), and only outputs with \(L(y) > \varepsilon'\) contribute. For \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\), the outputs with \(L = 0\) and \(L = -2\ln 3\) never count. Only \((0, 0)\), with \(p = \frac9{16}\) and \(L = 2\ln 3\), counts, and only while \(\varepsilon' < 2\ln 3\).
The curve. \(\delta(\varepsilon') = \frac9{16}\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon'}/9\big) = \frac{9 - e^{\varepsilon'}}{16}\) for \(0 \le \varepsilon' \le 2\ln 3\), and 0 beyond.
Check. \(\varepsilon' = 0\): \(\frac{8}{16} = \frac12\). \(\varepsilon' = \ln 3\): \(\frac{6}{16} = \frac38\). \(\varepsilon' = 2\ln 3\): \(0\). Enumeration of the four outputs and Equation 21.11 give the same three values.
Compared with basic composition. Basic composition says \((2\ln 3, 0)\), the end point of this curve, and is exact there. For two rounds there is nothing to gain at \(\delta = 0\). What the curve adds is every other point: for example, the pair is \((\ln 3, \frac38)\)-DP. A \(\delta\) of \(\frac38\) is useless for privacy, which is the point: with \(k = 2\) the loss has not had the chance to concentrate.

Composition gains come from many steps. With two steps the worst output has probability \(\frac9{16}\), and you cannot trade it for a small \(\delta\).
crumbs: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.4 The per-step δ

Exercise 4. The per-step \(\delta\). Prove the identity \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k \le k\delta\) used for advanced composition with \(\delta > 0\), and show that Equation 21.11 is non-trivial only for a target \(\delta_{\text{total}} > 1 - (1 - \delta)^k\). Check: with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), \(\delta = 5\times10^{-8}\), \(k = 100\) and \(\delta_{\text{total}} = 10^{-5}\), the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) is 4.4469 and advanced composition gives 5.9926. (Optimal composition)







TipSolution






The inequality is a union bound. \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k\) is the probability that at least one of \(k\) independent events of probability \(\delta\) happens: some step shows its flag. The union bound gives at most \(k\delta\). (Or by induction: \((1 - \delta)^{k} \ge (1 - \delta)^{k-1} - \delta \ge 1 - (k - 1)\delta - \delta\).)
The floor of Equation 21.11. \(\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon') \ge 0\), so the right side of Equation 21.11 is at least \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k\) for every \(\varepsilon'\). This floor is attained by the composed four-point pair: the flags have infinite loss. So no finite \(\varepsilon'\) achieves a smaller total \(\delta\), and the script returns \(\varepsilon' = \infty\) for a target of \(4\times10^{-6}\).
Above the floor. For a target \(\delta_{\text{total}} > 1 - (1 - \delta)^k\), solve \(\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon') = \frac{\delta_{\text{total}} - (1 - (1 - \delta)^k)}{(1 - \delta)^k}\), a pure randomized-response problem.
Check. \(1 - (1 - 5\times10^{-8})^{100} = 4.999988\times10^{-6}\), just below \(k\delta = 5\times10^{-6}\). That leaves about \(5\times10^{-6}\) for the randomized-response part, and the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) is 4.4469. Advanced composition with \(\delta' = 10^{-5} - 100 \times 5\times10^{-8} = 5\times10^{-6}\) gives 5.9926, and its \(\tanh\) form 5.4404.

The per-step \(\delta\) is spent outright, step by step; only what is left can be traded against \(\varepsilon'\).

section: 21.5 Which pairs factor through randomized response?
text:
21.5 Which pairs factor through randomized response?

Exercise 5. Which pairs factor through randomized response? For \(P = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\) and \(Q = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5)\), find the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for which Equation 21.10 is a valid channel, and write the channel. Hint: a row of \(K\) goes negative exactly where the pair violates \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Check: \(\varepsilon = \ln 2.5 = 0.9163\); the channel rows are then \((0.7, 0.3, 0)\) and \((0, 0.3, 0.7)\). (Randomized response is the worst)







TipSolution






Positivity. \(K(y \mid 0) \ge 0\) iff \(e^\varepsilon p(y) \ge q(y)\), and \(K(y \mid 1) \ge 0\) iff \(e^\varepsilon q(y) \ge p(y)\). Together: \(e^\varepsilon \ge \max_y\max(p/q, q/p)\), that is \(\varepsilon \ge \max_y|L(y)|\).
The ratios. \(p/q = 2.5, 1, 0.4\) on the three outputs. The largest \(|\ln(p/q)|\) is \(\ln 2.5 = 0.9163\). So the smallest valid \(\varepsilon\) is \(\ln 2.5\), the pair’s pure-DP level.
The channel. With \(e^\varepsilon = 2.5\), \(K(\cdot \mid 0) = (2.5P - Q)/1.5 = (1.05, 0.45, 0)/1.5 = (0.7, 0.3, 0)\) and \(K(\cdot \mid 1) = (2.5Q - P)/1.5 = (0, 0.3, 0.7)\).
Check. \(t = 2.5/3.5 = 0.7143\), and \(t(0.7, 0.3, 0) + (1 - t)(0, 0.3, 0.7) = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) = P\). Below \(\ln 2.5\) the construction fails: at \(\varepsilon = 0.8\), \(K(\cdot \mid 0) = (0.7448, 0.3, -0.0448)\) has a negative entry, at the third output, where \(q/p = 2.5 > e^{0.8}\).

At the tight level each row of the channel puts zero mass on one output: randomized response’s “report 0” can never produce the output that most favours \(D'\).

title: 21  Exercises: Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.6 Composing Gaussians exactly

Exercise 6. Composing Gaussians exactly. Show that \(k\) Gaussian mechanisms with noise \(\sigma\) on sensitivity-1 queries, composed non-adaptively, have the same \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) as one Gaussian pair with shift \(\sqrt k/\sigma\). Hint: the privacy loss of each step is normal; use Part 1’s Gaussian pair. Then explain the gap in Figure 21.4 by comparing the mean loss \(k/(2\sigma^2)\) with \(k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) for the per-step \(\varepsilon_0\) at \(\delta_0 = 5\times10^{-9}\). Check: for \(\sigma = 20\) and \(k = 1{,}000\), the exact \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is 7.511, the true mean loss is 1.25, and \(k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 29.93\). (Optimal composition, Gaussian pair)







TipSolution






One step. The worst pair of a sensitivity-1 Gaussian mechanism is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). With \(\mu = 1/\sigma\), Part 1 (Divergences, the Gaussian pair) shows that its privacy loss under \(P\) is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\).
\(k\) steps. By Fact 2 of the chapter, the total loss is the sum of \(k\) independent such losses: normal with mean \(k\mu^2/2\) and variance \(k\mu^2\).
One pair with shift \(\mu_k = \sqrt k\mu\) has loss with mean \(\mu_k^2/2 = k\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu_k^2 = k\mu^2\): the same distribution.
Same loss, same curve. By Fact 1, \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) depends on the pair only through the distribution of \(L\) under \(P\). So the two curves agree. (The same holds in the other direction by symmetry.)
Check. \(\mu_k = \sqrt{1000}/20 = 1.5811\), and solving the Gaussian \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) by bisection gives \(\varepsilon = 7.511\).
The gap. The true mean loss of the run is \(k\mu^2/2 = 1000/800 = 1.25\). The per-step point at \(\delta_0 = 5\times10^{-9}\) is \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.2453\), and optimal composition must assume the worst mechanism with that \(\varepsilon_0\), randomized response, whose mean loss per step is \(\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). Over \(k\) steps that is \(29.93\), 24 times the truth. The fluctuation term \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\) with the remaining \(\delta' = 5\times10^{-6}\) is 38.32 on top.
Why. A Gaussian step’s loss is rarely as large as \(\varepsilon_0\): \(\varepsilon_0\) was chosen so that it is exceeded only with probability about \(\delta_0\). Randomized response with the same \(\varepsilon_0\) has loss \(\pm\varepsilon_0\) on every output. Replacing each Gaussian step by its worst-case \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) stand-in inflates both the mean and the spread of the total.

The \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) summary of one step is a worst case over a whole class, and composing worst cases compounds the loss. Composing the actual loss distributions avoids it.

21.7 Two different steps

Exercise 7. Two different steps. Compose randomized response at \(\varepsilon_1 = \ln 3\) with randomized response at \(\varepsilon_2 = \ln 2\). List the four outputs with their probabilities and losses, and compute \(\delta(\varepsilon')\) at \(\varepsilon' = 0\), \(\ln\frac32\) and \(\ln 2\). Check: \(\frac12\), \(\frac38\) and \(\frac13\). (Fact 1, Fact 2)







TipSolution






The two steps. The first is truthful with probability \(\frac34\), the second with \(\frac23\).
The four outputs (Table 21.2). On \(D\) the probabilities multiply. On \(D'\) “truthful” and “flipped” swap roles. By Fact 2 the loss adds: \(\pm\ln 3 \pm \ln 2\).

\(\delta(0)\). The outputs with \(e^L > 1\) count: \(\frac12(1 - \frac16) + \frac14(1 - \frac23) = \frac5{12} + \frac1{12} = \frac12\).
\(\delta(\ln\frac32)\). Only \(e^L = 6\) counts: \(\frac12(1 - \frac{3/2}{6}) = \frac12\cdot\frac34 = \frac38\).
\(\delta(\ln 2)\). Again only \(e^L = 6\): \(\frac12(1 - \frac26) = \frac13\). And \(\delta(\ln 6) = 0\), the basic composition point \((\ln 3 + \ln 2, 0)\).

With different \(\varepsilon_i\) the loss takes \(2^k\) distinct values in general, not \(k + 1\). For two steps you can list them; for many, the exact computation is #P-complete, as Murtagh & Vadhan showed.

The solutions use the chapter’s notation. A selection problem has \(k\) candidates with scores \(u(D, r)\) of sensitivity \(\Delta\), and \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) = \max_r u(D, r)\). \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) and \(\mathrm{Gumbel}(\beta)\) are given by their scales, and logarithms are natural. AboveThreshold is the sparse vector algorithm of the chapter.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
Exercise 1. The factor 2 is needed. Use weights \(e^{\varepsilon u}\) (no 2) with \(\Delta = 1\) on \(k\) candidates and the neighbours \(u(D) = (1, 0, \dots, 0)\), \(u(D') = (0, 1, \dots, 1)\). Compute the privacy loss of the output “candidate 1” and show that it tends to \(2\varepsilon\) as \(k \to \infty\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) it is 1.3106 for \(k = 3\) and 1.9977 for \(k = 1000\). (Exponential mechanism, the two factors)







TipSolution






The pair is allowed. Every score moves by exactly 1, so \(\Delta = 1\). The scores are not monotone: candidate 1 goes down while all others go up.
On \(D\). Candidate 1 has weight \(e^\varepsilon\) and the other \(k - 1\) have weight 1, so \(\Pr[1 \mid D] = \dfrac{e^\varepsilon}{e^\varepsilon + k - 1}\).
On \(D'\). Candidate 1 has weight 1 and the others \(e^\varepsilon\), so \(\Pr[1 \mid D'] = \dfrac{1}{1 + (k - 1)e^\varepsilon}\).
The ratio splits into the derivation’s two factors: \[\frac{\Pr[1 \mid D]}{\Pr[1 \mid D']} = \underbrace{e^\varepsilon}_{\text{numerator}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{1 + (k - 1)e^\varepsilon}{e^\varepsilon + k - 1}}_{\text{normalizer}}. \tag{22.1}\]
The values. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the script gives a privacy loss of 1.0000 for \(k = 2\) (the normalizer factor is exactly 1), 1.3106 for \(k = 3\), 1.7761 for \(k = 10\) and 1.9977 for \(k = 1000\). The closed form and the mechanism’s probabilities agree to four decimals.
The limit. Divide numerator and denominator of the normalizer factor by \(k - 1\): it tends to \(e^\varepsilon/1 = e^\varepsilon\). The ratio tends to \(e^{2\varepsilon}\), so the loss tends to \(2\varepsilon\).

With the correct weights \(e^{\varepsilon u/2}\) the same calculation gives at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\cdot e^{\varepsilon/2} = e^\varepsilon\).
The two factors of the privacy proof are both reached here: candidate 1’s weight drops by \(e^\varepsilon\), and the normalizer, dominated by the \(k - 1\) competitors, rises by nearly \(e^\varepsilon\). Monotone scores cannot do both at once, which is why only they may drop the 2.
crumbs: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.2 A private median

Exercise 2. A private median. Records take values in \(\{0, 1, \dots, 100\}\). Use the exponential mechanism over \(r \in \{0, \dots, 100\}\) with score \(u(D, r) = -\big|\#\{i : x_i < r\} - \#\{i : x_i > r\}\big|\). Show that \(\Delta u = 1\) under add/remove, and use Equation 22.5 to show that with probability at least 0.95 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the output’s score is within 15.22 of the best score. When some candidate splits the data evenly, this means \(\big|\#\{x_i < r\} - \#\{x_i > r\}\big| \le 15.22\). Hint: \(k = 101\) and \(t = \ln 20\). (Utility theorem)







TipSolution





Sensitivity.

Fix a candidate \(r\) and write \(a = \#\{x_i < r\}\), \(c = \#\{x_i > r\}\), so \(u = -|a - c|\).
Adding a record \(x\) increases \(a\) by 1 if \(x < r\), increases \(c\) by 1 if \(x > r\), and changes neither if \(x = r\). So \(a - c\) changes by at most 1.
By the reverse triangle inequality, \(\big||a' - c'| - |a - c|\big| \le |(a' - c') - (a - c)| \le 1\). Removing a record is the same step backwards. So \(\Delta u = 1\).
The script checks this by brute force on the dataset below: adding a record of every possible value and removing each distinct value, the largest change of any score is 1.

Utility.

There are \(k = 101\) candidates. With \(t = \ln 20\), \(e^{-t} = 0.05\).
Equation 22.5 gives a gap of at most \(\frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}(\ln k + t) = 2(\ln 101 + \ln 20) = 2\ln 2020 = 15.22\) with probability at least 0.95.
If some candidate \(r^*\) has as many records below it as above it, \(\mathrm{OPT} = 0\), and the gap is the selected candidate’s \(|a - c|\) itself.

A concrete dataset. Take \(n = 1001\) records \(x_i = \lfloor 100\,(i/1000)^2\rfloor\) for \(i = 0, \dots, 1000\), skewed toward 0. The median is 25. Values repeat (ten records equal 25), so no candidate splits the data evenly: at \(r = 25\), 500 records are below and 491 above, so \(\mathrm{OPT} = -9\). title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.3 The noisy maximum value

Exercise 3. The noisy maximum value. For independent \(G_r \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\beta)\), show that \(\max_r(u_r + G_r)\) is Gumbel with scale \(\beta\) and location \(\beta\ln\sum_re^{u_r/\beta}\), so its mean is \(\beta\big(\ln\sum_re^{u_r/\beta} + \gamma\big)\) with \(\gamma = 0.5772\) the Euler–Mascheroni constant. Check it on the five scores of Table 22.5 with \(\beta = 2\). Hint: \(\Pr[\max \le x] = \prod_rF(x - u_r)\). (Gumbel-max)







TipSolution






The maximum is below \(x\) when every term is. The terms are independent, and \(u_r + G_r \le x\) means \(G_r \le x - u_r\). With the Gumbel cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(F(g) = \exp(-e^{-g/\beta})\), \[\Pr\Big[\max_r(u_r + G_r) \le x\Big] = \prod_r\exp\big(-e^{-(x - u_r)/\beta}\big) = \exp\Big(-e^{-x/\beta}\sum_re^{u_r/\beta}\Big). \tag{22.2}\]
Recognize a shifted Gumbel. Write \(\sum_re^{u_r/\beta} = e^{\ell/\beta}\), that is \(\ell = \beta\ln\sum_re^{u_r/\beta}\). The CDF is \(\exp(-e^{-(x - \ell)/\beta})\): a Gumbel with scale \(\beta\) and location \(\ell\).
The mean of a Gumbel. For \(G \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(1)\), substitute \(w = e^{-g}\): \(\mathbb E G = \int_0^\infty(-\ln w)\,e^{-w}\,dw = -\Gamma'(1) = \gamma\). Scaling and shifting give \(\mathbb E\max = \ell + \beta\gamma\).
Check. For scores \((4, 3, 3, 1, 0)\) and \(\beta = 2\): \(\ell = 2\ln(e^2 + 2e^{1.5} + e^{0.5} + 1) = 5.8890\), and the mean is \(5.8890 + 2\times0.5772 = 7.0434\). A million simulated draws give 7.0430.

The location \(\ell\) is the “soft maximum” of the scores: it lies between \(\max_ru_r = 4\) and \(\max_ru_r + \beta\ln k = 4 + 2\ln5 = 7.2189\).
The noisy maximum is a smooth function of all the scores, not of the winner’s alone. Releasing it is a separate numeric query, which needs its own budget; report-noisy-max releases only the index.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.4 Splitting the budget of AboveThreshold

Exercise 4. Splitting the budget of AboveThreshold. With \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon_1)\) and \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\), redo the accuracy derivation to get \(\alpha = \max\big(2\Delta\ln(2/\beta)/\varepsilon_1,\ 4\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)/\varepsilon_2\big)\), and minimize it over \(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon\). Check: for \(k = 1000\), \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\Delta = 1\), the equal split gives 84.77 and the best split gives 49.76, with \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.148\). (Laplace tails, union bound)







TipSolution






Threshold noise. \(\Pr[|\rho| \ge \alpha/2] = e^{-(\alpha/2)\varepsilon_1/\Delta}\). This is at most \(\beta/2\) when \(\alpha \ge 2\Delta\ln(2/\beta)/\varepsilon_1\).
Query noise. By the union bound, \(\Pr[\max_i|\nu_i| \ge \alpha/2] \le k\,e^{-(\alpha/2)\varepsilon_2/(2\Delta)}\). This is at most \(\beta/2\) when \(\alpha \ge 4\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)/\varepsilon_2\).
Both. On the event that both noises are below \(\alpha/2\), which has probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the answers are \(\alpha\)-accurate exactly as in the chapter. So \(\alpha\) is the larger of the two requirements.
Minimize. Write \(a = 2\Delta\ln(2/\beta)\) and \(c = 4\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)\). As \(\varepsilon_1\) grows, \(a/\varepsilon_1\) falls and \(c/(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_1)\) rises, so the maximum is smallest where they are equal: \(a/\varepsilon_1 = c/\varepsilon_2 = \alpha^*\). Then \(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = (a + c)/\alpha^* = \varepsilon\), so \[\alpha^* = \frac{a + c}{\varepsilon} = \frac{2\Delta\ln(2/\beta) + 4\Delta\ln(2k/\beta)}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \varepsilon_1 = \frac{a}{a + c}\,\varepsilon. \tag{22.3}\]
Numbers. With \(k = 1000\), \(\beta = 0.05\): \(a = 2\ln40 = 7.38\) and \(c = 4\ln40000 = 42.39\). The equal split gives \(\max(14.76, 84.77) = 84.77\), which is Dwork & Roth’s \(8(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta))\). The best split gives \(\alpha^* = 49.76\) with \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.148\) and \(\varepsilon_2 = 0.852\).

The threshold noise is drawn once and the query noise \(k\) times, so the union bound makes the query noise the bottleneck. Giving it 85% of the budget improves the accuracy by 41% at the same privacy.

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.5 No query noise

Exercise 5. No query noise. In the two-query counterexample for Algorithm 5 of Table 22.6, with \(T = 0\) and \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2)\), compute \(\Pr[\bot\top \mid D]\) and \(\Pr[\bot\top \mid D']\). Check: 0.1967 and 0. (Reading a proof for the step that fails)







TipSolution






On \(D\), \(f = (0, 1)\). The first query says \(\bot\) when \(0 < \rho\), and the second says \(\top\) when \(1 \ge \rho\). So \(\Pr[\bot\top \mid D] = \Pr[0 < \rho \le 1]\).
Laplace CDF. \(\Pr[\rho \le 1] = 1 - \frac12e^{-1/2}\) and \(\Pr[\rho \le 0] = \frac12\), so the probability is \(\frac12(1 - e^{-1/2}) = 0.1967\). A million simulated runs give 0.1968.
On \(D'\), \(f = (1, 0)\). Now \(\bot\) needs \(1 < \rho\) and \(\top\) needs \(0 \ge \rho\). No value of \(\rho\) does both, so the probability is 0. A million simulated runs never produced \(\bot\top\).
Which step fails. In the AboveThreshold proof, step 3 shifts \(\nu_k\) to keep the \(\top\) consistent after \(\rho\) has been shifted for the \(\bot\)s. Without \(\nu_k\) there is nothing to shift, and the two conditions can become incompatible.

A probability that is positive on one dataset and zero on its neighbour has infinite privacy loss: one observation of \(\bot\top\) proves the data are \(D\), not \(D'\).

title: 22  Exercises: Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.6 Two candidates

Exercise 6. Two candidates. For two candidates whose scores differ by \(d\), compute the probability that the better one is selected by the exponential mechanism with weights \(e^{u/b}\) and by Laplace report-noisy-max with scale \(b\). Hint: the difference of two independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) variables has \(\Pr[Z_1 - Z_2 > x] = \frac12e^{-x/b}(1 + \frac{x}{2b})\) for \(x \ge 0\). Check: at \(d = b\), 0.7311 against 0.7241. Compare with the 50-model example, where Laplace noise did better. (Gumbel-max, Laplace differences)







TipSolution






Exponential mechanism. \(\Pr[\text{better}] = \dfrac{e^{d/b}}{e^{d/b} + 1} = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-d/b}}\), the logistic function of \(d/b\).
The difference of two Laplace variables. \(Z_2\) is symmetric, so \(Z_1 - Z_2\) has the law of \(Z_1 + Z_2\), whose density is the convolution \(\int\frac{1}{4b^2}e^{-|y|/b - |x - y|/b}\,dy\). For \(x \ge 0\), split at \(y = 0\) and \(y = x\): the pieces \(y < 0\) and \(y > x\) each give \(\frac b2e^{-x/b}\), and \(0 \le y \le x\) gives \(xe^{-x/b}\). So the density is \(\frac{1}{4b}\big(1 + \frac{|x|}{b}\big)e^{-|x|/b}\).
Its tail. \(\int_x^\infty\big(1 + \frac yb\big)e^{-y/b}\,dy = (2b + x)\,e^{-x/b}\), so \(\Pr[Z_1 - Z_2 > x] = \frac12e^{-x/b}\big(1 + \frac{x}{2b}\big)\).
Laplace report-noisy-max. The better candidate loses when \(Z_2 - Z_1 > d\), so \(\Pr[\text{better}] = 1 - \frac12e^{-d/b}\big(1 + \frac{d}{2b}\big)\).
Numbers. Table 22.2 compares the two.

Against the 50 models. With two candidates the exponential mechanism is better at every gap in the table. On the 50 models of the chapter, with the same scale \(b = 2\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), Laplace noise picks the best model with probability 0.4241 against 0.3935 and has the smaller expected gap, 1.40 against 1.54.

Neither private argmax dominates the other: which one selects better depends on how many competitors are close to the top. Both have the same privacy guarantee, so the choice is about accuracy on the score profiles you expect.

title: 23  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.1 Local sensitivity of the mean
Exercises for Beyond global sensitivity, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_sensitivity.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_sensitivity.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Datasets have a fixed size \(n\), neighbours differ in one replaced record, \(d\) is the Hamming distance, and \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) are the parameters of differential privacy (DP). Sorted values are \(x_1 \le \dots \le x_n\) in \([0, \Lambda]\), padded with \(x_i = 0\) for \(i \le 0\) and \(x_i = \Lambda\) for \(i > n\). \(A^{(k)}(D)\) is the largest local sensitivity within distance \(k\) of \(D\), and \(S^*_\beta(D) = \max_k e^{-k\beta}A^{(k)}(D)\). “The ages” are the chapter’s 1,001 synthetic ages (seed 0), with \(\Lambda = 100\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\).

title: 23  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
Exercise 1. Local sensitivity of the mean. For values in \([0, \Lambda]\) under the replace relation, show \(\mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{mean}}(D) = \max_i\max(x_i, \Lambda - x_i)/n\), and deduce \(\Lambda/(2n) \le \mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{mean}}(D) \le \Lambda/n\). Why can smooth sensitivity never gain more than a factor of 2 over global sensitivity for the mean? Check: the 1,001 ages of the chapter include an age clipped to 0, so \(\mathrm{LS} = \Delta = 0.0999\). (Local sensitivity)







TipSolution






One replacement. Replacing \(x_i\) by \(x'\) changes the sum by \(x' - x_i\), and the mean by \((x' - x_i)/n\).
Worst replacement of \(x_i\). Over \(x' \in [0, \Lambda]\), \(|x' - x_i|\) is largest at an endpoint: \(x' = 0\) gives \(x_i\), and \(x' = \Lambda\) gives \(\Lambda - x_i\). So the largest change is \(\max(x_i, \Lambda - x_i)/n\).
Worst record. Maximize over \(i\): \(\mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{mean}}(D) = \max_i\max(x_i, \Lambda - x_i)/n\).
Bounds. For any \(a \in [0, \Lambda]\), \(\max(a, \Lambda - a) \ge \Lambda/2\) (the two numbers add up to \(\Lambda\), so the larger is at least half), and \(\max(a, \Lambda - a) \le \Lambda\). So \(\Lambda/(2n) \le \mathrm{LS} \le \Lambda/n = \Delta\), the global sensitivity.
At most a factor of 2. Every smooth upper bound satisfies \(S^*_\beta(D) \ge \mathrm{LS}(D) \ge \Lambda/(2n) = \Delta/2\). Noise scaled by \(S^*\) is therefore at least half the global noise, before even paying the \(1/\alpha\) factor of the admissible noise.
The ages. The smallest age is 0 (six ages were clipped to 0), so \(\max(x_i, \Lambda - x_i) = 100\) for that record and \(\mathrm{LS} = 100/1001 = 0.0999 = \Delta\).

Local sensitivity helps when the statistic is insensitive on typical data but not in the worst case. For the mean, every dataset is within a factor of 2 of the worst case, so clipping, not smoothing, is the tool.

title: 23  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.2 A sharper Cauchy

Exercise 2. A sharper Cauchy. Show that \(\sup_{u \ge 0}\gamma u^{\gamma-1}/(1 + u^\gamma) = (\gamma - 1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\), so for the Cauchy the sliding constant is 1 rather than \(\gamma = 2\). Redo the pure-DP condition with this constant and find the largest \(\alpha\) for \(\beta = \varepsilon/6\). Check: \(\alpha = \varepsilon/2\), and the noise scale for the median age drops from 0.979 to 0.326. (Admissible noise)







TipSolution






Find the maximum. Let \(g(u) = \gamma u^{\gamma-1}/(1 + u^\gamma)\). It is 0 at \(u = 0\) (for \(\gamma > 1\)) and tends to 0 as \(u \to \infty\), so its maximum is at a critical point. By the quotient rule, \(g'(u) = 0\) when \[(\gamma - 1)u^{\gamma-2}(1 + u^\gamma) = \gamma u^{\gamma-1}\cdot u^{\gamma-1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\gamma - 1)(1 + u^\gamma) = \gamma u^\gamma\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u^\gamma = \gamma - 1. \tag{23.1}\]
Evaluate. There \(1 + u^\gamma = \gamma\), so \(g = u^{\gamma-1} = (\gamma - 1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\). A numerical maximum on a fine grid agrees (Table 23.1).

Redo the privacy loss. In step 4 of the chapter’s derivation, the mean value theorem now gives a sliding term of at most \(c_\gamma\alpha\) with \(c_\gamma = (\gamma - 1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\). The scale term (\(\beta\)) and the dilation term (\(\gamma\beta\)) are unchanged. So the condition becomes \(c_\gamma\alpha + (\gamma + 1)\beta \le \varepsilon\).
The Cauchy. With \(\gamma = 2\), \(c_2 = 1\) and \(\beta = \varepsilon/6\): \(\alpha \le \varepsilon - 3\varepsilon/6 = \varepsilon/2\).
The median age. \(S^*_{1/6} = 0.1632\) does not change, since \(\beta\) did not. The noise scale \(S^*/\alpha\) goes from \(6S^*/\varepsilon = 0.979\) to \(2S^*/\varepsilon = 0.326\), three times smaller.

Constants in admissibility lemmas are usually stated for convenience, not optimality. A direct bound on the privacy loss of your one noise distribution can recover a constant factor in the error.

title: 23  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.3 Other quantiles

Exercise 3. Other quantiles. Generalize Equation 23.15 to the \(r\)-th order statistic and compute the smooth sensitivity of the 90th percentile (\(r = 901\)) of the 1,001 ages with \(\beta = 1/6\). Why is it larger than the median’s although its local sensitivity is smaller? Check: \(\mathrm{LS} = 0.0114\), \(S^* = 0.2666\) at \(k = 7\). (Smooth sensitivity)







TipSolution






Local sensitivity. Replacing one record moves the \(r\)-th order statistic to anywhere in \([x_{r-1}, x_{r+1}]\) (Fact 4 of the chapter with \(j = r\), and the same two replacements, by 0 and by \(\Lambda\), attain both ends). So \(\mathrm{LS}_r(D) = \max(x_r - x_{r-1}, x_{r+1} - x_r)\).
Distance \(k\). The derivation of the median formula used the rank \(m\) only through “exactly \(m\) values are at or below the order statistic”. Replacing \(m\) by \(r\) everywhere gives \[A^{(k)}_r(D) = \max_{0 \le t \le k+1}\big(x_{r+t} - x_{r+t-k-1}\big), \tag{23.2}\] with the same padding: the windows now slide around rank \(r\). The script’s function order_stat_a_profile takes \(r\) as a parameter, and the median is the case \(r = (n + 1)/2\).
Compute. For the ages, \(x_{901} = 55.21\), \(\mathrm{LS} = 0.0114\), and \(S^*_{1/6} = 0.2666\) at \(k = 7\). The median has \(\mathrm{LS} = 0.1386\) but \(S^*_{1/6} = 0.1632\), also at \(k = 7\). With Cauchy noise the 90th percentile gets scale \(6S^*/\varepsilon = 1.599\).
Why the order flips. The local sensitivity is one gap, and a single gap is noisy: the 90th percentile happened to sit between two close values. The smooth sensitivity is governed by \(A^{(7)}\), the span of 8 consecutive values. Near the 90th percentile the data are sparser than near the median (the normal density is lower about 1.2 standard deviations above the mean), so 8 consecutive values span more.

Smooth sensitivity reflects the density of the data around the statistic, not one lucky gap. Quantiles in the tails cost more noise than the median.

title: 23  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.4 Sizing the proposal

Exercise 4. Sizing the proposal. With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), how large must \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D)\) be for propose-test-release to answer with probability at least 0.99? For the ages, what is the smallest \(b\) that achieves it? Check: distance 18 (17.73 rounded up), pass probability 0.9924; \(b = A^{(17)} = 0.7892\). (Propose-test-release)







TipSolution






The pass probability. With threshold \(T = \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon = 13.82\) and distance \(d \ge T\), the test passes when \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon) > T - d\), which has probability \(1 - \frac12e^{-\varepsilon(d - T)}\).
Solve for 0.99. \(\frac12e^{-\varepsilon(d - T)} \le 0.01\) means \(d \ge T + \ln(50)/\varepsilon = 13.82 + 3.91 = 17.73\).
Round up. The distance counts records, so it is an integer: \(d \ge 18\). At \(d = 18\) the pass probability is \(1 - \frac12e^{-(18 - 13.82)} = 0.9924\).
Translate into \(b\). \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) = \min\{k : A^{(k)}(D) > b\}\), and \(A^{(k)}\) is non-decreasing in \(k\). So \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) \ge 18\) exactly when \(A^{(17)}(D) \le b\).
The ages. \(A^{(17)} = 0.7892\), so the smallest proposal that passes with probability 0.99 is \(b = 0.7892\) years; the script confirms \(\operatorname{dist}_{0.7892} = 18\). The chapter’s \(b = 1\) has distance 21, with room to spare.

Propose-test-release needs stability against about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) changes plus a few more for reliability. The proposal has to cover the local sensitivity at that distance, not at distance 1.

title: 23  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.5 The number of blocks

Exercise 5. The number of blocks. Approximate Equation 23.18 by \((\theta B/n)^2 + \theta^2/n + 2(R/(B\varepsilon))^2\) and find the minimizing \(B\) in closed form. Compare with the exact optimum over the divisors of \(n = 10{,}000\). Check: \(B^* = (2R^2n^2/(\theta\varepsilon)^2)^{1/4} = 265.9\); the best divisor is 250. (Bias–variance trade-off)







TipSolution






Where the approximation comes from. The bias \(\theta/(n_b - 1)\) with \(n_b = n/B\) is about \(\theta B/n\) when blocks are large, and the sampling variance \(\operatorname{Var}(z)/B\) is about \(\theta^2/n\), which does not depend on \(B\).
Differentiate \(g(B) = \theta^2B^2/n^2 + 2R^2/(B^2\varepsilon^2)\): \(g'(B) = 2\theta^2B/n^2 - 4R^2/(B^3\varepsilon^2)\).
Set to zero: \(B^4 = 2R^2n^2/(\theta^2\varepsilon^2)\), so \(B^* = \big(2R^2n^2/(\theta\varepsilon)^2\big)^{1/4}\). The second derivative is positive, so this is a minimum.
Numbers. With \(R = 5\), \(n = 10^4\), \(\theta = \varepsilon = 1\): \(B^* = (2 \times 25 \times 10^8)^{1/4} = 265.9\).
Exact optimum. \(B\) must divide \(n\) for equal blocks. Evaluating the exact error Equation 23.18 at every divisor, the best is \(B = 250\) (blocks of 40), with error \(0.0396\). The neighbouring divisors are worse: 200 gives \(0.0421\) and 400 gives \(0.0465\).

At the optimum, bias and noise are of the same size, and \(B^*\) grows like \(\sqrt{n}\): more data buys more, smaller blocks.

title: 23  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.6 Clipping exponential data

Exercise 6. Clipping exponential data. For \(X \sim \mathrm{Exponential}(1)\), show \(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+] = e^{-C}\) and, ignoring the sampling term, that the best clip bound solves \(e^{-2C} = 2C/(n\varepsilon)^2\). Check: \(C^* = 5.692\) for \(n = 1000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\); \(3.616\) for \(n = 100\) and \(7.834\) for \(n = 10{,}000\). (Clipping)







TipSolution






The bias. \(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+] = \int_C^\infty(x - C)e^{-x}\,dx\). Substitute \(u = x - C\): \(e^{-C}\int_0^\infty ue^{-u}\,du = e^{-C}\). (This is memorylessness: given \(X > C\), the excess is again \(\mathrm{Exponential}(1)\), with mean 1, and \(\Pr[X > C] = e^{-C}\).)
The objective without the sampling term: \(e^{-2C} + 2C^2/(n\varepsilon)^2\).
Differentiate and set to zero: \(-2e^{-2C} + 4C/(n\varepsilon)^2 = 0\), that is \(e^{-2C} = 2C/(n\varepsilon)^2\). The left side falls and the right side rises in \(C\), so there is exactly one root, which bisection finds.
Numbers. For \(n = 1000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(C^* = 5.692\), where the bias is \(e^{-5.692} = 0.0034\), the noise standard deviation \(\sqrt2\,C^*/1000 = 0.0080\), and their combined root-mean-square error \(0.0087\). For \(n = 100\), \(C^* = 3.616\); for \(n = 10{,}000\), \(C^* = 7.834\).
Growth with \(n\). Taking logarithms, \(2C^* = 2\ln(n\varepsilon) - \ln(2C^*)\), so \(C^* \approx \ln(n\varepsilon)\) minus a slowly growing correction: each factor of 10 in \(n\) adds about \(\ln 10 = 2.3\) minus a little, as the three values show.

For a light (exponential) tail, the clip bound grows only logarithmically with \(n\varepsilon\). For heavier tails, such as the chapter’s log-normal incomes, it grows much faster.

title: 23  Exercises: Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.7 Smoothness at work

Exercise 7. Smoothness at work. For the degenerate pair \(D = (0, 0, 0, 0, 100)\) and \(D' = (0, 0, 0, 100, 100)\) with \(\beta = 1/6\), compute \(A^{(k)}\) for both and the smooth sensitivities. Check that their ratio is at most \(e^\beta\), and explain why it is exactly \(e^\beta\) here. Check: \(S^*(D) = 84.648\) at \(k = 1\), \(S^*(D') = 100\), ratio \(1.1814 = e^{1/6}\). (Smooth sensitivity)







TipSolution






\(D\), distance 0. \(n = 5\), \(m = 3\), so \(\mathrm{LS}(D) = \max(x_3 - x_2, x_4 - x_3) = \max(0, 0) = 0\).
\(D\), distance \(k \ge 1\). With \(k = 1\) the windows are \(x_3 - x_1 = 0\), \(x_4 - x_2 = 0\) and \(x_5 - x_3 = 100\), so \(A^{(1)} = 100\): replace \(x_4 = 0\) by 100 and the median sits at the bottom of a gap of 100. Since \(A^{(k)} \le \Lambda = 100\), \(A^{(k)} = 100\) for all \(k \ge 1\) (Table 23.2).
\(D'\). Already \(\mathrm{LS}(D') = x_4 - x_3 = 100\), so \(A^{(k)} = 100\) for every \(k\).

Smooth sensitivities. For \(D'\) the maximum of \(e^{-k/6}\times100\) is at \(k = 0\): \(S^*(D') = 100\). For \(D\) the \(k = 0\) term is 0, and the largest of the rest is at \(k = 1\): \(S^*(D) = 100e^{-1/6} = 84.648\).
The ratio is \(100/84.648 = 1.1814 = e^{1/6}\), exactly the largest ratio smoothness allows.
Why it is tight. \(D\)’s largest discounted term is \(D'\) itself, one step away. So \(S^*(D)\) is \(S^*(D')\) discounted by exactly one factor \(e^{-\beta}\), which is step 2 of the chapter’s smoothness proof holding with equality.

Compare with local sensitivity, which jumps from 0 to 100 on this pair and makes the release on \(D\) deterministic. Smooth sensitivity sees \(D'\) coming and already adds noise of scale 84.6/α on \(D\).

title: 24  Exercises: Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
Exercise 1. The cost of Algorithm 1. Show that the expected number of uniform draws for \(\mathrm{Bernoulli}(e^{-\gamma})\) is \(e\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}e^{-j} + e^{-n}e^{\gamma - n}\) with \(n = \lfloor\gamma\rfloor\), and that it is below \(\frac{e}{1 - e^{-1}} + 1\) for every \(\gamma\). Check: 3.9414 for \(\gamma = 5/2\). (Algorithm 1, Equation 24.7)







TipSolution






One unit coin. For \(\gamma' \le 1\), the loop draws one uniform integer per coin \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_K\), so it costs \(K\) draws, and \(\mathbb E[K] = e^{\gamma'}\) by Equation 24.7. A coin with \(\gamma' = 1\) costs \(e\) on average.
Which coins run. Write \(\gamma = n + \phi\) with \(n = \lfloor\gamma\rfloor\) and \(0 \le \phi < 1\). The \((j + 1)\)-th of the \(n\) coins with probability \(e^{-1}\) runs only if the first \(j\) all came up 1, which has probability \(e^{-j}\). The final coin, with probability \(e^{-\phi}\), runs only if all \(n\) came up 1, with probability \(e^{-n}\).
Add the expected costs. A coin that runs costs on average what step 1 says, so by linearity of expectation \[\mathbb E[\text{draws}] = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}e^{-j}\cdot e + e^{-n}\cdot e^{\phi}, \tag{24.1}\] which is the claimed formula since \(\phi = \gamma - n\).
The bound. The first sum is below the full geometric series \(e\sum_{j \ge 0}e^{-j} = \frac{e}{1 - e^{-1}} = 4.3003\). For \(n \ge 1\) the last term is \(e^{\phi - n} \le e^{1 - 1} = 1\). For \(n = 0\) the whole cost is \(e^\gamma < e\). Either way the total is below \(4.3003 + 1 = 5.3003\).
Check. For \(\gamma = 5/2\): \(n = 2\), \(\phi = \frac12\), so the cost is \(e(1 + e^{-1}) + e^{-2}e^{1/2} = 3.7183 + 0.2231 = 3.9414\). Over 20,000 coins the script counts 3.9233 draws per coin. At \(\gamma = \frac12\) the formula gives \(e^{1/2} = 1.6487\) (simulated 1.6597) and at \(\gamma = 1\) it gives \(e + e^{-1} = 3.0862\) (simulated 3.0854).

The cost jumps at each integer: just below 1 it is \(e = 2.7183\), at 1 it is 3.0862, because the split always runs a final coin, even for \(\phi = 0\), where that coin costs exactly one draw.

section: 24.2 Discrete Laplace as a difference of geometrics
text:
24.2 Discrete Laplace as a difference of geometrics

Exercise 2. Discrete Laplace as a difference of geometrics. Let \(G_1, G_2\) be independent with \(\Pr[G = g] = (1 - r)r^g\) for \(g \ge 0\). Show that \(G_1 - G_2 \sim \mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\) with \(r = e^{-1/b}\), the integer version of “a difference of exponentials is Laplace” in Probability distributions. Check: \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = 0] = 0.4621\) for \(r = e^{-1}\). (Fact 3, convolution)







TipSolution






Condition on \(G_2\). For \(z \ge 0\), \(G_1 - G_2 = z\) means \(G_1 = g + z\) when \(G_2 = g\), for some \(g \ge 0\). The events for different \(g\) are disjoint, so \[\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = z] = \sum_{g \ge 0}(1 - r)r^{g + z}\cdot(1 - r)r^g = (1 - r)^2r^z\sum_{g \ge 0}r^{2g}. \tag{24.2}\]
Sum the geometric series. \(\sum_gr^{2g} = \frac{1}{1 - r^2} = \frac{1}{(1 - r)(1 + r)}\), so \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = z] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}r^z\).
Negative \(z\). \(G_1 - G_2\) and \(G_2 - G_1\) have the same distribution (swap the names), so \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = -z] = \Pr[G_1 - G_2 = z]\), and the PMF is \(\frac{1 - r}{1 + r}r^{|z|}\) for all \(z\). That is \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\).
Check. At \(r = e^{-1}\), \(\Pr[G_1 - G_2 = 0] = \frac{1 - e^{-1}}{1 + e^{-1}} = 0.4621\). The script sums the convolution numerically and finds it within \(4.3\times10^{-19}\) of the PMF for every \(|z| \le 10\).

Algorithm 2 builds one geometric and a fair sign instead of two geometrics, because the sign trick needs only one coin; both give the same distribution.

24.3 Variance of the discrete Laplace

Exercise 3. Variance of the discrete Laplace. Show \(\frac{2r}{(1 - r)^2} = \frac{1}{2\sinh^2(1/(2b))}\), deduce that it is below \(2b^2\), and show that \(2b^2 - \operatorname{Var}Z \to \frac16\) as \(b \to \infty\). Check: 1.8413 at \(b = 1\) and 199.8334 at \(b = 10\). Hint: \(\sinh x \ge x\) and \(\sinh^2x = x^2 + x^4/3 + O(x^6)\). (Discrete Laplace)







TipSolution





Let \(x = \frac{1}{2b}\), so \(r = e^{-2x}\).

Rewrite. Divide the numerator and the denominator by \(r\): \(\frac{2r}{(1 - r)^2} = \frac{2}{(r^{-1/2} - r^{1/2})^2} = \frac{2}{(e^x - e^{-x})^2} = \frac{2}{4\sinh^2x} = \frac{1}{2\sinh^2x}\).
The bound. \(\sinh x = x + x^3/6 + \dots \ge x\) for \(x \ge 0\), so \(\frac{1}{2\sinh^2x} \le \frac{1}{2x^2} = 2b^2\), with strict inequality for every finite \(b\).
The gap. \(\sinh^2x = x^2(1 + x^2/3 + O(x^4))\), so \(\frac{1}{2\sinh^2x} = \frac{1}{2x^2}\big(1 - \frac{x^2}{3} + O(x^4)\big) = 2b^2 - \frac16 + O(1/b^2)\).

text:
24.4 Accuracy of the geometric mechanism

Exercise 4. Accuracy of the geometric mechanism. Show \(\Pr[|Z| \ge k] = \frac{2r^k}{1 + r}\) for \(k \ge 1\). For a count released at \(\varepsilon = 1\), find the smallest \(k\) with \(\Pr[|Z| > k] \le 0.05\), and compare with the continuous Laplace at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). Check: \(\Pr[|Z| \ge 3] = 0.0728\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), and \(k = 3\). (Discrete Laplace tails)







TipSolution






One tail. \(\Pr[Z \ge k] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\sum_{z \ge k}r^z = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\cdot\frac{r^k}{1 - r} = \frac{r^k}{1 + r}\).
Both tails. By symmetry, \(\Pr[|Z| \ge k] = \frac{2r^k}{1 + r}\) for \(k \ge 1\). (For \(k = 0\) it is 1, not \(\frac{2}{1 + r}\), because 0 is counted once.)
At \(\varepsilon = 1\) (\(b = 1\), \(r = e^{-1}\)): \(\Pr[|Z| \ge 3] = 2e^{-3}/(1 + e^{-1}) = 0.0728\) and \(\Pr[|Z| \ge 4] = 0.0268\). \(\Pr[|Z| > k] = \Pr[|Z| \ge k + 1]\), so the smallest \(k\) with \(\Pr[|Z| > k] \le 0.05\) is \(k = 3\): the released count is within 3 of the truth with probability at least 95%. For the continuous \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\), \(\Pr[|X| \ge 3] = e^{-3} = 0.0498\).
At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) (\(b = 10\)): the script finds the smallest radius is 30. The continuous Laplace has \(\Pr[|X| \ge k] = e^{-k/b} \le 0.05\) for \(k \ge b\ln20 = 29.96\). At large scales the two agree.

At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the comparison with the continuous Laplace is between an integer radius and a real one: the discrete noise can’t be 2.5, so its tail at 3 includes the mass the continuous one puts on \([2.5, 3)\).

text:
24.5 The acceptance rate of Algorithm 3

Exercise 5. The acceptance rate of Algorithm 3. Derive Equation 24.19 and show that \(A \to \sqrt{\pi/2}\,e^{-1/2}\) as \(\sigma \to \infty\). Check: \(A = 0.6629\) at \(\sigma^2 = 4\) and 0.7601 at \(\sigma^2 = 10^4\). Hint: \(\sigma/t \to 1\), and \(\sum_ye^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}/(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma) \to 1\) by Equation 24.17. (Rejection sampling, Poisson summation)







TipSolution






Average the acceptance over the proposal. \(A = \sum_y\Pr[Y = y]\,e^{-(|y| - \sigma^2/t)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) with \(\Pr[Y = y] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}e^{-|y|/t}\).
Combine the exponents, as in step 1 of the sampler’s derivation: \(-\frac{|y|}{t} - \frac{(|y| - \sigma^2/t)^2}{2\sigma^2} = -\frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\sigma^2}{2t^2}\). So \[A = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\,e^{-\sigma^2/(2t^2)}\sum_ye^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}, \tag{24.3}\] which is Equation 24.19.
Each factor as \(\sigma \to \infty\). \(t = \lfloor\sigma\rfloor + 1\) satisfies \(\sigma < t \le \sigma + 1\), so \(\sigma/t \to 1\) and \(e^{-\sigma^2/(2t^2)} \to e^{-1/2}\). Next, \(\frac{1 - r}{1 + r} = \tanh\frac{1}{2t}\), which is \(\frac{1}{2t}(1 + O(1/t^2))\). Finally Equation 24.17 at \(c = 0\) gives \(\sum_ye^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)} = \sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(1 + 2e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2} + \dots)\), so the sum is \(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma\) up to an error that vanishes like \(e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2}\).
Multiply. \(A \approx \frac{1}{2t}\cdot e^{-1/2}\cdot\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma \to \frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2}e^{-1/2} = \sqrt{\pi/2}\,e^{-1/2} = 0.7602\).
Check (Table 24.2).

24.6 Sums of discrete Gaussians

Exercise 6. Sums of discrete Gaussians. Compute the PMF of the sum of two independent \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\) variables and compare it with \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) for \(\sigma^2 = \frac14\), 1 and 4. Show that the sum’s variance is \(2\operatorname{Var}X\), and explain why it differs from the variance of \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) at small \(\sigma\). Check: at \(\sigma^2 = \frac14\), \(\Pr[\text{sum} = 0] = 0.6414\) against 0.5641. (Discrete Gaussian, Equation 24.15)







TipSolution






The convolution. \(\Pr[X_1 + X_2 = z] = \frac{1}{Z^2}\sum_xe^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}e^{-(z - x)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), with \(Z\) the discrete Gaussian normalizer.
Complete the square. \(x^2 + (z - x)^2 = 2(x - z/2)^2 + z^2/2\). So \[\Pr[X_1 + X_2 = z] = \frac{e^{-z^2/(4\sigma^2)}}{Z^2}\sum_xe^{-(x - z/2)^2/\sigma^2}. \tag{24.4}\] The factor \(e^{-z^2/(4\sigma^2)}\) is the \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) shape. The sum over \(x\) is the lattice sum of Equation 24.17 with variance \(\sigma^2/2\) and shift \(c = z/2\): an integer for even \(z\), a half-integer for odd \(z\).
Why it is not a discrete Gaussian. By the lemma, the lattice sum is larger at integer shifts. So even \(z\) get a little more weight than \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) gives them, and odd \(z\) a little less. By Equation 24.17, the ratio of the two values is \(\frac{1 + 2e^{-\pi^2\sigma^2} + \cdots}{1 - 2e^{-\pi^2\sigma^2} + \cdots}\), because \(2\pi^2(\sigma^2/2)k^2 = \pi^2\sigma^2k^2\) and \(\cos(2\pi k\cdot\frac12) = (-1)^k\).
Variance. Variances of independent variables add, so \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1 + X_2) = 2\operatorname{Var}X\), which is \(2\sigma^2\) minus twice the deficit of Equation 24.15. \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 2\sigma^2)\) has its own, much smaller deficit, because the deficit decays like \(e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2}\) and \(\sigma^2\) has doubled.

section: 24.7 The support argument as a test
text:
24.7 The support argument as a test

Exercise 7. The support argument as a test. In the 12-bit toy, the test “say \(D\) when \(y \notin \mathcal Y_{D'}\), and \(D'\) otherwise” never says \(D\) when the data are \(D'\), so its false negative rate is 0. Using the hypothesis-testing form of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, show that the toy sampler is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\) when \(\delta < 0.4791\), and find the bound the reverse test gives. Then show that after snapping to \(\Lambda = 1\) and clamping to \([-10, 10]\), every integer in \([-10, 10]\) is reachable from both inputs. Check: the reverse test gives \(\delta \ge 0.2033\). (Support argument, snapping)







TipSolution






The test. Say “\(D\)” when \(y \in S = \mathcal Y_D \setminus \mathcal Y_{D'}\), and “\(D'\)” otherwise. With the convention of The definition of differential privacy, the false positive rate \(\alpha\) is the chance of saying “\(D'\)” when the data are \(D\), and the false negative rate \(\beta\) the chance of saying “\(D\)” when they are \(D'\). Here \(\beta = \Pr[M(D') \in S] = 0\), because \(M(D')\) never lands in \(S\), and \(\alpha = 1 - \Pr[M(D) \in S] = 1 - 0.4791\) (Table 24.2).
The constraint. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP makes every test satisfy \(\alpha + e^\varepsilon\beta \ge 1 - \delta\); this is the hypothesis-testing form in The definition of differential privacy, and also the definition applied to the event \(S\) on which the test says “\(D\)”. With \(\beta = 0\) the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) multiplies nothing, and the inequality reads \(1 - 0.4791 \ge 1 - \delta\), that is, \(0.4791 \le \delta\). So for \(\delta < 0.4791\) no \(\varepsilon\) works.
The reverse test. Swap the roles: say “\(D'\)” when \(y \in S' = \mathcal Y_{D'} \setminus \mathcal Y_D\), and “\(D\)” otherwise. Its false positive rate is \(\Pr[M(D) \in S'] = 0\) and its true positive rate is \(\Pr[M(D') \in S'] = 0.2033\). DP must hold in both directions, and the other inequality of the hypothesis-testing form, \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\cdot\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\), then gives \(\delta \ge 0.2033\). The direction from \(D\) gives the stronger bound.
Snapping. With \(b = 1\), an output \(k \in \{-9, \dots, 9\}\) arises from input \(f \in \{0, 1\}\) when the rounded noise lands in an interval of width 1 around \(k - f\), which lies in \([-10.5, 9.5]\). The noise magnitudes \(\mathrm{round}(\ln(1/u))\) run from about \(2^{-12}\) up to \(40\ln2 \approx 27.7\), and consecutive ones differ by at most about \(2^{-11}\) of their size (consecutive \(u\) differ by a relative step of at most \(2^{-11}\), and \(\ln\) turns a relative step into an additive one). So every interval of width 1 below 27.7 contains noise values, with either sign. The clamp sends everything beyond \(\pm9.5\) to \(\pm10\), which both inputs reach. So all 21 integers in \([-10, 10]\) are reachable from both inputs, and the script confirms both supports have exactly 21 points with \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = 0\).

The support argument gives a lower bound on \(\delta\) from one single event, without any statistics. Auditing tools use exactly such events, found by search, to refute claimed guarantees.

title: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
Exercise 1. Warner’s forced-response variant. Each person answers truthfully with probability \(s\) and otherwise reports a fair coin. Show that this is randomized response with keep probability \(t = (1 + s)/2\), and find its \(\varepsilon_0\). Check: \(s = \frac12\) gives \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3 = 1.0986\). (Local randomizer)







TipSolution






The report equals the true bit in two ways. Either the person answers truthfully (probability \(s\)), or they toss the coin and it happens to show their bit (probability \((1 - s)\cdot\frac12\)). So \(\Pr[\text{report} = x] = s + \frac{1-s}{2} = \frac{1+s}{2} = t\), for both values of \(x\).
The report is the flipped bit otherwise, with probability \(1 - t = \frac{1-s}{2}\). A mechanism on one bit is determined by these two numbers, so this is randomized response with keep probability \(t\).
Its level. As in the table of output probabilities for randomized response, the largest ratio between the two rows is \(t/(1 - t)\), so \[\varepsilon_0 = \ln\frac{t}{1-t} = \ln\frac{1+s}{1-s}. \tag{25.1}\]
Check. \(s = \frac12\) gives \(t = 0.75\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3 = 1.0986\), Warner’s two coins. \(s = 0.25\) gives \(t = 0.625\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.5108\); \(s = 0.1\) gives \(t = 0.55\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.2007\).

For small \(s\), \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln\frac{1+s}{1-s} \approx 2s\): the truthful fraction is half the privacy level.

title: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.2 Why \(p = \frac12\)

Exercise 2. Why \(p = \frac12\). Among unary encodings with \(\frac{p(1-q)}{q(1-p)} = e^{\varepsilon_0}\), minimize the rare-value variance \(q(1-q)/(p-q)^2\) over \(p\). Show the minimum is at \(p = \frac12\). Check: at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) the minimum is 3.683, and the symmetric choice gives 3.918. (Debiasing, optimization)







TipSolution





Write \(a = e^{\varepsilon_0}\), and work with odds: \(P = p/(1-p)\) and \(Q = q/(1-q)\). The constraint says exactly \(P = aQ\).

Rewrite both pieces in odds. \(p = P/(1+P)\) and \(q = Q/(1+Q)\), so \[p - q = \frac{P - Q}{(1+P)(1+Q)}, \qquad q(1-q) = \frac{Q}{(1+Q)^2}. \tag{25.2}\]
The variance in one variable. Dividing, the factors \((1+Q)^2\) cancel: \[\frac{q(1-q)}{(p-q)^2} = \frac{Q(1+P)^2}{(P-Q)^2} = \frac{Q(1 + aQ)^2}{(a-1)^2Q^2} = \frac{(1 + aQ)^2}{(a-1)^2\,Q}. \tag{25.3}\]
Minimize over \(Q > 0\). The derivative of \((1 + aQ)^2/Q\) is \(\big(2aQ(1 + aQ) - (1 + aQ)^2\big)/Q^2 = (1 + aQ)(aQ - 1)/Q^2\). It is negative for \(aQ < 1\) and positive for \(aQ > 1\), so the minimum is at \(aQ = 1\), that is \(P = 1\), that is \(p = \frac12\). Then \(q = Q/(1+Q) = 1/(a + 1)\): optimized unary encoding.
The minimum value. At \(aQ = 1\), \((1 + 1)^2/((a-1)^2/a) = 4a/(a-1)^2\), the formula of the chapter.
Check at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\). \(4e/(e-1)^2 = 3.6827\). A grid search over \(p \in (0.25, 0.75]\) finds the minimum at \(p = 0.5000\) with the same value. Table 25.1 shows the curve around it; it is symmetric in \(p \leftrightarrow 1 - p\) because \((1 + aQ)^2/Q\) takes the same value at \(Q\) and at \(1/(a^2Q)\). The symmetric choice \(p = e^{1/2}/(e^{1/2} + 1) = 0.6225\) gives 3.9177.

3.6827
3.8361
4.3842






Since almost all bits are 0, what matters is how rarely a 0 becomes a 1; the optimum gives up accuracy on the single 1 to keep \(q\) small.
