title: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.3 How many people?

Exercise 3. How many people? At \(\varepsilon = 1\), how many people does randomized response need to estimate a fraction with standard deviation 0.001, and how many does the central Laplace mechanism need? Check: 920,674 local and 1,415 central. (Variance formulas)







TipSolution






Local. The standard deviation is \(\sqrt{e^\varepsilon/(n(e^\varepsilon - 1)^2)}\). Setting it to at most \(0.001\) and solving for \(n\): \(n \ge \frac{e^\varepsilon}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)^2}\cdot10^6\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the factor is \(e/(e-1)^2 = 0.9207\), so \(n \ge 920{,}674\) (rounding up).
Central. Under replace, the count of ones has sensitivity 1, and \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) on the count gives a fraction with standard deviation \(\sqrt2/(n\varepsilon)\). Setting it to at most \(0.001\): \(n \ge \sqrt2\times1000 = 1414.2\), so \(n \ge 1{,}415\).
Compare. The ratio is about 650. Halving the target standard deviation multiplies the local requirement by 4 but the central one only by 2: the \(\sqrt n\) gap seen from the side of sample sizes.

Local DP turns an error target \(\sigma\) into a sample size of order \(1/(\varepsilon^2\sigma^2)\); central DP into one of order \(1/(\varepsilon\sigma)\).
crumbs: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.4 Inverting the shuffle bound

Exercise 4. Inverting the shuffle bound. For \(n = 10^6\) and \(\delta = 10^{-8}\), find the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) for which Equation 25.12 gives \(\varepsilon \le 0.5\), and check the theorem’s condition. Check: \(\varepsilon_0 = 5.809\); the condition allows up to 8.093. (Bisection)







TipSolution






The bound increases with \(\varepsilon_0\). Both \(\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\) and the bracket increase with \(\varepsilon_0\), and \(\ln(1 + u)\) is increasing. So the set of allowed \(\varepsilon_0\) is an interval \([0, \varepsilon_0^*]\), and \(\varepsilon_0^*\) solves “bound \(= 0.5\)”.
The condition. \(\ln\big(n/(16\ln(2/\delta))\big) = \ln\big(10^6/(16\times19.11)\big) = 8.093\). The theorem applies only up to there.
Bisect on \([0, 8.093]\): at the upper end the bound exceeds 0.5, at 0 it is 0, so a root lies in between. Bisection gives \(\varepsilon_0^* = 5.809\), where the bound equals 0.5000. This is inside the condition.
Check the pieces. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 5.809\): \(e^{\varepsilon_0} = 333.3\), \(\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} = \tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 0.9940\), \(\ln(4/\delta) = 19.81\), the square-root term \(8\sqrt{333.3\times19.81}/\sqrt{10^6} = 0.6500\) and the \(1/n\) term \(8\times333.3/10^6 = 0.0027\). Their sum times \(0.9940\) is \(u = 0.6487\), and \(\ln(1 + u) = 0.5000\). Using \(u\) itself, the small-\(\varepsilon\) approximation, would overstate \(\varepsilon\) by 30% at this size.

A million users let each report be almost unrandomized (\(e^{\varepsilon_0} \approx 333\)) while the shuffled collection is \((0.5, 10^{-8})\)-DP.
crumbs: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.5 Sybils in the shuffle

Exercise 5. Sybils in the shuffle. An adversary controls \(m\) of the \(n\) senders. Show that the honest people’s guarantee is Equation 25.12 with \(n - m\) in place of \(n\). With \(n = 10^4\), \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), compare \(m = 0\) and \(m = 5{,}000\). Check: 0.5009 and 0.6535. (Post-processing)







TipSolution






Split the multiset. The shuffled output is the multiset union of the \(n - m\) honest reports and the \(m\) adversarial ones. The adversary chose its own reports, so it knows them.
The full output is a post-processing of the honest part. Given the honest multiset \(H\), the adversary’s view is \(H \cup A\), where \(A\) is a fixed (or independently random) multiset that does not depend on the honest records. A function of \(H\) and independent randomness is post-processing (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
The honest part is a shuffle of \(n - m\) reports. Its neighbouring datasets replace one honest record, and Theorem 3.1 applies with \(n - m\) people, under its condition with \(n - m\).
So the guarantee for an honest person is Equation 25.12 evaluated at \(n - m\). It cannot be better: the adversary can always remove its own reports, so they hide nobody.
Numbers. With \(m = 0\): \(n = 10{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 0.5009\) (condition: \(\varepsilon_0 \le 3.763\)). With \(m = 5{,}000\): \(5{,}000\) honest people, \(\varepsilon = 0.6535\) (condition: \(\varepsilon_0 \le 3.070\)). With \(m = 9{,}000\) only 1,000 honest people remain, the condition allows only \(\varepsilon_0 \le 1.460\), and the theorem says nothing at \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\).

Halving the honest crowd multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by about \(\sqrt2\) (here 1.30, slightly less because of the logarithm), and too few honest users void the guarantee entirely.
crumbs: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.6 Splitting Laplace noise

Exercise 6. Splitting Laplace noise. Show that if \(G_i, G'_i\) are independent \(\mathrm{Gamma}(1/n, b)\) (shape \(1/n\), scale \(b\)), then \(\sum_{i=1}^n(G_i - G'_i) \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\). Hint: compare moment generating functions; \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) has \(1/(1 - \lambda^2b^2)\). Check by simulation for \(n = 100\), \(b = 2\). Check: variance \(2b^2 = 8\). (Infinite divisibility)







TipSolution






Gamma moment generating function. For \(G \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(k, b)\) and \(\lambda < 1/b\), \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda G}] = (1 - b\lambda)^{-k}\). For \(-G'\), replace \(\lambda\) by \(-\lambda\): \((1 + b\lambda)^{-k}\).
One client’s share. \(G_i\) and \(G'_i\) are independent, so for \(|\lambda| < 1/b\), \[\mathbb E[e^{\lambda(G_i - G'_i)}] = (1 - b\lambda)^{-1/n}(1 + b\lambda)^{-1/n} = (1 - b^2\lambda^2)^{-1/n}. \tag{25.4}\]
The sum. The \(n\) shares are independent, so the moment generating functions multiply: \(\big((1 - b^2\lambda^2)^{-1/n}\big)^n = 1/(1 - b^2\lambda^2)\), the Laplace one.
Same moment generating function on an interval around 0, same distribution. This is the uniqueness theorem for moment generating functions (for example Billingsley, Probability and Measure, section 30).
Simulation. With \(n = 100\) and \(b = 2\), 200,000 sums give mean \(-0.0077\), variance 8.025 (exact \(2b^2 = 8\)), and \(\Pr[|X| \ge 4] = 0.1361\) against the exact \(e^{-2} = 0.1353\).

Laplace noise can be distributed exactly, so a distributed protocol can give pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP; but Gamma shares are real-valued, and secure aggregation over the integers needs a discrete analogue (differences of Pólya variables split the discrete Laplace the same way).
crumbs: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 25  Exercises: Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.7 Planning for dropouts

Exercise 7. Planning for dropouts. 100 clients calibrate distributed Gaussian noise for \((1, 10^{-6})\) with \(\Delta_2 = \sqrt2\). If 30% drop out after the noise was planned, what \(\varepsilon\) results? How much noise per client keeps \(\varepsilon = 1\) if up to 30% may drop out? Check: \(\varepsilon = 1.212\); per-client \(\sigma = 0.714\) instead of 0.597. (Gaussian calibration)







TipSolution






Planned noise. The exact Gaussian calibration at \((1, 10^{-6})\) and \(\Delta_2 = \sqrt2\) gives total \(\sigma = 5.975\), so each of the 100 clients adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2/100)\), standard deviation 0.597.
Thirty clients drop out. The sum now has 70 shares, total variance \(0.7\sigma^2\), and the Gaussian mechanism with noise \(\sigma\sqrt{0.7}\) is \((1.212, 10^{-6})\)-DP: about 21% more \(\varepsilon\) than promised. The guarantee falls to \(\varepsilon = 2\) only when the honest fraction drops to 0.279.
Over-provision. To keep total variance \(\sigma^2\) with only 70 shares, each client adds \(\sigma^2/70\): standard deviation \(5.975/\sqrt{70} = 0.714\).
The cost. If nobody drops out, the sum carries \(100/70 = 1.429\) times the variance needed, so the error is \(\sqrt{1.429} = 1.20\) times the central one.

Over-provisioning trades a fixed accuracy loss for a guarantee that survives the worst case you planned for.

26.1 Histograms under replace neighbours
Exercises for Lower bounds: what privacy costs, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_lower_bounds.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/solutions_lower_bounds.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(M\) is a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, \(\alpha\) an error and \(\beta\) a failure probability, and the random dataset of the fingerprinting section has attribute means \(p_j\) uniform on \([-1, 1]\) and records \(x_i \in \{\pm1\}^d\) with \(\mathbb E[x_{ij} \mid p] = p_j\). The examples use \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\beta = 0.05\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\).
crumbs: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
Exercise 1. Histograms under replace neighbours. Redo the histogram lower bound with datasets of a fixed size \(n\): \(D_0\) is \(n\) copies of an element \(x_0\), and \(D_x\) replaces \(k\) of them by \(x \ne x_0\). Show \(\alpha \ge \frac12\big(\ln((N - 1)(1 - \beta))/\varepsilon - 1\big)\), and show that the Laplace mechanism’s error doubles. Check: at \(N = 10^6\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\beta = 0.05\), the lower bound is still 6.38 and the Laplace error becomes 33.57. (Packing)







TipSolution






The candidates. For each \(x \ne x_0\) there is one dataset \(D_x\), so \(m = N - 1\). Each is \(k\) replacements away from \(D_0\).
Their histograms. \(h(D_x) = (n - k)e_{x_0} + k\,e_x\). For \(x \ne y\), the two histograms agree in bin \(x_0\) and differ by \(k\) in bins \(x\) and \(y\), so \(\|h(D_x) - h(D_y)\|_\infty = k\).
Disjoint regions. As in the chapter, the \(\ell_\infty\) balls of radius \(\alpha\) around them are disjoint when \(k > 2\alpha\). Take \(k = \lfloor2\alpha\rfloor + 1 \le 2\alpha + 1\).
Packing lemma with \(m = N - 1\): \(2\alpha + 1 \ge \ln((N - 1)(1 - \beta))/\varepsilon\), which rearranges to the claim.
The number. \(\ln(N - 1)\) and \(\ln N\) differ by about \(1/N = 10^{-6}\), so the bound is 6.3821 under both relations.
The upper bound doubles. Replacing a record lowers one count by 1 and raises another by 1, so the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity is 2 and the Laplace scale is \(2/\varepsilon\). Every quantile of \(\max_j|\eta_j|\) scales with it: \(2\times16.79 = 33.57\) (the script computes \(2 \times 16.785\ldots\) before rounding).

The lower bound does not care about the neighbouring relation, because both relations put the packing datasets \(k\) steps from \(D_0\). The upper bound does, because sensitivity depends on it. So under replace neighbours the gap between Laplace and the lower bound is about twice as large.
crumbs: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 26.2 What packing can force under approximate DP
text:
26.2 What packing can force under approximate DP

Exercise 2. What packing can force under approximate DP. Starting from Equation 26.2, show that \(m\) disjoint regions force \(m\big(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) - k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\big) \le 1\), and that as \(m \to \infty\) this forces only \(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) \le k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\). Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), \(\beta = 0.05\) the limit is \(k = 12.26\), so the forced integer group distance is 13 for \(m = 2^{20}\) and for \(m = 2^{1000}\) alike, against \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon = 13.82\). (Group privacy, packing)







TipSolution






Group privacy for each region. Equation 26.2 with \(D = D_i\), \(D'' = D_0\) and \(S = G_i\): \(1 - \beta \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_i] + \delta_k\).
Solve for the share of \(D_0\): \(\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_i] \ge e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) - e^{-k\varepsilon}\delta_k\).
Bound the \(\delta\) term. \(e^{-k\varepsilon}\delta_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{(j - k)\varepsilon}\). Each of the \(k\) terms is at most the largest, \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) (at \(j = k - 1\)), so \(e^{-k\varepsilon}\delta_k \le k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\).
Sum over the disjoint regions: \(1 \ge \sum_i\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_i] \ge m\big(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) - k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\big)\).
The limit. Call the bracket the floor. If it is positive, step 4 fails for large enough \(m\), so an accurate mechanism must have a \(k\) where the floor is \(\le 0\). As \(m \to \infty\), that is all step 4 says: \(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) \le k\,e^{-\varepsilon}\delta\).
The numbers. Bisection finds the floor’s zero at \(k = 12.26\). At \(k = 12\) the floor is \(0.95e^{-12} - 12e^{-1}\times10^{-6} = 5.83\times10^{-6} - 4.41\times10^{-6} = 1.42\times10^{-6}\), and \(m = 2^{20} \approx 1.05\times10^6\) makes \(m\) times it 1.49, more than 1. So \(k \le 12\) is impossible and \(k \ge 13\) is forced. At \(k = 13\) the floor is already negative, so no larger \(m\), not even \(2^{1000}\), forces more.

Under approximate DP, packing hits a ceiling near \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) that no number of candidates can lift. The ceiling is 12.26 rather than 13.82 because the \(\delta\) term carries the factor \(k\), which costs a further \(\ln k/\varepsilon\).

title: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 26.3 The lemma for a shrunk mean
text:
26.3 The lemma for a shrunk mean

Exercise 3. The lemma for a shrunk mean. For \(f = c\,\bar x\) with \(0 \le c \le 1\), show that \(\mathbb E[f\sum_i(x_i - p)] = 2c/3\) exactly, and that the bound in Equation 26.12 is \(\frac23 - 2(1 - c)\mathbb E|\bar x|\). Compute \(\mathbb E|\bar x|\) for \(n = 1\) and its limit as \(n \to \infty\). Check: for \(n = 5\), \(\mathbb E|\bar x| = 0.6\), so \(c = 0.75\) gives correlation 0.5000 against the bound 0.3667. (Fingerprinting lemma)







TipSolution






The correlation. By the equality in Equation 26.12, \(\mathbb E[f\sum_i(x_i - p)] = 2\mathbb E[p\,f] = 2c\,\mathbb E[p\,\bar x]\). Given \(p\), \(\mathbb E[\bar x \mid p] = p\), so \(\mathbb E[p\,\bar x] = \mathbb E[p^2] = \int_{-1}^1\frac{p^2}2\,dp = \frac13\). The correlation is \(2c/3\).
The bound. \(|f - \bar x| = |c\bar x - \bar x| = (1 - c)|\bar x|\), so \(\frac23 - 2\mathbb E|f - \bar x| = \frac23 - 2(1 - c)\mathbb E|\bar x|\).
\(n = 1\). \(\bar x = x_1 \in \{\pm1\}\), so \(\mathbb E|\bar x| = 1\).
\(n \to \infty\). \(\bar x \to p\) by the law of large numbers, and \(|\bar x| \le 1\), so \(\mathbb E|\bar x| \to \mathbb E|p| = \int_{-1}^1\frac{|p|}2\,dp = \frac12\). The script gives 0.5050 at \(n = 100\).
\(n = 5\). Summing over the six possible counts of \(+1\) and integrating over \(p\) gives \(\mathbb E|\bar x| = 0.6000\). Table 26.1 compares the two sides.




Table 26.1: The fingerprinting lemma for the shrunk mean \(c\,\bar x\) with \(n = 5\) records, computed exactly.

The bound always holds and is tight only at \(c = 1\). Its slack is \(\frac{2c}3 - \big(\frac23 - 1.2(1 - c)\big) = (1.2 - \frac23)(1 - c) = 0.5333(1 - c)\): the lemma charges an estimate twice its error, \(1.2(1 - c)\), while shrinking costs only \(\frac23(1 - c)\) in correlation.

title: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
26.4 Padding recovers \(1/\alpha\)

Exercise 4. Padding recovers \(1/\alpha\). Let \(M\) release the means of \(n\) records with \(\ell_\infty\) error \(\alpha\). Pad a dataset of \(n_0\) records with \(n - n_0\) records, half all \(+1\) and half all \(-1\), run \(M\), and rescale. Show that this gives an equally private mechanism for \(n_0\) records with error \(\alpha n/n_0\), choose \(n_0\) so that this error is \(\alpha_0\), and conclude \(n \ge \frac{\alpha_0}{\alpha}\cdot\frac{(2/3 - 2\alpha_0 - 4\beta)d}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d}\) (up to rounding). Find the best \(\alpha_0\). Check: \(\alpha_0 = \frac16 - \beta\), and the constant \(\alpha_0(\frac23 - 2\alpha_0 - 4\beta) = (\frac23 - 4\beta)^2/8 = 0.0272\) at \(\beta = 0.05\); at \(d = 10^4\) the bound is 15.8 records for \(\alpha = 0.1\) and 158.4 for \(\alpha = 0.01\). (Fingerprinting, reductions)







TipSolution






The padded dataset. Given a small dataset \(S\) of \(n_0\) records, form \(\tilde D = S \cup P\), where \(P\) has \((n - n_0)/2\) copies of \((+1, \dots, +1)\) and as many of \((-1, \dots, -1)\). The padding sums to 0 in every coordinate, so the mean of \(\tilde D\) is \(\frac{n_0}{n}\bar x_S\).
The new mechanism. \(M'(S) = \operatorname{clip}\big(\frac{n}{n_0}M(\tilde D)\big)\). When \(M\) is within \(\alpha\) of the mean of \(\tilde D\) in every coordinate, \(\frac n{n_0}M(\tilde D)\) is within \(\frac n{n_0}\alpha\) of \(\bar x_S\), and clipping to \([-1, 1]\) cannot move it further away. So \(M'\) has error \(\alpha n/n_0\) with the same failure probability \(\beta\).
The same privacy. Replacing one record of \(S\) replaces one record of \(\tilde D\), and the padding does not depend on \(S\). So \(M'\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP whenever \(M\) is; rescaling and clipping are post-processing.
Choose \(n_0\). Take \(n_0 = \lceil\alpha n/\alpha_0\rceil\), so that the error \(\alpha n/n_0\) is at most \(\alpha_0\). This needs \(\alpha_0 \ge \alpha\), since padding can only add records.
Apply Equation 26.13 to \(M'\) with \(\alpha' = \alpha_0 + 2\beta\): \(n_0 \ge (\frac23 - 2\alpha_0 - 4\beta)d/R\) with \(R = (e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d\). Since \(n_0 \le \alpha n/\alpha_0 + 1\), ignoring the \(+1\) gives \(n \ge \frac{\alpha_0}\alpha(\frac23 - 2\alpha_0 - 4\beta)\frac dR\).
The best \(\alpha_0\). \(\phi(\alpha_0) = \alpha_0(\frac23 - 4\beta - 2\alpha_0)\) is a downward parabola with \(\phi'(\alpha_0) = \frac23 - 4\beta - 4\alpha_0 = 0\) at \(\alpha_0 = \frac16 - \beta\). There \(\frac23 - 4\beta - 2\alpha_0 = \frac13 - 2\beta = 2\alpha_0\), so \(\phi = 2(\frac16 - \beta)^2 = (\frac23 - 4\beta)^2/8\). At \(\beta = 0.05\): \(\alpha_0 = 0.1167\) and \(\phi = 0.0272\).
The numbers. At \(d = 10^4\), \(R = 1.7183\times100 + 0.04 = 171.87\). For \(\alpha = 0.1\): \(n \ge 0.0272\times10^4/(0.1\times171.87) = 15.8\). For \(\alpha = 0.01\): ten times more, 158.4.

Padding is a general trick: a lower bound for constant accuracy becomes one for accuracy \(\alpha\) at a cost of a factor \(1/\alpha\) in \(n\). With it the fingerprinting bound has the shape \(\sqrt d/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) of the Gaussian mechanism’s upper bound.

title: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 26.5 How many attributes does tracing need?
text:
26.5 How many attributes does tracing need?

Exercise 5. How many attributes does tracing need? Using Equation 26.18 with \(\sigma = 0\), find the number of attributes \(d\) at which the tracing attack has advantage 0.5 for \(n = 100\) and for \(n = 200\). Check: \(d = 5678\) and \(d = 22{,}274\); the ratio \(d/n^2\) is about 0.56 in both cases. (Tracing, normal approximation)







TipSolution






The advantage. With \(m = 2d/(3n)\) and \(s = \sqrt{d(2/15 + 8/(15n))}\), the advantage is \(2\Phi(m/(2s)) - 1\). Setting it to 0.5 gives \(\Phi(m/(2s)) = 0.75\), so \(m/(2s) = \Phi^{-1}(0.75) = 0.6745\).
Solve for \(d\). \(m/s = \frac{2\sqrt d}{3n\sqrt{2/15 + 8/(15n)}}\), so \(\sqrt d = 1.349\times\frac{3n}2\sqrt{2/15 + 8/(15n)}\).
\(n = 100\): \(\sqrt{0.13333 + 0.00533} = 0.3724\), so \(\sqrt d = 1.349\times150\times0.3724 = 75.35\) and \(d = 5678\).
\(n = 200\): \(\sqrt{0.13333 + 0.00267} = 0.3688\), so \(\sqrt d = 1.349\times300\times0.3688 = 149.2\) and \(d = 22{,}274\).
The ratio. \(d/n^2 = 0.5678\) and \(0.5568\). Apart from the small \(8/(15n)\) term, \(d\) is proportional to \(n^2\).

Doubling the number of people quadruples the number of attributes the attacker needs. That is the \(n \approx \sqrt d\) of the fingerprinting bound, read from the attacker’s side.
crumbs: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
26.6 Tracing with a reference sample

Exercise 6. Tracing with a reference sample. The attacker does not know \(p\) but has \(m\) fresh records from the population, with mean \(\hat p\). Show that the score \(\langle\bar x, y - \hat p\rangle\) has the same mean gap \(2d/(3n)\) and a variance larger by the factor \(1 + 1/m\) (ignoring terms of order \(1/(nm)\)). Check: at \(n = 50\), \(d = 2000\), \(m = 50\), the predicted advantage is 0.563, and the simulation gives 0.563. (Tracing, robust traceability)







TipSolution





Work with one coordinate and drop the index \(j\). Given \(p\), the dataset, the reference sample and a fresh target are independent.

Non-member mean. \(y\) and \(\hat p\) both have mean \(p\) and are independent of \(\bar x\), so \(\mathbb E[\bar x(y - \hat p)] = \mathbb E[\bar x]\cdot0 = 0\).
Member mean. For \(y = x_i\): \(\mathbb E[\bar x\,x_i] - \mathbb E[\bar x]\,\mathbb E[\hat p]\). The first term is \(\frac1n\mathbb E[x_i^2] + \frac{n - 1}np^2 = \frac1n + \frac{n-1}np^2\); the second is \(p^2\). The difference is \(\frac{1 - p^2}n\), as with a known \(p\). Averaging and summing over coordinates gives the same gap \(2d/(3n)\).
Non-member variance. \(y - \hat p\) has mean 0 and variance \((1 - p^2) + (1 - p^2)/m = (1 - p^2)(1 + \frac1m)\), and it is independent of \(\bar x\). The coordinates are independent, so cross terms vanish, and \(\operatorname{Var} = (1 + \frac1m)\sum_j\mathbb E\big[\bar x_j^2(1 - p_j^2)\big] = (1 + \frac1m)\,d\big(\frac2{15} + \frac8{15n}\big)\), the known-\(p\) variance times \(1 + \frac1m\). (The member’s variance differs from this by terms of order \(d/n\) and smaller, which the normal approximation ignores.)
The numbers. At \(n = 50\), \(d = 2000\): gap 26.67, standard deviation \(16.97\times\sqrt{1.02} = 17.14\), so the predicted advantage is \(2\Phi(26.67/(2\times17.14)) - 1 = 0.563\). The simulation over 200 datasets gives a member mean of 26.15, a non-member standard deviation of 17.11 and an advantage of 0.563.

An estimated population costs the attacker almost nothing: with as many reference records as there are members, the advantage drops only from 0.568 (known \(p\)) to 0.563. This is the robustness that made genomic tracing practical, since public reference panels supply \(\hat p\).
crumbs: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 26  Exercises: Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
26.7 Reconstruction implies \(\varepsilon\)

Exercise 7. Reconstruction implies \(\varepsilon\). A reconstruction attack recovers 90% of a database of uniform bits from a release claimed to be \((\varepsilon, 10^{-6})\)-DP. What is the smallest \(\varepsilon\) the claim can have? Check: \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\big((0.9 - 10^{-6})/0.1\big) = 2.1972\); at 99% it is 4.5951. (Fact 3)







TipSolution






The bound on recovery. By Equation 26.19, an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP release lets any reconstruction recover a fraction of at most \((e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\) of uniform bits, in expectation.
Solve for \(\varepsilon\). \(r(e^\varepsilon + 1) \le e^\varepsilon + \delta\) rearranges to \(e^\varepsilon(1 - r) \ge r - \delta\), so \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{r - \delta}{1 - r}\).
\(r = 0.9\): \(\ln(0.899999/0.1) = \ln 9.0000 = 2.1972\).
\(r = 0.99\): \(\ln(0.989999/0.01) = \ln 99.0 = 4.5951\).
Conversely, at \(\varepsilon = 1\) no attack can recover more than \((e + 10^{-6})/(e + 1) = 0.7311\) of the bits.

Each extra “nine” in the recovery rate adds about \(\ln 10 = 2.3\) to the \(\varepsilon\) the attack proves. The \(10^{-6}\) barely matters here; \(\delta\) would need to be comparable to \(1 - r\) to change the answer.

title: 27  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.1 Randomized response at order 2
Exercises for Rényi differential privacy, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_renyi_dp.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_renyi_dp.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is tracked by the curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) of a mechanism \(M\); \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) are its outputs on neighbours, \(r = p/q\) the likelihood ratio and \(L = \ln r\) the privacy loss. Differential privacy (DP) without qualifier means \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence is the limit of \(D_\alpha\) as \(\alpha \to 1\). Logarithms are natural, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) throughout.

title: 27  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
Exercise 1. Randomized response at order 2. Show that \(\varepsilon(2) = \ln\big(1 + \chi^2(P\|Q)\big)\) for randomized response, with \(\chi^2(P\|Q) = \frac{(2p - 1)^2}{p(1 - p)}\). Check: 0.8473 for \(p = 0.75\) and 0.1542 for \(p = 0.6\). For \(p = \frac12 + \gamma\) with small \(\gamma\), show \(\varepsilon(2) \approx 16\gamma^2\) and KL \(\approx 8\gamma^2\). (Special orders of the Rényi divergence)







TipSolution






Order 2 is the second moment of the likelihood ratio. By Fact 1 of the chapter at \(\alpha = 2\), \(e^{D_2(P\|Q)} = \mathbb E_Q[r^2]\). Write \(r^2 = 1 + 2(r - 1) + (r - 1)^2\) and use \(\mathbb E_Q[r] = 1\): \(\mathbb E_Q[r^2] = 1 + \mathbb E_Q[(r - 1)^2] = 1 + \chi^2(P\|Q)\), with \(\chi^2 = \sum_y (p(y) - q(y))^2/q(y)\).
The two outputs of randomized response. From Table 27.2, \(p(y) - q(y) = \pm(2p - 1)\) on the two outputs, where \(p\) is the keep-probability, and \(q(y)\) is \(1 - p\) on one output and \(p\) on the other. So \[\chi^2 = \frac{(2p-1)^2}{1 - p} + \frac{(2p-1)^2}{p} = \frac{(2p - 1)^2}{p(1-p)}. \tag{27.1}\]
Check. For \(p = 0.75\): \(\chi^2 = 0.25/0.1875 = 1.3333\), and \(\ln 2.3333 = 0.8473\), the value of Table 27.3. For \(p = 0.6\): \(\chi^2 = 0.04/0.24 = 0.1667\), and \(\ln 1.1667 = 0.1542\).
Small \(\gamma\), order 2. With \(p = \frac12 + \gamma\), \(2p - 1 = 2\gamma\) and \(p(1 - p) = \frac14 - \gamma^2\). So \(\chi^2 = \frac{4\gamma^2}{1/4 - \gamma^2} = 16\gamma^2 + O(\gamma^4)\), and \(\ln(1 + x) = x + O(x^2)\) gives \(\varepsilon(2) = 16\gamma^2 + O(\gamma^4)\).
Small \(\gamma\), KL. The KL divergence is \(\mathbb E_P[L] = p\ln\frac{p}{1-p} + (1 - p)\ln\frac{1-p}{p} = (2p - 1)\ln\frac{p}{1-p}\). Here \(\ln\frac{1/2 + \gamma}{1/2 - \gamma} = \ln(1 + 2\gamma) - \ln(1 - 2\gamma) = 4\gamma + O(\gamma^3)\). So KL \(= 2\gamma \cdot 4\gamma + O(\gamma^4) = 8\gamma^2 + O(\gamma^4)\).
Numerically, at \(p = 0.55\) (\(\gamma = 0.05\)): \(\varepsilon(2) = 0.03961\) against \(16\gamma^2 = 0.04000\), and KL \(= 0.02007\) against \(8\gamma^2 = 0.02000\).

For a weak mechanism the curve is about \(\alpha\) times the KL divergence at moderate orders: \(\varepsilon(2) \approx 2\,\)KL. A curve that is linear in \(\alpha\) is what Concentrated DP builds on.

title: 27  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.2 Composing Laplace mechanisms three ways

Exercise 2. Composing Laplace mechanisms three ways. Run \(k = 100\) Laplace mechanisms with \(b = 10\) (each \(0.1\)-DP) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Compute \(\varepsilon\) by basic composition, by advanced composition with \(\delta' = \delta\), and by RDP with Mironov’s conversion over ORDERS. Check: 10, 5.2981 (with the \(\tanh\) term; 5.8502 with the textbook term) and 5.0705 at \(\alpha = 6.3\). Explain why RDP wins although each Laplace step is pure DP. (Composition, conversion)







TipSolution






Basic composition adds the \(\varepsilon_0 = 1/b = 0.1\) of the steps: \(100 \times 0.1 = 10\), with \(\delta = 0\).
Advanced composition with \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), \(\delta_0 = 0\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\) gives \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 5.2981\). With the textbook mean term \(k\varepsilon_0(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\) it is 5.8502.
RDP. Each step has the Laplace curve Equation 27.8 with \(b = 10\). Composition multiplies it by 100 (Equation 27.10). Mironov’s conversion (Equation 27.17), minimized over ORDERS, picks \(\alpha = 6.3\). There a single step has \(\varepsilon(6.3) = 0.02898\), so the composed curve is \(2.8983\), and the tail term is \(\ln(1/\delta)/5.3 = 2.1723\). The total is 5.0705.
Why RDP wins. Pure DP charges every step its worst case, \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), as if the privacy loss were always at its maximum. At order 6.3 the Laplace curve is 0.02898, less than a third of \(\varepsilon_0\): the loss of a Laplace step is usually far below its maximum, and the moderate orders see that. Composition adds these small numbers, and the conversion is paid once.
It does not always win. For \(k = 10\) steps, basic composition gives 1.0000, while RDP gives 1.0090 and advanced composition 1.5674. The RDP order there is 512, the top of the grid, so a longer grid would do a little better (Exercise 5). For \(k = 1000\), basic composition gives 100.0000, advanced composition 20.1701 and RDP 19.6905. RDP’s advantage over advanced composition is small for pure DP mechanisms; its large gains come from mechanisms like the Gaussian whose \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) points hide a whole curve (Table 27.7). An accountant can always report the smallest of the valid bounds.

Composing in RDP and converting once is never much worse than the classical theorems for pure DP steps, and it handles Gaussian and Laplace steps in the same ledger.

title: 27  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.3 The moments accountant’s tail bound

Exercise 3. The moments accountant’s tail bound. Show that Abadi et al.’s bound \(\delta = \min_\lambda\exp(K(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon)\) is Equation 27.17 solved for \(\delta\). For the Gaussian with \(\sigma = 1\), find the optimal \(\lambda\) for a given \(\varepsilon\) in closed form. Check: at \(\varepsilon = 3\), \(\lambda^* = 2.5\) and \(\delta = 4.394 \times 10^{-2}\). (Change of measure, Chernoff)







TipSolution






Rewrite the moment in RDP terms. By Equation 27.15, \(K(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1)\). With \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\), the exponent is \(K(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon = (\alpha - 1)\big(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon\big)\).
Solve Mironov’s conversion for \(\delta\). At order \(\alpha\), Equation 27.17 says \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\). Solving, \(\ln\delta = (\alpha - 1)\big(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon\big)\), which is the exponent of step 1. So at each order the two bounds are the same pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), read in opposite directions.
The two optimizations agree. Abadi et al. fix \(\varepsilon\) and choose \(\lambda\) to make \(\delta\) smallest; Mironov fixes \(\delta\) and chooses \(\alpha\) to make \(\varepsilon\) smallest. Both search the same family of valid pairs. The script checks a round trip: Mironov’s best \(\varepsilon\) for \(\sigma = 1\) is 5.2985 (at \(\alpha = 5.8\)), and the tail bound at that \(\varepsilon\) returns \(\delta = 1.000 \times 10^{-5}\) at \(\lambda = 4.8\), the same order.
The Gaussian in closed form. With \(\sigma = 1\), \(K(\lambda) = \lambda(\lambda + 1)/2\) (the chapter’s Gaussian example with \(\mu = 1\)). The exponent \(\lambda(\lambda + 1)/2 - \lambda\varepsilon\) has derivative \(\lambda + \frac12 - \varepsilon\), which vanishes at \(\lambda^* = \varepsilon - \frac12\).
Substitute: \(\lambda^*(\lambda^* + 1)/2 - \lambda^*\varepsilon = (\varepsilon - \tfrac12)\big[\tfrac12(\varepsilon + \tfrac12) - \varepsilon\big] = -\tfrac12(\varepsilon - \tfrac12)^2\). So \(\delta = \exp\big(-(\varepsilon - \tfrac12)^2/2\big)\).
Check. At \(\varepsilon = 3\): \(\lambda^* = 2.5\) and \(\delta = e^{-3.125} = 4.394 \times 10^{-2}\); the grid search finds the same \(\lambda\), because \(\alpha = 3.5\) is on the grid. At \(\varepsilon = 4\): \(\lambda^* = 3.5\) and \(\delta = 2.187 \times 10^{-3}\).

The bound \(\delta = e^{-(\varepsilon - 1/2)^2/2}\) is a Gaussian tail in \(\varepsilon\): the Chernoff bound for a normal privacy loss with mean and variance 1/2 and 1.

title: 27  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
section: 27.4 The weak triangle inequality on three Gaussians
text:
27.4 The weak triangle inequality on three Gaussians

Exercise 4. The weak triangle inequality on three Gaussians. Take \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(R = \mathcal N(0.5, 1)\), \(Q = \mathcal N(1.5, 1)\) and \(\alpha = 3\). Evaluate both sides of Equation 27.12 for \(u = 2\), \(u = 1.5\) and \(u = 3\). Check: left side 3.3750; right sides 3.4375, 4.1562 and 3.5000. Then minimize the right side over \(u\) for shifts \(a\) (from \(P\) to \(R\)) and \(b\) (from \(R\) to \(Q\)). Check: the best exponent is \(u^* = 1 + \frac{b(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha a} = 2.3333\), where the right side equals the left side, 3.3750. Explain the equality through the equality case of Hölder’s inequality. (Hölder’s inequality)







TipSolution





Unit-variance normals with shift \(s\) have \(D_\alpha = \alpha s^2/2\) (Equation 3.15). Here \(a = 0.5\), \(b = 1\) and the total shift is \(a + b = 1.5\).

Left side. \(D_3(P\|Q) = 3 \times 1.5^2/2 = 3.3750\).
\(u = 2\), \(v = 2\). The orders are \(u\alpha = 6\) and \(v(\alpha - 1) + 1 = 5\). The right side is \(\frac{3 - 1/2}{2}\cdot\frac{6 \times 0.25}{2} + \frac{5 \times 1}{2} = 1.25 \times 0.75 + 2.5 = 3.4375\).
\(u = 1.5\), \(v = 3\). Orders 4.5 and 7: \(\frac{3 - 2/3}{2}\cdot\frac{4.5 \times 0.25}{2} + \frac{7}{2} = 4.1562\).
\(u = 3\), \(v = 1.5\). Orders 9 and 4: \(\frac{3 - 1/3}{2}\cdot\frac{9 \times 0.25}{2} + \frac{4}{2} = 3.5000\).
The right side as a function of \(u\). With \(v = u/(u - 1)\), \[\mathrm{RHS}(u) = \frac{\alpha u - 1}{u(\alpha - 1)}\cdot\frac{u\alpha a^2}{2} + \Big(\frac{u}{u-1}(\alpha - 1) + 1\Big)\frac{b^2}{2} = \frac{\alpha(\alpha u - 1)a^2}{2(\alpha - 1)} + \Big(1 + \frac{(\alpha - 1)u}{u - 1}\Big)\frac{b^2}{2}. \tag{27.2}\]
Minimize. \(\frac{d}{du}\frac{u}{u - 1} = -\frac{1}{(u-1)^2}\), so the derivative is \(\frac{\alpha^2a^2}{2(\alpha - 1)} - \frac{(\alpha - 1)b^2}{2(u - 1)^2}\). It vanishes at \((u - 1)^2 = \frac{(\alpha - 1)^2b^2}{\alpha^2a^2}\), that is, \(u^* = 1 + \frac{b(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha a} = 1 + \frac{2}{1.5} = 2.3333\), with \(v^* = 1.75\). The orders become 7 and 4.5, and the right side is 3.3750, equal to the left side.
Why equality is possible. Hölder’s inequality \(\mathbb E_R[XY] \le (\mathbb E_RX^u)^{1/u}(\mathbb E_RY^v)^{1/v}\) is an equality exactly when \(X^u\) is a constant multiple of \(Y^v\). Here \(X = (p/r)^\alpha\) and \(Y = (r/q)^{\alpha - 1}\). For normals with equal variance, \(\ln(p/r)\) and \(\ln(r/q)\) are both linear in \(y\), with slopes proportional to \(-a\) and \(-b\). So \(X^u = cY^v\) holds when the slopes match, \(u\alpha a = v(\alpha - 1)b\). With \(v = u/(u - 1)\) this gives \((u - 1)\alpha a = (\alpha - 1)b\), the same \(u^*\) as step 6.

The weak triangle inequality loses nothing for Gaussians when \(u\) is tuned to the two shifts. The fixed choice \(u = 2\) is what group privacy uses, and its loss is small (3.4375 against 3.3750 here).

title: 27  Exercises: Rényi differential privacy
section: 27.5 The edge of the order grid
text:
27.5 The edge of the order grid

Exercise 5. The edge of the order grid. For a single Gaussian step at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), find the noise multiplier above which the continuous optimum \(\alpha^*\) of Equation 27.18 exceeds the largest order 512. Check: \(\sigma > 106.5\). At \(\sigma = 200\), how much does the grid lose against the continuous optimum? Check: 0.02893 against 0.02401, a factor 1.205. (Calculus, the order grid)







TipSolution






The threshold. \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\) exceeds 512 when \(\sigma > 511/\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} = 511/4.7985 = 106.5\).
Just below the edge. At \(\sigma = 100\), \(\alpha^* = 480.9\). The grid has no order between 256 and 512, so it uses 512 and gets 0.04813 against the continuous 0.04804, a loss of 0.2%.
Beyond the edge. At \(\sigma = 200\), \(\alpha^* = 960.7\), but the largest order is 512. The converted \(\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) is convex in \(\alpha\) and still decreasing at 512, so the grid’s best is the last order: 0.02893, against 0.02401 at \(\alpha^*\), a factor 1.205.
Remedy. Add larger orders (1024, 2048, …) when the noise is large, or optimize \(\alpha\) continuously when the curve has a closed form. Both converted values are still well above the exact \(\varepsilon = 0.01251\) of this mechanism; that remaining slack is the conversion’s, not the grid’s.

A fixed grid is a convenience for adding curves of different mechanisms. Check that the chosen order is not at the edge of the grid; if it is, the grid is too short.

title: 28  Exercises: From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
Exercise 1. The optimal constant, in general. Show that \(\sup_z (1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+ e^{-(\alpha - 1)z}\) is attained at \(z^* = \varepsilon - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\), and that the ratio of the improved to Mironov’s \(\delta\) is \(\frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\), with \(\alpha\) times this ratio tending to \(1/e\). Check: at \(\alpha = 2\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(c^* = 9.196986\times10^{-2}\); \(\alpha\) times the ratio is 0.5000, 0.3874, 0.3697, 0.3681 at \(\alpha = 2, 10, 100, 1000\). (Calculus, majorizing an integrand)







TipSolution






Only \(z > \varepsilon\) matters. For \(z \le \varepsilon\) the positive part is 0. For \(z > \varepsilon\) the function is \(f(z) = e^{-(\alpha - 1)z} - e^{\varepsilon - \alpha z}\).
Stationary point. \(f'(z) = e^{-\alpha z}\big(\alpha e^\varepsilon - (\alpha - 1)e^z\big)\). The bracket is positive for small \(z\) and negative for large \(z\), and vanishes at \(e^{z} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}e^\varepsilon\), so \(f\) rises and then falls, with its maximum at \(z^* = \varepsilon + \ln\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1} = \varepsilon - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\).
Value. \(f(z^*) = e^{-\alpha z^*}(e^{z^*} - e^\varepsilon) = e^{-\alpha z^*}\frac{e^\varepsilon}{\alpha - 1}\), and \(e^{-\alpha z^*} = e^{-\alpha\varepsilon}(1 - 1/\alpha)^\alpha\), so \(c^* = \frac{e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}}{\alpha - 1}(1 - 1/\alpha)^\alpha\).
Check. At \(\alpha = 2\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\): \(z^* = 1 + \ln 2 = 1.6931\) and \(c^* = e^{-1}\cdot\frac14 = 9.196986\times10^{-2}\). The maximum of \(f\) over a grid of two million points gives the same seven digits.
The ratio. Mironov’s bound uses \(c = e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\); both bounds multiply \(c\) by the same \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\). So the ratio is \(c^*/c = \frac{(1 - 1/\alpha)^\alpha}{\alpha - 1} = \frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\), using \(\frac{1 - 1/\alpha}{\alpha - 1} = \frac1\alpha\).
The limit. \(\alpha\) times the ratio is \((1 - 1/\alpha)^{\alpha - 1} = \exp\big((\alpha - 1)\ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\big)\). With \(\ln(1 - x) = -x - x^2/2 - \dots\) and \(x = 1/\alpha\), the exponent is \(-(\alpha - 1)/\alpha - O(1/\alpha) \to -1\). The script gives 0.5000, 0.3874, 0.3697 and 0.3681 at \(\alpha = 2, 10, 100, 1000\), approaching \(1/e = 0.3679\).

So at large orders the improved conversion divides Mironov’s \(\delta\) by about \(e\alpha\): the gain is largest in \(\delta\) exactly where it is smallest in \(\varepsilon\), because \(\ln(e\alpha)\) is divided by \(\alpha - 1\).

section: 28.2 Best orders for a linear curve
text:
28.2 Best orders for a linear curve

Exercise 2. Best orders for a linear curve. For \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), derive Mironov’s best order and value and Equation 28.13, and evaluate both at \(\rho = 0.5\) and \(\rho = 0.005\) for \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and \(10^{-10}\). Check: at \(\rho = 0.5\), \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), Mironov 7.286 at order 7.786 and improved 6.839 at order 7.483. (Optimization over α)







TipSolution






Mironov. \(g(\alpha) = \rho\alpha + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\) has \(g'(\alpha) = \rho - \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{(\alpha - 1)^2}\) and \(g'' > 0\). The zero is \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\). At it, \(\rho\alpha^* = \rho + \sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\) and \(\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha^* - 1} = \sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\), so \(\varepsilon^* = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\).
Improved. \(h(\alpha) = \rho\alpha + \ln(1 - 1/\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta) - \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\). The derivative of the middle term is \(\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}\); the derivative of the last is \(-\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)} - \frac{\ln(1/\delta) - \ln\alpha}{(\alpha - 1)^2}\). They cancel in part, leaving \(h'(\alpha) = \rho - \frac{\ln(1/(\alpha\delta))}{(\alpha - 1)^2}\), whose zero is Equation 28.13.
Solve it. Rewrite as \(\alpha = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/(\alpha\delta))/\rho}\) and iterate from Mironov’s \(\alpha^*\). The right side changes slowly with \(\alpha\) (through \(\ln\alpha\)), so the iteration converges; the script’s residual \(\rho(\alpha - 1)^2 - \ln(1/(\alpha\delta))\) is at most \(8.9\times10^{-16}\).
Values. Table 28.1. At \(\rho = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-10}\), Mironov gives 7.286 at order 7.786 and the improved conversion 6.839 at order 7.483. Evaluating \(g\) directly at Mironov’s \(\alpha^*\) reproduces each \(\varepsilon^*\).

title: 28  Exercises: From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
28.3 One order’s boundary at small \(a\)

Exercise 3. One order’s boundary at small \(a\). For a single order \(\alpha\), show from the second inequality of Equation 28.11 that every test has power \(1 - b \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha}a^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\), and that keeping the second term at its value 1 for \(b = 1\) gives the approximation \(1 - b \approx (e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)} - 1)^{1/\alpha}a^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\). For the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\), compare both with the exact single-order boundary at \(a = 10^{-6}\) for orders 2 and 8, and say when the slope picture of Figure 28.2 is accurate. Check: at order 2, \(1.6487\times10^{-3}\), \(1.3108\times10^{-3}\) and exact \(1.3118\times10^{-3}\); at order 8 all three are \(1.8622\times10^{-4}\). (Test region, asymptotics)







TipSolution






A bound that always holds. The second inequality of Equation 28.11 is \((1 - b)^\alpha a^{1 - \alpha} + b^\alpha(1 - a)^{1 - \alpha} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\). The second term is non-negative, so \((1 - b)^\alpha \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}a^{\alpha - 1}\). Taking the \(\alpha\)-th root gives \(1 - b \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha}a^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\) for every \(a\): on log axes a line of slope \((\alpha - 1)/\alpha\).
The approximation. At small \(a\) the allowed power is small, so \(b\) is near 1 and the second term \(b^\alpha(1 - a)^{1 - \alpha}\) is near 1. Moving it to the right side as 1 gives \((1 - b)^\alpha a^{1 - \alpha} \lesssim e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)} - 1\), which is the approximation. It is not a bound: \(b^\alpha \approx 1 - \alpha(1 - b)\) is a little below 1, so the exact boundary allows slightly more power.
The ratio of the two. The approximation divided by the bound is \((1 - e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)})^{1/\alpha}\), the same at every \(a\). With \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\) it is 0.7951 at order 2, where \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha) = 1\), and 1.0000 at order 8, where \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha) = 28\) and \(e^{-28}\) is negligible.
Against the exact boundary. Table 28.2 compares both with the exact single-order boundary, computed by bisection with both inequalities of Equation 28.11. At order 2 and \(a = 10^{-6}\) the bound gives \(1.6487\times10^{-3}\), the approximation \(1.3108\times10^{-3}\) and the exact boundary \(1.3118\times10^{-3}\). At order 8 all three are \(1.8622\times10^{-4}\).

28.4 Composing Laplace mechanisms in RDP

Exercise 4. Composing Laplace mechanisms in RDP. Extend Exercise 2 of Rényi DP with the improved conversion. One hundred Laplace mechanisms each with \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\): compare basic composition, advanced composition in its textbook form (composition), and the improved conversion of the summed curve, 100 times the Laplace RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\big[\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_0} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha\varepsilon_0}\big]\) (Mironov 2017). Check: 10.000, 5.850 and 4.533 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). (Composition in RDP, conversion)







TipSolution






Check the curve. A Riemann sum of \(p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\) for \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1/\varepsilon_0)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, 1/\varepsilon_0)\) gives 0.009644 at \(\alpha = 2\) and 0.065854 at \(\alpha = 20\), equal to the formula. For comparison, \(\alpha\varepsilon_0^2/2\) is 0.010000 and 0.100000: the Laplace curve is below the generic \(\varepsilon\)-DP bound of the chapter’s claim 3.
Basic composition. \(k\varepsilon_0 = 100 \times 0.1 = 10.000\), with \(\delta = 0\).
Advanced composition, textbook form. \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)} + k\varepsilon_0(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1) = 5.850\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
RDP. Composition adds curves, so the total is \(100\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\). The improved conversion over the grid gives 4.533 at order 5.8; Mironov’s gives 5.071 at order 6.3.
Using only the ε-DP bound. Replacing the Laplace curve by \(\min(\varepsilon_0, \alpha\varepsilon_0^2/2)\) gives 4.729. That is the Gaussian number of the chapter: \(100 \times \alpha\varepsilon_0^2/2 = \alpha/2\), the RDP curve of a Gaussian with \(\mu = 1\).

RDP beats advanced composition here even with the crude conversion, and the exact Laplace curve gains a further 0.196 over the generic bound.

section: 28.6 When is the improved conversion optimal for one order?
text:
28.6 When is the improved conversion optimal for one order?

Exercise 6. When is the improved conversion optimal for one order? Show that for any pair, the improved bound exceeds the true \(\delta\) by at least \(c^*\,\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\mathbf 1[L \le \varepsilon]]\), and use the worst two-outcome pair to explain why the improved conversion is optimal at large orders and not at small ones. Check: at \(\mu = 1\), improved and optimal are 11.1266 and 10.6680 at order 2, and 5.2141 and 5.2141 at order 8. (Optimal conversion, data processing)







TipSolution






The gap as an expectation. The improved bound is \(c^*e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)} \ge c^*\,\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\) by the RDP curve (Fact 2 of the chapter). The true \(\delta\) is \(\mathbb E_P[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\) (Fact 1). So the gap is at least \(\mathbb E_P\big[c^*e^{(\alpha - 1)L} - (1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big]\).
Split by \(L\). Where \(L > \varepsilon\) the integrand is \(\ge 0\), because \(c^*e^{(\alpha - 1)z}\) lies above \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\) everywhere. Where \(L \le \varepsilon\) the second term is 0. Dropping the first part leaves the claimed lower bound \(c^*\,\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\mathbf 1[L \le \varepsilon]]\).
The worst pair cannot avoid it. The optimal conversion for one order is attained by a two-outcome pair (the chapter’s test region). One outcome carries the large loss, near \(z^*\); the other must carry almost all the mass, at a loss near 0, because \(P\) and \(Q\) both sum to 1. That outcome contributes about \(c^* \times 1\) to the gap. So the improved \(\delta\) exceeds the optimal \(\delta\) by about \(c^*\).
Compare \(c^*\) with δ. At the improved \(\varepsilon\), \(c^*/\delta\) is 0.687 at order 1.5, 0.368 at order 2, 0.002 at order 4 and essentially 0 at order 8 (\(c^* = 6.914\times10^{-18}\)). Since \(c^* \propto e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}/(\alpha - 1)\), it is negligible against \(\delta\) once \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon\) clearly exceeds \(\ln(1/\delta)\).
In ε. Table 28.4 gives the two conversions for the Gaussian’s single values \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\). The optimal one uses the forward constraint \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\) alone, as the improved conversion does. At order 2 the improved conversion gives 11.1266 against the optimal 10.6680; at order 8 both give 5.2141.

29.1 Laplace in a zCDP budget
Exercises for Concentrated differential privacy, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_concentrated_dp.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_concentrated_dp.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zero-concentrated differentially private (\(\rho\)-zCDP) when its Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve satisfies \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\) for all \(\alpha > 1\); \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy (DP) is the guarantee you report; \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\), and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) throughout, so \(\ell = 11.5129\). Divergences are Kullback–Leibler (KL) or Rényi.

title: 29  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
Exercise 1. Laplace in a zCDP budget. The Laplace mechanism with scale \(b\) on a sensitivity-1 query is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(\varepsilon = 1/b\). Using its exact RDP curve (Equation 3.19 with \(t = \varepsilon\)), find numerically the smallest \(\rho\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\), and compare it with \(\varepsilon^2/2\) and with randomized response at the same \(\varepsilon\). Check: the smallest \(\rho\) is the KL divergence \(t + e^{-t} - 1 = 0.3679\), reached as \(\alpha \to 1\). (Pure DP to zCDP, tightness)







TipSolution






The curve. The outputs on neighbours are \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) and \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, b)\), a shift of \(t = 1/b = \varepsilon\) scale units. By Equation 3.19, \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)t} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha t}\right). \tag{29.1}\] The script evaluates it in log space, so large orders do not overflow.
The smallest \(\rho\) is the largest ratio. \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\) for all \(\alpha\) exactly when \(\rho \ge \sup_{\alpha > 1}\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha\). Table 29.1 evaluates the ratio at \(t = 1\).




Table 29.1: The RDP curve of the Laplace mechanism with \(t = \varepsilon = 1\) and its slope from the origin.

The ratio is largest as \(\alpha \to 1\). There \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \to D_{\mathrm{KL}} = t + e^{-t} - 1\) (the KL divergence of the Laplace pair, from Divergences), and \(\alpha \to 1\). On the fine grid of orders the maximum of \(\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha\) is \(0.3679\), equal to the KL divergence \(0.3679\).
Compare. The general bound is \(\varepsilon^2/2 = 0.5000\); randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\) needs \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) = 0.4621\); the Laplace mechanism only \(0.3679\).

The general \(\varepsilon^2/2\) is a convenient upper bound, not the cost of any mechanism at fixed \(\varepsilon\). Every \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is a post-processing of randomized response (Composition), so none needs more than randomized response’s \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) = 0.4621\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (Equation 29.7). The Laplace mechanism, whose privacy loss reaches \(\pm\varepsilon\) only in its tails, needs \(0.3679\). Charging it \(\varepsilon^2/2\) is safe but overcharges by a factor \(0.5000/0.3679 = 1.36\); the sharp \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) still overcharges by \(0.4621/0.3679 = 1.26\).

title: 29  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.2 Calibrating σ for many steps

Exercise 2. Calibrating \(\sigma\) for many steps. Derive Equation 29.12. Then find the noise multiplier that makes \(k = 100\) Gaussian steps \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP by the simple conversion, and the \(\varepsilon\) that the improved conversion and the exact Gaussian profile give for that \(\sigma\). Check: \(\sigma = 49.01\). (Optimizing over α, inverting a conversion)







TipSolution






Inversion. The simple conversion Equation 29.10 is \(\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}\), increasing in \(\rho\). Put \(x = \sqrt\rho \ge 0\): \(x^2 + 2\sqrt\ell\,x = \varepsilon\). Add \(\ell\) to both sides: \((x + \sqrt\ell)^2 = \varepsilon + \ell\). So \(x = \sqrt{\varepsilon + \ell} - \sqrt\ell\) (the other root is negative), and every \(\rho \le x^2\) meets the target. That is Equation 29.12.
The total budget. With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\ell = 11.5129\), \(\rho = 0.02082\).
Split it over the steps. Composition adds \(\rho\), so each of the 100 steps may spend \(\rho/100 = 2.0820 \times 10^{-4}\). A Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) spends \(1/(2\sigma^2)\), so \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{2\rho/100} = \sqrt{100}/\sqrt{2\rho} = 49.01\).
Check the other conversions. 100 steps at \(\sigma = 49.01\) give back \(\rho = 0.02082\) and \(\varepsilon = 1.0000\) by the simple formula. The improved conversion gives \(0.8118\). The composition of 100 Gaussian steps is itself a Gaussian pair with \(\mu = \sqrt{2\rho}\), whose exact \(\varepsilon\) is \(0.7416\).

Calibrating with the simple formula buys a guarantee that is really about \(\varepsilon = 0.74\). Calibrating with the exact Gaussian profile instead would let you use less noise for the same reported \(\varepsilon\).

29.3 Hölder for two steps

Exercise 3. Hölder for two steps. Write out Equation 29.15 for \(m = 2\) and \(\alpha = 2\), and check it on \(P = \mathrm{Bern}(0.2)\), \(Q = \mathrm{Bern}(0.8)\) with \(R = \mathrm{Bern}(0.4)\) and with \(R = \mathrm{Bern}(0.5)\). When does it hold with equality? Check: the left side is \(1.1787\); the right side is \(1.1872\) for \(R = \mathrm{Bern}(0.4)\) and \(1.1787\) for \(R = \mathrm{Bern}(0.5)\). (Hölder’s inequality, group privacy)







TipSolution






The orders. With group size \(m = 2\) and \(\alpha = 2\): the first order is \(\frac{m\alpha - 1}{m - 1} = 3\), the coefficient \(\frac{m\alpha}{m\alpha - 1} = \frac43\), and the second order \(m\alpha = 4\): \[D_2(P\|Q) \le \tfrac43D_3(P\|R) + D_4(R\|Q). \tag{29.2}\] The Hölder exponents are \(u = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{\alpha(m - 1)} = \frac32\) and \(v = \frac{m\alpha - 1}{\alpha - 1} = 3\), and indeed \(\frac23 + \frac13 = 1\).
Evaluate. Each divergence is a two-term sum, \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha-1}\ln\sum_y P(y)^\alpha Q(y)^{1-\alpha}\). Table 29.2 lists the values.




Table 29.2: The triangle-like inequality for \(m = 2\), \(\alpha = 2\), \(P = \mathrm{Bern}(0.2)\), \(Q = \mathrm{Bern}(0.8)\).

When equality holds. Hölder’s inequality \(\mathbb E[XY] \le (\mathbb E X^u)^{1/u}(\mathbb E Y^v)^{1/v}\) is an equality when \(X^u\) and \(Y^v\) are proportional. Here \(X = (P/R)^\alpha\) and \(Y = (R/Q)^{\alpha - 1}\), ratios of the densities at an output drawn from \(R\), so \(X^u = (P/R)^3\) and \(Y^v = (R/Q)^3\): equality needs \(\ln(P/R) - \ln(R/Q)\) to be the same for every outcome. For Bernoulli distributions that means the log-odds of \(R\) sit exactly halfway between those of \(P\) and \(Q\). The log-odds of \(0.2\), \(0.4\), \(0.5\), \(0.8\) are \(-1.3863\), \(-0.4055\), \(0.0000\), \(1.3863\), so \(\mathrm{Bern}(0.5)\) is the midpoint and \(\mathrm{Bern}(0.4)\) is not.
The link to the Gaussian. A chain of Gaussians \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathcal N(2, \sigma^2)\) has the same structure: both log-ratios are linear in \(y\) with the same slope, so they differ by a constant. That is why group privacy \(k^2\rho\) is exact for the Gaussian mechanism.

The inequality loses nothing when the middle dataset is “halfway” in the sense of the privacy loss. For the Gaussian mechanism every chain of neighbours is like that.

title: 29  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.4 A mixed pipeline

Exercise 4. A mixed pipeline. A pipeline runs 20 propose-test-release steps, each \((0.25, 10^{-8})\)-DP, and 50 Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 5\). Find its \(\rho\), its \(\delta_a\), and \(\varepsilon\) at total \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) with the improved conversion. Check: \(\rho = 1.625\). (Approximate zCDP)







TipSolution






Each stability step. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP step is \(\delta\)-approximately \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP, so each costs \(\rho = 0.25^2/2 = 0.03125\) and fails with probability \(10^{-8}\).
Each Gaussian step costs \(1/(2 \cdot 25) = 0.020\) and never fails.
Compose. \(\rho = 20 \times 0.03125 + 50 \times 0.020 = 1.6250\) and \(\delta_a = 1 - (1 - 10^{-8})^{20} = 2.0000 \times 10^{-7}\).
Convert. Spend the rest of the \(\delta\) on the conversion: \(\delta' = 10^{-5} - \delta_a\). The improved conversion at \(\rho = 1.625\) and this \(\delta'\) gives \(\varepsilon = 9.463\), at total \(\delta = \delta_a + \delta' = 10^{-5}\) (the third property of the approximate zCDP section, its conversion, which allows \(\delta_a + (1 - \delta_a)\delta' \le 10^{-5}\)).
Compare. Treating the two kinds of steps separately, the Gaussians alone (\(\rho = 1\)) convert to \(\varepsilon = 7.084\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5} - 2 \times 10^{-7} = 9.8 \times 10^{-6}\), and basic composition of the stability steps adds \(20 \times 0.25 = 5\), for \(12.084\).

Twenty steps of \(\varepsilon = 0.25\) cost 5 under basic composition but only \(\rho = 0.625\) in the zCDP ledger, because they compose like Gaussian steps. That is the point of approximate zCDP.

title: 29  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.5 The subsampled Gaussian at order 2

Exercise 5. The subsampled Gaussian at order 2. From Equation 29.18, show \(\varepsilon(2) = \ln\big(1 + q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\big)\), and evaluate it for \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\). Then show that the lower bound Equation 29.21 is positive exactly when \(\alpha > 1 + 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\). Check: \(\varepsilon(2) = 1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\). (Binomial expansion)







TipSolution






The three terms of \(A_2\). In Equation 29.18 with \(\alpha = 2\), \(j = 0\) gives \((1 - q)^2\), \(j = 1\) gives \(2q(1 - q)e^0\), and \(j = 2\) gives \(q^2e^{(4 - 2)/(2\sigma^2)} = q^2e^{1/\sigma^2}\).
Add. \((1 - q)^2 + 2q(1 - q) = (1 - q)(1 + q) = 1 - q^2\), so \(A_2 = 1 - q^2 + q^2e^{1/\sigma^2} = 1 + q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\).
Divide \(\ln A_2\) by \(\alpha - 1 = 1\). For \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\): the closed form and the binomial sum both give \(1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\). Without subsampling, \(\varepsilon(2) = 1\), so subsampling at 1% buys a factor of about 5,800 at this order: \(1/q^2 = 10^4\), divided by \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 = e - 1 = 1.72\).
Where the lower bound turns positive. \(\rho_0\alpha + \frac{\alpha\ln q}{\alpha - 1} > 0\) with \(\rho_0 = 1/(2\sigma^2)\) and \(\alpha > 1\) means \(\frac{\alpha - 1}{2\sigma^2} > \ln(1/q)\), that is \(\alpha > 1 + 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\).
Check. For \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), the threshold is \(10.21\). The bound is \(-0.1169\) at \(\alpha = 10\) and \(0.4343\) at \(\alpha = 11\).

The threshold \(1 + 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\) is where the curve bends in Figure 29.4: below it the rare event “the record is in every sample” is too rare to matter, above it that event dominates.

title: 29  Exercises: Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.6 The tCDP conversion

Exercise 6. The tCDP conversion. Derive Equation 29.20 and apply it to \(10{,}000\) steps of the running example with \(\omega = 4\) and \(\omega = 8\), saying which branch applies. Check: \(7.469\) and \(8.289\). (Constrained optimization over α)







TipSolution






Admissible orders. \((\rho, \omega)\)-truncated concentrated DP (tCDP) bounds \(D_\alpha\) by \(\rho\alpha\) for \(\alpha \in (1, \omega)\), and at \(\alpha = \omega\) too, because \(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing and lower semicontinuous in \(\alpha\), so \(D_\omega \le \lim_{\alpha \uparrow \omega}D_\alpha \le \rho\omega\). Mironov’s conversion at any such order gives \(g(\alpha) = \rho\alpha + \ell/(\alpha - 1)\).
The unconstrained minimum. \(g\) is convex with minimizer \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\) and minimum \(\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}\) (the chapter’s conversion section).
First branch. If \(\alpha^* \le \omega\), which is \(\ell \le (\omega - 1)^2\rho\), the minimizer is admissible.
Second branch. Otherwise \(g' < 0\) on all of \((1, \omega]\) (a convex function decreases before its minimizer), so the best admissible order is \(\omega\): \(\varepsilon = \rho\omega + \ell/(\omega - 1)\).
\(\omega = 4\). Per step \(\rho = 9.0789 \times 10^{-5}\) (chapter, Table 29.7), so \(10{,}000\) steps give \(\rho = 0.9079\). Then \((\omega - 1)^2\rho = 8.171 < \ell = 11.5129\): second branch, \(\varepsilon = 7.469\). The unconstrained minimizer \(\alpha^* = 4.561\) lies beyond \(\omega\).
\(\omega = 8\). \(\rho = 1.1171\) and \((\omega - 1)^2\rho = 54.736 \ge \ell\): first branch, with \(\alpha^* = 4.210 \le 8\), and \(\varepsilon = 8.289\).

A larger \(\omega\) makes more orders available but forces a larger slope, because the line has to clear the curve on more orders. Here the slope wins, and the smaller truncation point gives the better \(\varepsilon\).

title: 30  Exercises: f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.1 The Laplace mechanism is GDP
Exercises for the chapter on differential privacy (DP) as a trade-off curve, f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy, each with a worked solution. Try each exercise before opening its solution. The script code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_gaussian_dp.py computes every number quoted here; run it with uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/solutions_gaussian_dp.py.
The solutions use the chapter’s notation. \(\mu\)-Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) means the trade-off curve \(G_\mu(a) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) - \mu)\). A test has type I error \(a\) and type II error \(b\), and \(\alpha\) is reserved for Rényi orders. \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), the privacy loss is \(L = \ln(p/q)\), and Dong, Roth & Su (2022) is cited as Dong et al. Three more acronyms appear: the total variation (TV) distance, the central limit theorem (CLT) for composition, and differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), written DP-SGD.

title: 30  Exercises: f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
Exercise 1. The Laplace mechanism is GDP. Find the smallest \(\mu\) such that the Laplace mechanism with \(\varepsilon = 1\) is \(\mu\)-GDP, that is \(G_\mu \le T(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1), \mathrm{Lap}(1, 1))\) everywhere. Check numerically that the binding point is on the diagonal, derive the closed form this gives, and prove that it suffices. What \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) does this GDP summary report, and what is the truth? Check: \(\mu = 1.0301\) (the same as Part 1’s Gaussian with equal TV); the GDP summary gives \(\varepsilon = 4.5301\), while the mechanism is \((1, 0)\)-DP. (Ordering trade-off curves, symmetry)







TipSolution





Write \(T_\varepsilon = T(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1/\varepsilon), \mathrm{Lap}(1, 1/\varepsilon))\), Part 1’s Laplace curve with \(\kappa = \varepsilon\).

Both curves are symmetric. \(G_\mu\) is symmetric (Part 1, Exercise 1), and \(T_\varepsilon\) is too: its first and last pieces, \(1 - e^\varepsilon a\) and \(e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - a)\), are reflections of each other, and the middle piece \(b = e^{-\varepsilon}/(4a)\) is symmetric in \(a\) and \(b\).
A necessary condition on the diagonal. On the diagonal \(a = b\), \(G_\mu(a) = a\) means \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) - \mu = \Phi^{-1}(a) = -\Phi^{-1}(1 - a)\), so \(a = \Phi(-\mu/2)\). The Laplace curve meets the diagonal on its middle piece: \(a^2 = e^{-\varepsilon}/4\), so \(a = \frac12e^{-\varepsilon/2}\). For \(G_\mu \le T_\varepsilon\) the Gaussian must cross the diagonal no further out, \(\Phi(-\mu/2) \le \frac12 e^{-\varepsilon/2}\), that is \[\mu \ge \mu^* = 2\,\Phi^{-1}\big(1 - \tfrac12e^{-\varepsilon/2}\big). \tag{30.1}\]
It is also sufficient. Both curves are symmetric, so by the duality of the chapter (step 3 there) each is the upper envelope of its lines \(f_{\varepsilon',\delta(\varepsilon')}\), \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\). Since \(f_{\varepsilon',\delta}\) falls as \(\delta\) grows, \(G_\mu \le T_\varepsilon\) holds as soon as \(\delta_G(\varepsilon') \ge \delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}(\varepsilon')\) for every \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\), where \(\delta_G\) is Equation 30.10 at \(\mu = \mu^*\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}(\varepsilon') = 1 - e^{(\varepsilon' - \varepsilon)/2}\) for \(\varepsilon' \le \varepsilon\) and 0 beyond (the Laplace profile of Part 3, The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, Exercise 2). Let \(D(\varepsilon') = \delta_G(\varepsilon') - \delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}(\varepsilon')\).

At \(\varepsilon' = 0\): \(\delta_G(0) = 2\Phi(\mu^*/2) - 1 = 1 - 2\Phi(-\mu^*/2) = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon/2} = \delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}(0)\) by the choice of \(\mu^*\), so \(D(0) = 0\).
The slope. Part 3 (Exercise 3 of The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms) showed \(\delta_G'(\varepsilon') = -e^{\varepsilon'}\Phi(v)\) with \(v = -\varepsilon'/\mu^* - \mu^*/2\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{Lap}}'(\varepsilon') = -\frac12e^{(\varepsilon' - \varepsilon)/2}\) on \([0, \varepsilon]\). So \(D' \ge 0\) exactly when \(h(\varepsilon') = e^{\varepsilon'/2}\Phi(v) \le \frac12e^{-\varepsilon/2} = \Phi(-\mu^*/2) = h(0)\).
\(h\) is non-increasing. \(h'(\varepsilon') = e^{\varepsilon'/2}\big[\frac12\Phi(v) - \varphi(v)/\mu^*\big]\). Since \(v \le -\mu^*/2 < 0\), the Mills-ratio bound \(\Phi(v) < \varphi(v)/|v|\) (Concentration inequalities) gives \(\Phi(v)/\varphi(v) < 1/|v| \le 2/\mu^*\), so \(h' < 0\).
Conclusion. \(h(\varepsilon') \le h(0)\), so \(D' \ge 0\) and \(D \ge 0\) on \([0, \varepsilon]\). Beyond \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{Lap}} = 0 \le \delta_G\). Hence \(G_{\mu^*} \le T_\varepsilon\), and with step 2, \(\mu^*\) is the smallest \(\mu\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\).

The script confirms it numerically. It finds the smallest \(\mu\) with \(G_\mu \le T_\varepsilon\) on a grid of 1,999 values of \(a\) by bisection. For \(\varepsilon = 1\) it gives \(\mu = 1.0301\), equal to the closed form 1.0301, and the two curves come closest (they touch) at \(a = 0.3035\), the grid point next to the diagonal point \(\frac12e^{-1/2} = 0.3033\). For \(\varepsilon = 0.5\): \(\mu = 0.5618\) from both, touching at \(a = 0.3895\), next to \(0.3894\).
The same as matching TV. The diagonal point of a symmetric curve is where the best advantage \(1 - a - b = 1 - 2a\) is attained (Part 1). So \(\mu^*\) is the Gaussian shift with the same total variation as the Laplace pair, \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1 = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon/2}\), which Part 1 found to be 1.0301 at \(\kappa = 1\).
What the summary reports. By Equation 30.10, 1.0301-GDP gives \(\varepsilon = 4.5301\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (and 0.5618-GDP gives 2.2706). The Laplace mechanism is \((1, 0)\)-DP.

The GDP summary of a Laplace mechanism is tight at one point, the diagonal, and very loose in the tails: the Laplace privacy loss is bounded by \(\varepsilon\), while every \(G_\mu\) has an unbounded one.

30.2 Group privacy

Exercise 2. Group privacy. Let \(h(a) = 1 - f(a)\) be the largest power at type I error \(a\) that a curve \(f\) allows. Show that if \(T(P, Q) \ge f\) and \(T(Q, R) \ge f\), then \(T(P, R) \ge 1 - h(h(a))\), so an \(f\)-DP mechanism is \(\big(1 - h^{\circ k}\big)\)-DP for groups of \(k\) records (Dong et al., Theorem 2.14). For \(f = G_\mu\), show that \(1 - h^{\circ k} = G_{k\mu}\). What \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) does a 0.5-GDP mechanism give a group of 2 and a group of 4, and what does Part 3’s group property (Equation 19.6) give when applied to the single point \((1.9931, 10^{-5})\) instead? Check: groups of 2 and 4 are 1-GDP and 2-GDP, so \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\) and \(9.9973\). From the point, a group of 4 gets \((7.9724, 4.57\times10^{-3})\), while 2-GDP has \(\delta(7.9724) = 5.20\times10^{-4}\). (Trade-off curves as power bounds, GDP)







TipSolution






A curve bounds power. \(T(P, Q) \ge f\) says that every test \(\phi\) with \(\mathbb E_P\phi \le a\) has type II error at least \(f(a)\), that is, power \(\mathbb E_Q\phi \le 1 - f(a) = h(a)\). Since \(f\) is non-increasing, \(h\) is non-decreasing.
Chain the bounds. Take a test \(\phi\) of \(P\) against \(R\) with \(\mathbb E_P\phi \le a\). Read as a test of \(P\) against \(Q\), it has power \(\mathbb E_Q\phi \le h(a)\). Read as a test of \(Q\) against \(R\), its type I error is \(\mathbb E_Q\phi \le h(a)\), so its power is \(\mathbb E_R\phi \le h(\mathbb E_Q\phi) \le h(h(a))\), using that \(h\) is non-decreasing. So its type II error against \(R\) is at least \(1 - h(h(a))\), and \(T(P, R) \ge 1 - h\circ h\).
Groups. Datasets that differ in \(k\) records are joined by a path \(D = D_0 \simeq D_1 \simeq \dots \simeq D_k\). Applying step 2 along the path \(k - 1\) times gives \(T(M(D_0), M(D_k)) \ge 1 - h^{\circ k}\).
The Gaussian case. For \(f = G_\mu\), \(h(a) = 1 - \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) - \mu) = \Phi(\mu - \Phi^{-1}(1 - a)) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(a) + \mu)\), using \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) = -\Phi^{-1}(a)\). Each application of \(h\) adds \(\mu\) inside \(\Phi\), so \(h^{\circ k}(a) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(a) + k\mu)\) and \(1 - h^{\circ k}(a) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) - k\mu) = G_{k\mu}(a)\). The script checks \(1 - h(h(a)) = G_{2\mu}(a)\) at \(\mu = 0.5\) on a grid of 1,999 values of \(a\): the largest difference is \(2.2\times10^{-16}\). For the Gaussian mechanism the bound is tight, because a group of \(k\) shifts the mean by up to \(k\) sensitivities.
The numbers. A 0.5-GDP mechanism is 1-GDP for groups of 2 and 2-GDP for groups of 4, so by Equation 30.10 it gives \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\) and \(9.9973\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
Going through one point instead. 0.5-GDP gives \(\varepsilon = 1.9931\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Part 3’s group property turns \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) into \(\big(k\varepsilon, \delta\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\big)\):

30.3 A tensor product by hand

Exercise 3. A tensor product by hand. Show that \(f_{\varepsilon,0}\otimes f_{\varepsilon,0} = \max\big(f_{2\varepsilon,0}, f_{0,\tanh(\varepsilon/2)}\big)\), and read off its privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon')\) for \(0 \le \varepsilon' \le 2\varepsilon\) from the corners. Check: at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta(0) = 0.4621\), \(\delta(1) = 0.3378\), \(\delta(2) = 0\). (Tensor product, duality)







TipSolution





Let \(\pi = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), so randomized response reports the true bit with probability \(\pi\), and note \(2\pi - 1 = \tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) and \(\pi/(1 - \pi) = e^\varepsilon\).

The product pair. As in Table 30.5, the output pairs 11, 01 or 10, and 00 have likelihood ratios \(q/p = e^{2\varepsilon}\), \(1\) and \(e^{-2\varepsilon}\), and \(P\)-probabilities \((1 - \pi)^2\), \(2\pi(1 - \pi)\) and \(\pi^2\).
The corners. Adding outcomes in decreasing order of \(q/p\) gives the corners \((0, 1)\), \(\big((1 - \pi)^2, 1 - \pi^2\big)\), \(\big(1 - \pi^2, (1 - \pi)^2\big)\) and \((1, 0)\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) these are \((0.0723, 0.4656)\) and \((0.4656, 0.0723)\).
First segment. It has slope \(-e^{2\varepsilon}\) and starts at \((0, 1)\): \(b = 1 - e^{2\varepsilon}a\). It ends at the second corner because \(e^{2\varepsilon}(1 - \pi)^2 = \pi^2\).
Middle segment. Slope \(-1\) through \(\big((1 - \pi)^2, 1 - \pi^2\big)\): \(b = 1 - \pi^2 + (1 - \pi)^2 - a = 1 - (2\pi - 1) - a = 1 - \tanh(\varepsilon/2) - a\).
Last segment. Slope \(-e^{-2\varepsilon}\) through \((1, 0)\): \(b = e^{-2\varepsilon}(1 - a)\).
A convex polygon is the maximum of its lines. So the curve is \(\max\big(0, 1 - e^{2\varepsilon}a, e^{-2\varepsilon}(1 - a), 1 - \tanh(\varepsilon/2) - a\big)\). The first three terms make up \(f_{2\varepsilon,0}\) and the last (with 0) is \(f_{0,\tanh(\varepsilon/2)}\), as claimed. On a grid of 1,999 values of \(a\), the two sides differ by at most \(2.2\times10^{-16}\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), where \(\tanh(1/2) = 0.4621\).

The privacy profile. By the duality, \(\delta(\varepsilon') = \max_a(1 - f(a) - e^{\varepsilon'}a)\), and for a polygon the maximum is at a corner. The two interior corners, and the midpoint \((1 - \pi, 1 - \pi)\) of the middle segment, give \(1 - b - e^{\varepsilon'}a\) equal to \(\pi^2 - (1 - \pi)^2e^{\varepsilon'}\), \(\big(1 - (1 - \pi)^2\big) - (1 - \pi^2)e^{\varepsilon'}\) and \(\pi - (1 - \pi)e^{\varepsilon'}\). For \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\) the first is the largest: it beats the second by \((e^{\varepsilon'} - 1)(1 - \pi^2 - (1 - \pi)^2) = (e^{\varepsilon'} - 1)\,2\pi(1 - \pi) \ge 0\), and the midpoint value is the average of the two. So \[\delta(\varepsilon') = \pi^2 - (1 - \pi)^2e^{\varepsilon'}, \qquad 0 \le \varepsilon' \le 2\varepsilon, \tag{30.2}\] which reaches 0 at \(\varepsilon' = 2\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) (\(\pi^2 = 0.5344\), \((1 - \pi)^2 = 0.0723\)):

30.4 Inverting the duality

Exercise 4. Inverting the duality. Find the largest \(\mu\) such that \(\mu\)-GDP implies \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP. How many full-batch Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 20\) fit in that budget? How many DP-SGD steps with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) fit in budgets \(\varepsilon = 1, 2, 4\) according to the CLT? Check: \(\mu^* = 0.2681\); 28 full-batch steps; 418, 1463 and 4978 DP-SGD steps. (GDP duality, composition)







TipSolution






\(\delta(\varepsilon)\) grows with \(\mu\). A larger \(\mu\) gives a lower curve, so every supporting line moves down and \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 1 + G_\mu^*(-e^\varepsilon)\) goes up. So the set of \(\mu\) that satisfy \(\delta_\mu(1) \le 10^{-5}\) is an interval \([0, \mu^*]\), found by bisection on Equation 30.10: \(\mu^* = 0.2681\), where \(\delta_{\mu^*}(1) = 1.00\times10^{-5}\).
Full batch. \(k\) Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 20\) compose to \(\sqrt k/20\)-GDP (Equation 30.12). The budget allows \(\sqrt k/20 \le 0.2681\), so \(k \le (20 \times 0.2681)^2\), and the largest integer is \(k = 28\).
DP-SGD by the CLT. With \(\mu = q\sqrt{k(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) the budget allows \(k \le (\mu^*/q)^2/(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). With \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\):

text:
30.5 Berry–Esseen for randomized response

Exercise 5. Berry–Esseen for randomized response. Compute \(\mathrm{kl}\), \(\kappa_2\) and \(\bar\kappa_3\) for \(f_{\varepsilon_0,0}\), and show that Equation 30.14 gives \(\mu = 2\sqrt k\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) for \(k\) copies. Check: \(\mathrm{kl} = \varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 0.004996\) at \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\); at \(k = 100\), \(\mu = 1.0004\) and \(\gamma = 0.0562\). (CLT functionals)







TipSolution





Let \(t = \tanh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 2\pi - 1\) with \(\pi = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\).

The privacy loss under \(P\). Randomized response outputs the likely value with probability \(\pi\), where \(L = \ln(\pi/(1 - \pi)) = \varepsilon_0\), and the other value with probability \(1 - \pi\), where \(L = -\varepsilon_0\).
The functionals are moments of \(L\) (the chapter’s derivation, step 1):

\(\mathrm{kl} = \mathbb E_P L = \varepsilon_0\pi - \varepsilon_0(1 - \pi) = \varepsilon_0 t\);
\(\kappa_2 = \mathbb E_P L^2 = \varepsilon_0^2\);
\(\bar\kappa_3 = \mathbb E_P|L - \varepsilon_0t|^3 = \pi\,\varepsilon_0^3(1 - t)^3 + (1 - \pi)\,\varepsilon_0^3(1 + t)^3\). With \(\pi = (1 + t)/2\) this is \(\frac{\varepsilon_0^3(1 - t^2)}{2}\big((1 - t)^2 + (1 + t)^2\big) = \varepsilon_0^3(1 - t^2)(1 + t^2)\).

The variance. \(\kappa_2 - \mathrm{kl}^2 = \varepsilon_0^2(1 - t^2) = \varepsilon_0^2/\cosh^2(\varepsilon_0/2)\), using \(1 - \tanh^2 = 1/\cosh^2\).
\(\mu\) for \(k\) copies. Equation 30.14 gives \[\mu = \frac{2k\varepsilon_0t}{\sqrt{k\,\varepsilon_0^2/\cosh^2(\varepsilon_0/2)}} = 2\sqrt k\,\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\cosh(\varepsilon_0/2) = 2\sqrt k\,\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2). \tag{30.3}\]
\(\gamma\) for \(k\) copies. \(\gamma = \frac{0.56\,k\varepsilon_0^3(1 - t^2)(1 + t^2)}{\big(k\varepsilon_0^2(1 - t^2)\big)^{3/2}} = \frac{0.56\,(1 + t^2)\cosh(\varepsilon_0/2)}{\sqrt k}\).
Check. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\): \(\mathrm{kl} = 0.1\tanh(0.05) = 0.004996\). At \(k = 100\): \(\mu = 20\sinh(0.05) = 1.0004\) and \(\gamma = 0.0562\), from the closed form and from the general formula alike.

30.6 A sanity limit for the subsampled CLT

Exercise 6. A sanity limit for the subsampled CLT. Put \(q = 1\) in Equation 30.17 and compare with the exact \(\sqrt k/\sigma\). Which way is it off, and why does the derivation not apply? Check: the ratio, the same for every \(k\), is 1.3108 for \(\sigma = 1\), 1.0659 for \(\sigma = 2\) and 1.0101 for \(\sigma = 5\). (Subsampled CLT, expansions)







TipSolution






The formula at \(q = 1\). \(\mu_{\mathrm{CLT}} = \sqrt{k(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\), while full-batch training is exactly \(\sqrt k/\sigma\)-GDP. Their ratio is \(\sigma\sqrt{e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1}\), independent of \(k\).
Which way. \(e^x - 1 \ge x\) for all \(x\), so \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1) \ge 1\): the formula over-states \(\mu\) at \(q = 1\). As \(\sigma\) grows, \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 \approx 1/\sigma^2\) and the ratio tends to 1.

Why the derivation fails. Step 3 of the derivation expanded \(\ln(1 + qW)\) to second order, which needs \(qW\) small. At \(q = 1\), \(\ln(1 + W) = (y - \frac12)/\sigma^2\) exactly: the loss is Gaussian with variance \(1/\sigma^2\), not \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\). The expansion replaced the variance of \(\ln(1 + W)\) by the variance of \(W\), which is larger, and the gap grows as \(\sigma\) shrinks (Table 30.5).
The regime. The CLT formula is meant for \(q \to 0\) with \(q\sqrt k\) fixed. There \(qW\) is small with high probability and the expansion is accurate, although for small \(\sigma\) the heavy right tail of \(W\) is exactly where it is least accurate.

Formulas derived for a limit regime should be checked at the edges of that regime; here the edge \(q = 1\) is known exactly and shows the formula’s bias.

title: 31  Exercises: Amplification by subsampling
